\section[\texttt{boolexpr} -- A boolean expression evaluator and a switch command]{\texttt{boolexpr} -- A boolean expression evaluator and a switch command}\label{pkg:boolexpr}
\index{Package!boolexpr}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/boolexpr}
\item[name] \texttt{boolexpr}
\item[caption] A boolean expression evaluator and a switch command
\item[author] Chervet, Florent
\index{Author!Chervet, Florent}
\item[copyright] Florent Chervet (2009)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 3.14
\item[description] (no language specified) The  \texttt{{\textbackslash}boolexpr} macro evaluates boolean expressions in a purely 
          expandable way.

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}boolexpr{\textbraceleft} A {\textbackslash}OR B {\textbackslash}AND 
          C {\textbraceright}} expands to 0 if the logical expression is TRUE. A, B, C may be: numeric 
          expressions such as: \texttt{x=y} , \texttt{x<>y} , \texttt{x>y} or \texttt{x<y} ;\\– 
          boolean switches: \texttt{{\textbackslash}iftrue 0{\textbackslash}else 1{\textbackslash}fi} ;\\– 
          conditionals: \texttt{{\textbackslash}ifcsname whatsit{\textbackslash}endcsname 0{\textbackslash}else 
          1{\textbackslash}fi} ;\\– another \texttt{{\textbackslash}boolexpr} : \texttt{{\textbackslash}boolexpr{\textbraceleft} 
          D {\textbackslash}OR E {\textbackslash}AND F {\textbraceright}:} 

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}boolexpr} may be used with \texttt{{\textbackslash}ifcase:} \\
          \begin{verbatim}
\ifcase\boolexpr{ A \OR B \AND C }
What to do if true
\else
What to do if false
\fi
          \end{verbatim}

          The  \texttt{{\textbackslash}switch} command (which is also expandable) has the form:
          \begin{verbatim}
\switch
\case{<boolean expression>} ...
\case{<boolean expression>} ...
...
\otherwise ...
\endswitch
          \end{verbatim}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/boolexpr/boolexpr.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./9811573736-boolexpr.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/boolexpr/README}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/boolexpr}

          The user gives the list of vertices and arrows to be included, just as when composing a matrix, and the 
          program takes care of computing the dimensions of the arrows and realizing the pagesetting. All the user 
          has to do about the arrows is to specify their type (monomorphism, pair of adjoint arrows, etc.) and

\section[\texttt{boxhandler} -- Flexible Captioning and Deferred Box/List Printing]{\texttt{boxhandler} -- Flexible Captioning and Deferred Box/List Printing}\label{pkg:boxhandler}
\index{Package!boxhandler}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/boxhandler}
\item[name] \texttt{boxhandler}
\item[caption] Flexible Captioning and Deferred Box/List Printing
\item[author] Segletes, Steven B.
\index{Author!Segletes, Steven B.}
\item[copyright] Steven B. Segletes (2008)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.30
\item[description] (no language specified) The package allows the user to optimise presentation of LaTeX tables and figures. Boxhandler will lay 
          out table and figure captions with a variety of stylistic apperances, and will also allow figures and 
          tables to be ''wrapped'' in a manner consistent with many business and government documents.

          For a document that might appear in different venues with different formatting, boxhandler permits the 
          creation of a LaTeX source document that can, with a single-line change in the source code, produce an 
          output that has very different layout from the baseline configuration, not only in terms of caption style, 
          but more importantly in terms of the locations where figures, tables and lists appear (or not) in the 
          document.

          Deferral routines also allow one to keep all figure and table data in a separate source file, while nonetheless 
          producing a document with figures and tables appearing in the desired location.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/boxhandler/boxhandler.pdf}

\section[\texttt{brclc} -- Support 16-bit (double) calculations in LaTeX]{\texttt{brclc} -- Support 16-bit (double) calculations in LaTeX}\label{pkg:brclc}
\index{Package!brclc}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/brclc}
\item[name] \texttt{brclc}
\item[caption] Support 16-bit (double) calculations in LaTeX
\item[author] Radgen, Bernd
\index{Author!Radgen, Bernd}
\item[copyright] Bernd Radgen (1999)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 0.1.3
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a preprocessor  \emph{brclc} (written in C; a DOS executable is available), 
          and a package, which processes a LaTeX file that's been run through the preprocessor (the output of the 
          preprocessor tells LaTeX how to process the \texttt{{\textbackslash}clc} commands in 
          the in the LaTeX file. The script \emph{testclc} (available as a shell script or a DOS batch

\section[\texttt{breqn} -- Automatic line breaking of displayed equations]{\texttt{breqn} -- Automatic line breaking of displayed equations}\label{pkg:breqn}
\index{Package!breqn}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/breqn}
\item[name] \texttt{breqn}
\item[caption] Automatic line breaking of displayed equations
\item[author] Robertson, Will
\index{Author!Robertson, Will}
\item[author] Madsen, Lars
\index{Author!Madsen, Lars}
\item[author] Wright, Joseph
\index{Author!Wright, Joseph}
\item[author] Høgholm, Morten
\index{Author!Høgholm, Morten}
\item[author] Downes, Michael J.
\index{Author!Downes, Michael J.}
\item[copyright] Michael J. Downes (1997-2003)
\item[copyright] Morten Høgholm (2007-2008)
\item[copyright] Will Robertson (2007-2020)
\item[copyright] Ulrike Fischer (2020)
\item[copyright] Lars Madsen (2007-2014)
\item[copyright] Joseph Wright (2010-2017)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.98l (2021-10-28)
\item[last changes] 2021-10-28
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides solutions to a number of common difficulties in writing displayed equations and 
          getting high-quality output. For example, it is a well-known inconvenience that if an equation must be 
          broken into more than one line, ‘left...right’ constructs cannot span lines. The breqn package makes 
          them work as one would expect whether or not there is an intervening line break.

          The single most ambitious goal of the package, however, is to support automatic linebreaking of displayed 
          equations. Such linebreaking cannot be done without substantial changes under the hood in the way formulae 
          are processed; the code must be watched carefully, keeping an eye on possible glitches.

          The bundle also contains the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/flexisym}{flexisym} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathstyle}{mathstyle} packages, 
          which are both designated as support for breqn.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/breqn/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/breqn/breqn.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./9338792980-breqn.pdf|

\item[description] (no language specified) The bundledoc package is a post-processor for the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/snapshot}{snapshot} package 
          that bundles together all the classes, packages and files needed to build a given LaTeX document. It 
          reads the \texttt{.dep} file that \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/snapshot}{snapshot} produces, 
          finds each of the files mentioned therein, and archives them into a single .tar.gz (or .zip, or whatever) 
          file, suitable for moving across systems, transmitting to a colleague, etc.

          A script,  \texttt{arlatex} , provides an alternative ''archiving'' mechanism, creating a 
          single LaTeX file that contains all of the ancillary files of a LaTeX document, together with the document 
          itself, using the \texttt{filecontents*} environment.

\section[\texttt{businesscard-qrcode} -- Business cards with QR-Code]{\texttt{businesscard-qrcode} -- Business cards with QR-Code}\label{pkg:businesscard-qrcode}
\index{Package!businesscard-qrcode}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/businesscard-qrcode}
\item[name] \texttt{businesscard-qrcode}
\item[caption] Business cards with QR-Code
\item[author] Wäckerlin, Marc
\index{Author!Wäckerlin, Marc}
\item[license] lgpl = GNU Lesser General Public License (free)
\index{License!lgpl}
\index{License!GNU Lesser General Public License}
\item[version] 1.2 (2018-08-15)
\item[last changes] 2018-08-15
\item[year] 2018
\index{Year!2018}
\item[description] (no language specified) What happens when you give your visiting card to someone? Either they manually type the text into their 
          computer or mobile phone, or it will end up in a box and be forgotten. Nowadays data is required electronically, 
          not on paper. Here is the solution: A visiting card with QR-Code that contains a full  \href{https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6350}{vcard} so 
          that it can be scanned with an app on the mobile phone and thereby automatically imported into the electronic 
          contacts. This also works well when you are offline and bluetooth transfer fails. So here is the highly 
          configurable business card or visiting card with full vcard as QR-Code, ready to send to online printers. 
          You can specify the exact size of the paper and the content within the paper, inluding generation of 
          crop marks.

          The package depends on the following other LaTeX packages:  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/calc}{calc} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/crop}{crop} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dejavu}{DejaVuSans} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/etoolbox}{etoolbox} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontawesome}{fontawesome} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontenc}{fontenc} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/geometry}{geometry} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/kvoptions}{kvoptions} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/marvosym}{marvosym} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/qrcode}{qrcode} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/varwidth}{varwidth} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/wrapfig}{wrapfig} .

          The package needs XeLaTeX for working properly.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Example of use (2)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/xetex/latex/businesscard-qrcode/examples/peter-muster-example-company-zuerich.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) The package allows the construction of proof trees in the style of the sequent calculus and many other

          some centre point specified with the command {\textbackslash}fCenter. This is the style often used

\section[\texttt{bxcoloremoji} -- Use color emojis more conveniently]{\texttt{bxcoloremoji} -- Use color emojis more conveniently}\label{pkg:bxcoloremoji}
\index{Package!bxcoloremoji}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/bxcoloremoji}
\item[name] \texttt{bxcoloremoji}
\item[caption] Use color emojis more conveniently
\item[author] Yato, Takayuki
\index{Author!Yato, Takayuki}
\item[copyright] Takayuki YATO (aka. “ZR”) (2017-2024)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 1.0a
\item[description] (no language specified) This package lets users output color emojis in LaTeX documents. Compared to other packages with similar 
          functionality, this package has the following merits:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item It supports all major LaTeX engines.
          \item Emojis can be entered as the characters themselves, as their Unicode code values, or as their short names.
          \item It works reasonably well in PDF strings when using hyperref.
          \item Emojis can be handled properly even in Japanese typesetting environments.
          \end{itemize}
This package has been widely used among the Japanese LaTeX community, but there are already many emoji 
          packages on CTAN and in TeX Live. To avoid uploading a large amount of emoji image data that are essentially 
          identical, the package was revised in version 1.0 so that the image output was delegated to the twmojis 
          package. Therefore, this package now contains no image data.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{List of Emoji Short Names}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/bxcoloremoji/bxcoloremoji-shortnames.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a new command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}newfontx} . It is similar 
          to the old (and deprecated) command \texttt{{\textbackslash}newfont} in function, but 
          is more compatible with NFSS. In particular, one can safely change font size after invoking a font command 
          defined by \texttt{{\textbackslash}newfontx} . The new command will be useful to users 
          who know much of the old \texttt{{\textbackslash}newfont} command, but are unfamiliar 
          with the details of NFSS.

\item[description] (no language specified) The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hologo}{hologo} package provides many useful logos of 
          popular (and not so popular) TeX-family software. However, its interface is a bit cumbersome because 
          you must type \texttt{{\textbackslash}hologo{\textbraceleft}BibTeX{\textbraceright}} instead 
          of \texttt{{\textbackslash}BibTeX} .

          This package makes it possible to import some of the logos provided by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hologo}{hologo} as 
          single commands, such as \texttt{{\textbackslash}BibTeX} .

          Additionally, the package provides logos of some TeX-family software that is popular mainly in Japan. 
          These logos can be imported in the same way as those provided by the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}hologo} command.

          \texttt{bxtexlogo} depends on \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hologo}{hologo} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cjhebrew}{cjhebrew} (if \texttt{{\textbackslash}logoAleph} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}logoLamed} are 
          used).

\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/bxwareki}
\item[name] \texttt{bxwareki}
\item[caption] Convert dates from Gregorian to Japanese calender
\item[author] Yato, Takayuki
\index{Author!Yato, Takayuki}
\item[copyright] Takayuki YATO (aka. “ZR”) (2018-2023)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 0.7 (2023-07-07)
\item[last changes] 2023-07-07
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) This LaTeX package provides commands to convert from the Gregorian calendar (e. g. 2018/8/28) to the 
          Japanese rendering of the Japanese calendar (e. g. Heisei 30 nen 8 gatsu 28 nichi; actually with kanji 
          characters). You can choose whether the numbers are written in Western numerals or kanji numerals.

          Note that the package only deals with dates in the year 1873 or later, where the Japanese calendar is 
          really a Gregorian calendar with a different notation of years.

\section[\texttt{c2latex} -- Simple conversion of C programs to LaTeX]{\texttt{c2latex} -- Simple conversion of C programs to LaTeX}\label{pkg:c2latex}
\index{Package!c2latex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/c2latex}
\item[name] \texttt{c2latex}
\item[caption] Simple conversion of C programs to LaTeX
\item[author] Ramsdell, John D
\index{Author!Ramsdell, John D}
\item[copyright] John D. Ramsdell (1991)
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version] 1.1
\item[description] (no language specified) c2latex provides simple support for documentation of C programming. Given a C source file in which the 
          comments have been written in LaTeX, c2latex converts the C source file into a LaTeX source file. It 
          can be used to produce typeset listings of C programs and/or documentation associated with the program.

          The C source given to c2latex usually has the following form: It starts with a large comment containing 
          LaTeX commands that start a document along with any initial text. Then there is a sequence of comment 
          and code pairs, with the comment explaining the code to follow. The source file is ended by a comment 
          containing LaTeX commands that finish the document. The source of c2latex is distributed in this form.
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/c2latex}

\item[description] (no language specified) Cabin is a humanist sans with four weights and true italics and small capitals. According to the designer, 
          Pablo Impallari, Cabin was inspired by Edward Johnston's and Eric Gill's typefaces, with a touch of modernism. 
          Cabin incorporates modern proportions, optical adjustments, and some elements of the geometric sans.

          \texttt{cabin.sty} supports use of the font under LaTeX, pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX; 
          it uses the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mweights}{mweights} , to manage the user’s view 
          of all those font weights.

          An  \texttt{sfdefault} option is provided to enable Cabin as the default text font. The \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontaxes}{fontaxes} package 
          is required for use with [pdf]LaTeX.

\item[description] (no language specified) The macros used were created for ghyph31.tex by Bernd Raichle (see the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dehyph}{German 
          hyphenation pattern files} for further details); the patterns were created using standard, conservative 
          hyphenation rules for Catalan. The results were then refined by running them through \texttt{patgen} , 
          which increased the number of hits.

          The results were checked against ''Diccionari Ortogràfic i de Pronúncia, Enciclopèdia Catalana''; no 
          incorrect results were detected, and misses amounted to less than 1\%.

          For Catalan, both  \texttt{{\textbackslash}lefthyphenmn} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}righthyphenmin} should 
          be set to 2.

\section[\texttt{calculation} -- Typesetting reasoned calculations,  also called calculationa\ldots]{\texttt{calculation} -- Typesetting reasoned calculations,  also called calculational proofs}\label{pkg:calculation}
\index{Package!calculation}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/calculation}
\item[name] \texttt{calculation}
\item[caption] Typesetting reasoned calculations,  also called calculational proofs
\item[author] Fokkinga, Maarten
\index{Author!Fokkinga, Maarten}
\item[copyright] Maarten Fokkinga (2014-2015)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The  \texttt{calculation} environment formats reasoned calculations, also called calculational 
          proofs.

          The notion of reasoned calculations or calculational proofs was originally advocated by Wim Feijen and 
          Edsger Dijkstra. The package accepts options  \texttt{fleqn} and \texttt{leqno} (with 
          the same effect as the LaTeX options \texttt{fleqn} and \texttt{leqno} , or may 
          inherit the options from the document class). It allows steps and expressions to be numbered (by LaTeX 
          equation numbers, obeying the LaTeX \texttt{{\textbackslash}label} command to refer 
          to these numbers), and a step doesn't take vertical space if its hint is empty. An expression in a calculation 
          can be given a comment; it is placed at the side opposite to the equation numbers. Calculations are allowed 
          inside hints although numbering and commenting is then disabled.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/calculation/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/calculation/calculation.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./7938280735-calculation.pdf|
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/calculation}

\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 2.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The captcont package provides the ability to continue the numbering in your float environment (figure, 
          table, etc.) with minimal overhead. This package adds three commands:  \texttt{{\textbackslash}caption*} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}captcont} , 
          and \texttt{{\textbackslash}captcont*} . Along with the \texttt{{\textbackslash}caption} command, 
          these give full control over the caption numbering, caption text and the entries in the list-of pages.

          The  \texttt{{\textbackslash}caption} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}captcont} commands 
          generate list-of page entries. The \texttt{{\textbackslash}caption} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}caption*} commands 
          increment the figure or table counter.

          Captcont also fully supports the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/subfigure}{subfigure} package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/captcont/captcont.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) The caption package provides many ways to customise the captions in floating environments like figure 
          and table, and cooperates with many other packages. Facilities include rotating captions, sideways captions, 
          continued captions (for tables or figures that come in several parts). A list of compatibility notes, 
          for other packages, is provided in the documentation.

          The package also provides the ''caption outside float'' facility, in the same way that simpler packages 
          like  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/capt-of}{capt-of} do.

          The package supersedes  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/caption2}{caption2} .

\index{Package!carlisle}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/carlisle}
\item[name] \texttt{carlisle}
\item[caption] David Carlisle’s small packages
\item[author] Carlisle, David
\index{Author!Carlisle, David}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version]  (2021-06-13)
\item[last changes] 2021-06-13
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) Many of David Carlisle’s more substantial packages stand on their own, or as part of the LaTeX  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latex-tools}{latex-tools} set; 
          this set contains:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Making  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dotlessj}{dotless ‘j’} characters for fonts that don’t have them;
          \item A method for  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ltxtable}{combining the capabilities} of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/longtable}{longtable} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tabularx}{tabularx} ;
          \item An environment for  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/plain-ltx}{including Plain TeX} in LaTeX documents;
          \item A jiffy to  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/remreset}{remove counters} from other counters’ reset lists (now obsolete as it has been incorporated into the LaTeX format);

\item[description] (no language specified) The carolmin and allcmin packages provide Metafont fonts based on the Carolingan Miniscules manuscript 
          book-hand used between the 8th and 12th century AD. The font consists of minuscules and digits, with 
          some appropriate period punctuation marks. Both normal and bold versions are provided. (Note that the 
          carolmin font is also available in  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/carolmin-t1}{Adobe Type 1 format} .)

          This is one of a  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bookhands}{set of manuscript fonts} . Access 
          to the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/docmfp}{docmfp} package is desirable but not essential.

\item[author] Bouajjaj, Jamal

\item[description] (no language specified) This package, a fork of 2pi’s  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/karnaugh-map}{karnaugh-map} package, 
          draws karnaugh maps with 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 variables. It also contains commands for filling the karnaugh 
          map with terms semi-automatically or manually. Last but not least it contains commands for drawing implicants 
          on top of the map.

          The name ''cartonaugh'' is a portmanteau of ''cartographer'' and ''karnaugh''.

          The package needs LuaLaTeX and depends on  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xparse}{xparse} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xstring}{xstring} .

          \item lengthier explanations of answers;
          \item citations.
          \end{itemize}
The formatting of all the macros is highly (and simply) customizable.

\section[\texttt{ccool} -- A key-value document command parser]{\texttt{ccool} -- A key-value document command parser}\label{pkg:ccool}
\index{Package!ccool}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ccool}
\item[name] \texttt{ccool}
\item[caption] A key-value document command parser
\item[author] Rogard, Erwann
\index{Author!Rogard, Erwann}
\item[copyright] Erwann Rogard (2020)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 3.2
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a key-value interface,  \texttt{{\textbackslash}Ccool} , on
   top of xparse’s document command parser. Global options control
   input processing and its expansion. By default, they are set to
   meet likely requirements, depending on context: the selected
   language, and which of text and math mode is active. These options
   can be overridden inline. This versality could find its use, for
   example, to encode notational conventions (such as \texttt{{\textbackslash}Real} → \texttt{{\textbackslash}mathbb{\textbraceleft}R{\textbraceright}} ) at the point where they are introduced in the
   document (“Let R denote real numbers”). Polymorphic commands can be
   generated by parameterizing the keys (for instance, one parameter
   value for style, another for a property). User input to \texttt{{\textbackslash}Ccool} can optionally be serialized. This can useful for
   typesetting documents sharing the same notation.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ccool/ccool.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3788995910-ccool.pdf|

\section[\texttt{cellspace} -- Ensure minimal spacing of table cells]{\texttt{cellspace} -- Ensure minimal spacing of table cells}\label{pkg:cellspace}
\index{Package!cellspace}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cellspace}
\item[name] \texttt{cellspace}
\item[caption] Ensure minimal spacing of table cells
\item[author] Noirel, Josselin
\index{Author!Noirel, Josselin}
\item[copyright] Josselin Noirel (2006-2026)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.9.1a (2026-01-24)
\item[last changes] 2026-01-24
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) It is well known that high or deep cells tend to touch the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}hline} s 
          of a \texttt{tabular} . This package provides a modifier \texttt{S} acting on 
          usual column types so that to ensure a minimal distance that can be controlled through two parameters \texttt{{\textbackslash}cellspacetoplimit} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}cellspacebottomlimit} .

          The approach employed by this package is noticeably simpler than that of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tabls}{tabls} , 
          which considers the dimensions of each entire row; whereas you can ask the cellspace only to look at 
          the cells of potentially difficult columns.

          The package depends on  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ifthen}{ifthen} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/array}{array} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/calc}{calc} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cellspace/README}

\section[\texttt{cfr-lm} -- Enhanced support for the Latin Modern fonts]{\texttt{cfr-lm} -- Enhanced support for the Latin Modern fonts}\label{pkg:cfr-lm}
\index{Package!cfr-lm}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cfr-lm}
\item[name] \texttt{cfr-lm}
\item[caption] Enhanced support for the Latin Modern fonts
\item[author] Rees, Clea F.
\index{Author!Rees, Clea F.}
\item[copyright] Clea F. Rees (2008-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.8 (2025-02-03)
\item[last changes] 2025-02-03
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package supports a number of features of the Latin Modern fonts which are not easily accessible via 
          the default (La)TeX support provided in the official distribution. In particular, the package supports 
          the use of the various styles of digits available, small-caps and upright italic shapes, and alternative 
          weights and widths. It also supports variable width typewriter and the ''quotation'' font. Version 2.004 
          of the Latin Modern fonts is supported.

          By default, the package uses proportional oldstyle digits and variable width typewriter but this can 
          be changed by passing appropriate options to the package. The package also supports using (for example) 
          different styles of digits within a document so it is possible to use proportional oldstyle digits by 
          default, say, but tabular lining digits within a particular table.

          The package requires the official Latin Modern distribution, including its (La)TeX support. The package 
          relies on the availability of both the fonts themselves and the official font support files. The package 
          also makes use of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/nfssext-cfr}{nfssext-cfr} package.

          Only the T1 and TS1 encodings are supported for text fonts. The set up of fonts for mathematics is identical 
          to that provided by Latin Modern.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Font tables}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/cfr-lm/doc/cfr-lm-tables.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3284702785-cfr-lm-tables.pdf|

\index{Package!checkend}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/checkend}
\item[name] \texttt{checkend}
\item[caption] Extend “improperly closed environment” messages
\item[author] Bezos López, Javier
\index{Author!Bezos López, Javier}
\item[copyright] Javier Bezos (2002-2019)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) When an environment is left open, LaTeX gives an error at the end of the document. However it only informs 
          about the first of them, while the rest are shown with meaningless errors:

          \begin{verbatim}
(\end occurred inside a group at level N)
          \end{verbatim}
This package replaces these errors with more useful messages which show which environments (in reverse 
          order) were not closed. There are no user macros: just use the package.

\item[description] (no language specified) The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/chemformula}{chemformula} package and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel-russian}{babel-russian} settings 
          ( \texttt{russian.ldf} ) both define macros named '' \texttt{{\textbackslash}ch} ''.

          The package  \texttt{chemformula-ru} undefines babel’s macro to prevent an error when both 
          packages are loaded together.

          Optionally it redefines the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}cosh} macro to print the hyperbolic 
          cosine in Russian notation and/or defines a new macro \texttt{{\textbackslash}Ch} for 
          that purpose.

\section[\texttt{chemmacros} -- A collection of macros to support typesetting chemistry docu\ldots]{\texttt{chemmacros} -- A collection of macros to support typesetting chemistry documents}\label{pkg:chemmacros}
\index{Package!chemmacros}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/chemmacros}
\item[name] \texttt{chemmacros}
\item[caption] A collection of macros to support typesetting chemistry documents
\item[author] Niederberger, Clemens
\index{Author!Niederberger, Clemens}
\item[copyright] Clemens Niederberger and Sonja K. (2022)
\item[copyright] Clemens Niederberger (2011-2021)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 6.2a
\item[description] (no language specified) The bundle offers a collection of macros and commands which are intended to make typesetting chemistry 
          documents faster and more convenient. Coverage includes some nomenclature commands, oxidation numbers, 
          thermodynamic data, newman projections, etc.

          The package relies on the following supporting packages:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/chemformula}{chemformula} , providing a command for typesetting chemical formulae and reactions (doing a similar task to that of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mhchem}{mhchem} );
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/chemgreek}{chemgreek} , offering support for use of greek letters; and
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ghsystem}{ghsystem} , providing for the UN globally harmonised chemical notation.
          \end{itemize}
The packages are written using current versions of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/expl3}{experimental 
          LaTeX 3 coding conventions} and the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/l3packages}{LaTeX 3 support 
          packages} .

\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a way to convert and include chemical structure graphics from various chemical 
          formats, such as ChemDraw files, MDL molfile or SMILES notations using Open Babel.

          To use this LaTeX package, it is necessary to enable execution of the following external commands via 
          \texttt{latex -shell-escape} .

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{obabel} (Open Babel)
          \item  \texttt{inkscape} or \texttt{rsvg-convert} (for SVG -> PDF/EPS conversion)

          The package provides an extensible system for formatting chemistry documents according to the conventions 
          of a number of leading journals. It also provides some handy chemistry-related macros.

          Chemstyle is much enhanced compared to its predecessor, and users of rsc are strongly encouraged to migrate 
          (all of the additional macros in the rsc LaTeX package are present in chemstyle).

          The package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/chemscheme}{chemscheme} is distributed with chemstyle; 
          chemstyle itself incorporates ideas that come from the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/trivfloat}{trivfloat} package; 
          the documentation uses the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/auto-pst-pdf}{auto-pst-pdf} package.

\item[name] \texttt{cherokee}
\item[caption] A font for the Cherokee script
\item[author] Stanier, Alan
\index{Author!Stanier, Alan}
\item[copyright] Alan Stanier (1994)
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version]  (2011-01-11)
\item[last changes] 2011-01-11
\item[year] 2011
\index{Year!2011}
\item[description] (no language specified) The Cherokee script was designed in 1821 by Segwoya.

          The alphabet is essentially syllabic, only 6 characters (a e i o s u) correspond to Roman letters: the 
          font encodes these to the corresponding roman letter. The remaining 79 characters have been arbitrarily 
          encoded in the range 38–122; the cherokee package provides commands that map each such syllable to the 
          appropriate character; for example, Segwoya himself would be represented  \texttt{{\textbackslash}Cse{\textbackslash}Cgwo{\textbackslash}Cya} .

          The font is distributed as Metafont source; it works very poorly in modern environments, and could do 
          with expert attention (if you are interested, please contact the CTAN team for details).

\item[description] (no language specified) This package offers commands to use and switch between chess fonts. It uses the LaTeX font selection 
          scheme (nfss).

          The package doesn't parse, format and print PGN input like e.g. the packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/skak}{skak} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texmate}{texmate} ; 
          the aim of the package is to offer writers of chess packages a bundle of commands for fonts, so that 
          they don't have to implement all these commands for themselves. A normal user can use the package to 
          print e.g. single chess symbols and simple diagrams.

          The documentation contains also a section about installation of chess fonts.

\section[\texttt{chroma} -- Chroma: a reference book of LaTeX colours]{\texttt{chroma} -- Chroma: a reference book of LaTeX colours}\label{pkg:chroma}
\index{Package!chroma}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/chroma}
\item[name] \texttt{chroma}
\item[caption] Chroma: a reference book of LaTeX colours
\item[author] Kern, Uwe
\index{Author!Kern, Uwe}
\item[license] nosource = No Source Available (not free)
\index{License!nosource}
\index{License!No Source Available}
\item[version] 1.00
\item[description] (no language specified) This reference book presents several lists of colours and their respective parameters in a number of 
          colour models. The lists are constructed either by parameters or by name.

          ‘Colours by parameters’ displays systematic series of colours, based on 3-tuples of numbers that are 
          interpreted as colour parameters in the ‘rgb’, ‘cmy’, and ‘hsb’ colour models.

          ‘Colours by name’ displays sets of colours that have been given specific names such that LaTeX users 
          do not have to care about their parametrisation. However, as soon as there is the intention to use these 
          colours outside the LaTeX world (e.g., website construction or drawing programs), the parameters suddenly 
          gain importance. For each colour name, we display:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item the colour itself plus the name of the underlying model,
          \item a 50\%-tint (mixture with ‘white’),
          \item a 50\%-tone (mixture with ‘gray’),
          \item a 50\%-shade (mixture with ‘black’), and
          \item the complementary colour.
          \end{itemize}
Additionally, for the base colours defined by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xcolor}{xcolor} package, 
          also all 50\%-mixes of base colour pairs are included.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/info/colour/chroma/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{The document itself}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/info/colour/chroma/chroma.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) The package supports drawing timelines and aims to be highly customisable. Extensive configuration options 
          are offered via a standard key-value interface based on pgfkeys. Custom colour schemes and styles are 
          supported, and the package includes documented examples of each. Memoization works out-of-the-box if 
          the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/memoize}{memoize} package is loaded.

          The code was developed as a result of questions concerning difficulties in customising the output of 
          existing packages for drawing timelines, which sometimes eschew  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgfkeys}{pgfkeys} and 
          are often challenging to configure, even when based on \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{PGF/TikZ} .

          rather than name, and organized into so-called collections.

          In \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texlive}{TeX Live} , they are in the directory \texttt{texmf-dist/fonts/cid} .

          among other places, for more information.

\section[\texttt{circuit-macros} -- M4 macros for electric circuit diagrams]{\texttt{circuit-macros} -- M4 macros for electric circuit diagrams}\label{pkg:circuit-macros}
\index{Package!circuit-macros}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/circuit-macros}
\item[name] \texttt{Circuit\_macros}
\item[caption] M4 macros for electric circuit diagrams
\item[author] Aplevich, Dwight
\index{Author!Aplevich, Dwight}
\item[copyright] J. D. Aplevich (2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 10.7
\item[description] (no language specified) A set of m4 macros for drawing high-quality electric circuits containing fundamental elements, amplifiers, 
          transistors, and basic logic gates to include in TeX, LaTeX, or similar documents. Some tools and examples 
          for other types of diagrams are also included.

          The macros can be evaluated to drawing commands in the pic language, which is very easy to understand 
          and which has a good power/complexity ratio. Pic contains elements of a simple programming language, 
          and is well-suited to line drawings requiring parametric or conditional components, fine tuning, significant 
          geometric calculations or repetition, or that are naturally block structured or tree structured. (The 
          m4 and pic processors are readily available for Unix and PC machines.)

          Alternative output macros can create TeX output to be read by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{pstricks} , 
          TikZ commands for use by the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{pgf} bundle, or SVG.

\section[\texttt{citation-style-language} -- Bibliography formatting with Citation Style Language]{\texttt{citation-style-language} -- Bibliography formatting with Citation Style Language}\label{pkg:citation-style-language}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/citation-style-language}
\item[name] \texttt{citation-style-language}
\item[caption] Bibliography formatting with Citation Style Language
\item[author] Lee, Zeping
\index{Author!Lee, Zeping}
\item[copyright] Zeping Lee (2021-2025)
\item[license] cc-by-sa-3 = CC BY-SA 3.0 (free)
\index{License!cc-by-sa-3}

\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 0.6.8 (2025-01-25)
\item[last changes] 2025-01-25
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The  \href{https://citationstyles.org/}{Citation Style Language} (CSL) is an XML-based 
          language that defines the formats of citations and bibliography. There are currently thousands of styles 
          in CSL including the most widely used APA, Chicago, Vancouver, etc. The citation-style-language package 
          is aimed to provide another reference formatting method for LaTeX that utilizes the CSL styles. It contains 
          a citation processor implemented in pure Lua ( \texttt{citeproc-lua} ) which reads bibliographic 
          metadata and performs sorting and formatting on both citations and bibliography according to the selected 
          CSL style. A LaTeX package ( \texttt{citation-style-language.sty} ) is provided to communicate 
          with the processor.

          \begin{itemize}

          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/drftcite}{drftcite} , which prints citation keys rather than numbers;\\
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/overcite}{overcite} , which prints citation numbers in a superscript position; and\\

\index{License!gpl2}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 2}
\item[version] 4.8.5
\item[description] (no language specified) CJK is a macro package for LaTeX, providing simultaneous support for various Asian scripts in many encodings 
          (including Unicode):

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Chinese (both traditional and simplified),
          \item Japanese,
          \item Korean and
          \item Thai.
          \end{itemize}
A special add-on feature is an interface to the Emacs editor (cjk-enc.el) which gives simultaneous, easy-to-use 
          support to a bunch of other scripts in addition to the above — Cyrillic, Greek, Latin-based scripts, 
          Russian and Vietnamese are supported.

          Greek, Cyrillic, ogham, phonetic and mathematical ranges, scribal abbreviations and other specialist 
          characters.

          numerals) and variant forms for particular languages.

\item[version] 0.4.3
\item[description] (no language specified) The clawxiv package provides LaTeX environments for typesetting text according to its authorial provenance 
          in documents that mix human and AI contributions. Three principal environments are provided:  \texttt{seniorquote} for 
          the corresponding human author, \texttt{aiquote} for an AI coauthor, and \texttt{coauthorquote} for 
          other human contributors. Convenient aliases \texttt{humanprompt} and \texttt{airesp} support 
          prompt/response interaction transcripts. The package is part of the ClawXiv framework for archiving human–AI 
          co-authored papers with full provenance tracking. A white paper is available at \href{https://lebadus.ai/Pdf/clawxiv\_whitepaper\_arxiv.pdf}{ClawXiv}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/clawxiv/clawxiv-sty-doc.pdf}

          and bold) with corresponding italics, plus light and thin upright (without italics). Clear Sans has minimized,

\item[version] 0.21.4
\item[description] (no language specified) The package enhances LaTeX’s cross-referencing features, allowing the format of references to be determined 
          automatically according to the type of reference. The formats used may be customised in the preamble 
          of a document;  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel} support is available (though 
          the choice of languages remains limited: currently Danish, Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Norwegian, 
          Russian, Spanish and Ukranian).

          The package also offers a means of referencing a list of references, each formatted according to its 
          type. In such lists, it can collapse sequences of numerically-consecutive labels to a reference range.

\section[\texttt{cleveref-icelandic} -- Icelandic grammatical declension for cleveref cross-referenc\ldots]{\texttt{cleveref-icelandic} -- Icelandic grammatical declension for cleveref cross-references}\label{pkg:cleveref-icelandic}

\item[description] (no language specified) The cleveref-icelandic package extends  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cleveref}{cleveref} with Icelandic declension support, allowing cross-references to figures, tables, equations, and sections to appear in the correct grammatical case (nominative, accusative, dative, genitive) in both singular and plural. Case can be specified explicitly by name (nom/acc/dat/gen or Icelandic abbreviations nf/þf/þgf/ef), by number (0–3), or automatically inferred from a preposition argument. Built-in declension tables are provided for the four most common reference types. Additional reference types and prepositions can be declared in the document preamble using \verb|\DeclareIcrefType| and \verb|\DeclareIscrefPreposition| .

\section[\texttt{cleveref-usedon} -- Adds forward-referencing functionality to the cleveref packa\ldots]{\texttt{cleveref-usedon} -- Adds forward-referencing functionality to the cleveref package}\label{pkg:cleveref-usedon}
\index{Package!cleveref-usedon}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cleveref-usedon}
\item[name] \texttt{cleveref-usedon}
\item[caption] Adds forward-referencing functionality to the cleveref package
\item[author] Pistre, Sven
\index{Author!Pistre, Sven}
\item[copyright] Sven Pistre (2023)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.4.0 (2023-04-21)
\item[last changes] 2023-04-21
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) Imagine you are reading a long mathematical text such as a text book or a thesis.

          There are plenty of supplementary lemmas, propositions, theorems and/or exercises throughout the whole 
          text.

          You ask yourself ''Gosh, while Lemma 1.12 is certainly an interesting result,  \emph{where} is 
          this result used later on in this long text? I really would find that helpful to decide \emph{why} I 
          should read the proof.''

          You can, of course, use the PDF search function of your viewer to look up the string ''Lemma 1.12'', 
          but wouldn’t it be more helpful if Lemma 1.12 already indicated all or at least its most useful/crucial 
          applications via an info message?

          This is what this package tries to address: The info message ''Used on p. 40, 43-45 and 101.'' would 
          then be printed to the header of Lemma 1.12.

          This is done by extending the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}cref} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}Cref} commands and giving them an optional argument \texttt{UsedOn} . Every time you wish to record a reference in the ''used on page list'', you would simply type \verb|\cref[UsedOn]{<LabelName>}| . If you use \texttt{{\textbackslash}cref} without this optional argument, this reference won’t be recorded in this page list.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cleveref-usedon/cleveref-usedon.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./6155545347-cleveref-usedon.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cleveref-usedon/README.md}
\item[contact] \textit{support}: \url{https://github.com/SvenPistre/cleveref-usedon/discussions}

\section[\texttt{clojure-pamphlet} -- A simple literate programming tool based on clojure's pamphl\ldots]{\texttt{clojure-pamphlet} -- A simple literate programming tool based on clojure's pamphlet system}\label{pkg:clojure-pamphlet}
\index{Package!clojure-pamphlet}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/clojure-pamphlet}
\item[name] \texttt{clojure-pamphlet}
\item[caption] A simple literate programming tool based on clojure's pamphlet system
\item[author] Lanchares, Ernesto
\index{Author!Lanchares, Ernesto}
\item[copyright] Ernesto Lanchares Sanchez (2019)
\item[license] gpl3+ = GNU General Public License, version 3 or newer (free)
\index{License!gpl3+}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 3 or newer}
\item[version] 1.3
\item[description] (no language specified) The Clojure pamphlet system is a system based on the Clojure literate system. In the Clojure's pamphlet 
          system you have your main LaTeX file, which can be compiled regularly. This file contains documentation 
          and source code (just like in other forms of literate programming). These code snippets are wrapped in 
          the  \texttt{chunk} environment, hence they can be recognized by the \texttt{tangler} in 
          order to extract them. Chunks can be included inside each other by the \texttt{getchunk} command 
          (which will be typesetted acordingly). Finally, the LaTeX file will be run through the \texttt{tangler} to 
          get the desired chunk of code.

\item[description] (no language specified) Defines a ‘closefrom’ macro to complement the ‘readfrom’ primitive. It operates by repeatedly reading 
          from a file until reaching EOF, which has the side-effect of closing the file.

          The macro might be useful to avoid running out of read files when using the MetaPost graph package to 
          process many data files that contain extra junk at the end. (In such circumstances, reading the files 
          will stop short of the end, so leaving the file open.)

\item[description] (no language specified) This is another tool for the automation of LaTeX document processing, like  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latexmk}{latexmk} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/arara}{arara} .

          The main feature of this tool is that it does not clutter your working directory with  \texttt{.aux} or \texttt{.log} or 
          other auxiliary files.

          It has of course the usual features of automation tools: It automatically re-runs (La)TeX for cross-references. 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/makeindex}{MakeIndex} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bibtex}{BibTeX} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/biber}{Biber} , 
          or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/glossaries}{makeglossaries} will be executed if a corresponding 
          option is set. Furthermore, cluttex can watch input files for changes (using an external program).

\index{Author!Knuth, Donald E.}
\item[license] knuth = Knuth License (free)
\index{License!knuth}
\index{License!Knuth License}
\item[description] (no language specified) Knuth's final iteration of his re-interpretation of a c.19 Modern-style font from Monotype. The family 
          is comprehensive, offering both sans and roman styles, and a monospaced font, together with mathematics 
          fonts closely integrated with the mathematical facilities of TeX itself.

          The base fonts are distributed as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cm-mf}{Metafont source} , 
          but autotraced PostScript Type 1 versions are available (one version in the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsfonts}{AMS 
          fonts} distribution, and also the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bakoma-fonts}{BaKoMa} distribution).

          The Computer Modern fonts have inspired many later families, notably the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ec}{European 
          Computer Modern} and the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lm}{Latin Modern} families.

\index{Author!Kryukov, Alexey}
\item[copyright] Alexej Kryukov (2003-2005)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 0.5
\item[description] (no language specified) The fonts are converted from Metafont sources of the Computer Modern font families, using textrace. Supported 
          encodings are: T1 (Latin), T2A (Cyrillic), LGR (Greek) and TS1. The package also includes Unicode virtual 
          fonts for use with Omega.

          The font set is not a replacement for any of the other Computer Modern-based font sets (for example, 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cm-super}{cm-super} for Latin and Cyrillic, or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cbgreek-complete}{cbgreek} for 
          Greek), since it is available at a single size only; it offers a compact set for ‘general’ working. The 
          fonts themselves are encoded to external standards, and virtual fonts are provided for use with TeX.

\item[last changes] 2021-02-06
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) The cmap package provides character map tables, which make PDF files generated by pdfLaTeX both searchable 
          and copy-able in acrobat reader and other compliant PDF viewers. Encodings supported are OT1, OT6, T1, 
          T2A, T2B, T2C and T5, together with LAE (Arabic), LFE (Farsi) and LGR (Greek) and a variant OT1tt for 
          cmtt-like fonts.

          The package’s main limitation currently is the inability to work with virtual fonts, because of limitations 
          of pdfTeX. This restriction may be resolved in a future version of pdfTeX.

\section[\texttt{cmdtrack} -- Check used commands]{\texttt{cmdtrack} -- Check used commands}\label{pkg:cmdtrack}
\index{Package!cmdtrack}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cmdtrack}
\item[name] \texttt{cmdtrack}
\item[caption] Check used commands
\item[author] Downes, Michael J.
\index{Author!Downes, Michael J.}
\item[copyright] TeX Users Group (2012)
\item[copyright] Michael John Downes (1999)
\item[license] lppl1 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1 (free)
\index{License!lppl1}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package keeps track of whether a command defined in a document preamble is actually used somewhere 
          in the document. After the package is loaded in the preamble of a document, all  \texttt{{\textbackslash}newcommand} (and 
          similar command definitions) between that point and the beginning of the document will be marked for 
          logging. At the end of the document a report of command usage will be printed in the TeX log, for example:

          
          \begin{itemize}
          \item '' \texttt{mdash was used on line 25} '';
          \item '' \texttt{ndash was never used} ''.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cmdtrack/cmdtrack.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./6884842306-cmdtrack.pdf|

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cmsd}
\item[name] \texttt{cmsd}
\item[caption] Interfaces to the CM Sans Serif Bold fonts
\item[author] Schmidt, Walter A.
\index{Author!Schmidt, Walter A.}
\item[author] Harcombe, Keiran
\index{Author!Harcombe, Keiran}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[description] (no language specified) Thr purpose of the package is to provide an alternative interface to the CM Sans Serif boldface fonts. 
          The EC (T1, Cork) encoded versions of the ‘CM Sans Serif boldface extended’ fonts differ considerably 
          from the traditionally (OT1) encoded ones: at large sizes, >10pt, they have thinner strokes and are much 
          wider. At 25pt they are hardly to be recognized as being ‘boldface’. This package attempts to make these 
          T1 fonts look like the traditional ones did. You do not need any new fonts; the package just changes 
          the way LaTeX makes use of the current ones.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cmsd/readme}

\section[\texttt{cmsrb} -- Computer Modern for Serbian and Macedonian]{\texttt{cmsrb} -- Computer Modern for Serbian and Macedonian}\label{pkg:cmsrb}
\index{Package!cmsrb}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cmsrb}
\item[name] \texttt{cmsrb}
\item[caption] Computer Modern for Serbian and Macedonian
\item[author] Stefanović, Uroš
\index{Author!Stefanović, Uroš}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 4.0 (2020-03-30)
\item[last changes] 2020-03-30
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides provides Adobe Type 1 Computer Modern fonts for the Serbian and Macedonian languages.

          Although the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cm-super}{cm-super} package provides great support 
          for cyrillic script in various languages, there remains a problem with italic variants of some letters 
          for Serbian and Macedonian.

          This package includes the correct shapes for italic letters  \texttt{{\textbackslash}cyrb} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}cyrg} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}cyrd} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}cyrp} , 
          and \texttt{{\textbackslash}cyrt} . It also offers some improvements in letters and 
          accents used in the Serbian language.

          Supported encodings are: T1, T2A, TS1, X2 and OT2. The OT2 encoding is modified so that it is now easy 
          to transcribe Latin text to Cyrillic.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/cmsrb/doc/cmsrb.pdf}

\section[\texttt{cntdwn} -- Support for countdowns, and for clocks in any timezone]{\texttt{cntdwn} -- Support for countdowns, and for clocks in any timezone}\label{pkg:cntdwn}
\index{Package!cntdwn}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cntdwn}
\item[name] \texttt{cntdwn}
\item[caption] Support for countdowns, and for clocks in any timezone
\item[author] Story, Donald P.
\index{Author!Story, Donald P.}
\item[copyright] D. P. Story (2010)
\item[license] lppl1 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1 (free)
\index{License!lppl1}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1}
\item[version] 0.6 (2014-11-26)
\item[last changes] 2014-11-26
\item[year] 2014
\index{Year!2014}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides three sets of timers:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item A short countdown (or count up) to an event. (Short being defined as less than a day.) The short countdown is designed for talks or presentations. There are three notification times, to announce to the speaker and audience that time is running out;
          \item A long countdown to an event in the (distant) future. There are three notifications up to the main event (when counter reaches 0 seconds), and three notifications following 0 seconds;
          \item Clock counters. The package allows you to create clocks that display time and date. Clocks can show local time or time in any foreign time zone.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cntdwn/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cntdwn/doc/cntdwn_man.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./9800869599-cntdwn_man.pdf|
\item[home page] \url{http://www.math.uakron.edu/~dpstory/cntdwn.html}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/cntdwn}

\item[version] 0.3 (2015-06-01)
\item[last changes] 2015-06-01
\item[year] 2015
\index{Year!2015}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package stores values of counters (which have been registered beforehand) on a per chapter base 
          and provides the values on demand in the 2nd LaTeX compilation run. In this way it is possible to know 
          how many sections etc. there are lying ahead and to react to these counter values, if needed.

          This is a preliminary version that has been tested with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/book}{book.cls} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/memoir}{memoir.cls} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/scrbook}{scrbook.cls} .

          The packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/assoccnt}{assoccnt} (by the same author) and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xparse}{xparse} are 
          needed as well.

\index{Package!cochineal}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cochineal}
\item[name] \texttt{cochineal}
\item[caption] Cochineal fonts with LaTeX support
\item[author] Sharpe, Michael
\index{Author!Sharpe, Michael}
\item[copyright] Michael Sharpe (2016-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[license] ofl = The SIL Open Font License (free)
\index{License!ofl}
\index{License!The SIL Open Font License}
\item[version] 1.085 (2024-03-08)
\item[last changes] 2024-03-08
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) Cochineal is a fork from the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/crimson}{Crimson fonts} (Roman, 
          Italic, Bold, BoldItalic only) released under the OFL by Sebastian Kosch. These remarkable fonts are 
          inspired by the famous oldstyle fonts in the garalde family (Garamond, Bembo) but, in the end, look more 
          similar to Minion, though with smaller xheight and less plain in detail. The Crimson fonts on which these 
          were based had roughly 4200 glyphs in the four styles mentioned above. Cochineal adds more than 1500 
          glyphs in those styles so that it is possible to make a TeX support collection that contains essentially 
          all glyphs in all styles. Bringing the Semibold styles up the same level would have required adding about 
          2000 additional glyphs, which I could not even contemplate.

          The fonts are provided in OpenType and PostScript formats.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/cochineal/README}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}

\item[name] \texttt{codedoc}
\item[caption] LaTeX code and documentation in LaTeX-format file
\item[author] Robbers, Yuri
\index{Author!Robbers, Yuri}
\item[author] Isambert, Paul
\index{Author!Isambert, Paul}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.3
\item[description] (no language specified) The CodeDoc class is an alternative to DocStrip (and others) to produce LaTeX code along with its documentation 
          without departing from LaTeX's ordinary syntax.

          The documentation is prepared like any other LaTeX document and the code to be commented verbatim is 
          simply delimited by an environment. When an option is turned on in the class options, this code is written 
          to the desired file(s).

          The class also includes fully customizable verbatim environments which provide the author with separate 
          commands to typeset the material and/or to execute it.

          LaTeX3 Programming Layer to parse and highlight source code and demos. It is more powerful than the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/listings}{listings} package,

\item[author] Scharrer, Martin
\index{Author!Scharrer, Martin}

\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.4c
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides macros to collect and process a macro argument (i.e., something which looks like 
          a macro argument) as a horizontal box rather than as a real macro argument.

          The ''arguments'' are stored as if they had been saved by  \texttt{{\textbackslash}savebox} or 
          by the \texttt{lrbox} environment. Grouping tokens \texttt{{\textbackslash}bgroup} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}egroup} may 
          be used, which allows the user to have the beginning and end of a group in different macro invocations, 
          or to place them in the begin and end code of an environment. Arguments may contain verbatim material 
          or other special use of characters.

          The macros were designed for use within other macros.

\item[description] (no language specified) Colophons are a once-common design device by which a book (or document) designer gave some information 
          to his readers about the design and makeup of the text. It typically includes the publisher (if not included 
          elsewhere in the document), font size, leading size, measure, and of course font face identification. 
          Sometimes it includes information about the tools used, as well. This package provides some highly configurable 
          macros, with sensible defaults, for producing colophons without having to muck around with a lot of manual 
          code.

\item[caption] Easy colorblind-safe typesetting
\item[author] Pfahler, Simon
\index{Author!Pfahler, Simon}

\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)

\item[version] 1.2.1 (2026-01-19)
\item[last changes] 2026-01-19
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) In colorblind-safe documents, the contents are presented in a way that the same information is conveyed 
          to readers regardless of a potential color vision deficiency. This package provides the tools necessary 
          for colorblind-safe typesetting in LaTeX. It provides color schemes for a wide range of applications.

          The most commonly used schemes are qualitative schemes, providing easily distinguishable colors for use 
          in graphics, but also for text coloring or highlighting. Additionally, diverging and sequential schemes 
          are included which can be used for encoding quantitative information using colors. This package incorporates 
          colorblind-safeness into the writing process, making it both less cumbersome and less error-prone.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/colorblind/colorblind_doc.pdf}

\section[\texttt{colorist} -- Write your articles or books in a colorful way]{\texttt{colorist} -- Write your articles or books in a colorful way}\label{pkg:colorist}
\index{Package!colorist}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/colorist}
\item[name] \texttt{colorist}
\item[caption] Write your articles or books in a colorful way
\item[author] XU, Jinwen
\index{Author!XU, Jinwen}
\item[copyright] Jinwen XU (2021-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version]  (2025-10-21)
\item[last changes] 2025-10-21
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package offers you a LaTeX style file and two classes to typeset articles or books in a colorful 
          way. These classes currently have native support for English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese (European 
          and Brazilian), and Spanish typesetting. They compile with any major TeX engine.

          You may also wish to consider the packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lebhart}{lebhart} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beaulivre}{beaulivre} , 
          which are enhanced versions of the classes provided here. They have unicode support, thus can only be 
          used with either XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX. Currently they have native support for Chinese (both simplified 
          and traditional), English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese (European and Brazilian), Russian 
          and Spanish typesetting, and also use more beautiful fonts.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/colorist/README.md}

\section[\texttt{combinedgraphics} -- Include graphic (EPS or PDF)/LaTeX combinations]{\texttt{combinedgraphics} -- Include graphic (EPS or PDF)/LaTeX combinations}\label{pkg:combinedgraphics}
\index{Package!combinedgraphics}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/combinedgraphics}
\item[name] \texttt{combinedgraphics}
\item[caption] Include graphic (EPS or PDF)/LaTeX combinations
\item[author] Schneider, Christian
\index{Author!Schneider, Christian}
\item[copyright] Christian Schneider (2009)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 0.2.2
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a macro ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}includecombinedgraphics} ) 
          for the inclusion of combined EPS/LaTeX and PDF/LaTeX graphics (an export format of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/gnuplot}{Gnuplot} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xfig}{Xfig} , 
          and maybe other programs). Instead of including the graphics with a simple \texttt{{\textbackslash}input} , 
          the \texttt{{\textbackslash}includecombinedgraphics} macro has some comforts:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item changing the font and color of the text of the LaTeX part; rescaling the graphics without affecting the font of the LaTeX part;
          \item automatic inclusion of the vector graphics part, as far as LaTeX part does not do it (e.g., for files exported from Gnuplot before version 4.2); and
          \item rescaling and rotating of complete graphics (similar to  \texttt{{\textbackslash}includegraphics} from the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphicx}{graphicx} package).
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/combinedgraphics/combinedgraphics.pdf}

\section[\texttt{commado} -- Expandable iteration on comma-separated and filename lists]{\texttt{commado} -- Expandable iteration on comma-separated and filename lists}\label{pkg:commado}
\index{Package!commado}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/commado}
\item[name] \texttt{commado}
\item[caption] Expandable iteration on comma-separated and filename lists
\item[author] Lück, Uwe
\index{Author!Lück, Uwe}
\item[copyright] Uwe Lück (2012)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] r0.11a
\item[description] (no language specified) The bundle provides two packages:  \texttt{commado} and \texttt{filesdo} .

          The package  \texttt{commado} provides the command \texttt{{\textbackslash}DoWithCSL} :

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}DoWithCSL{\textbraceleft}< \emph{cmd} >{\textbraceright}{\textbraceleft}< \emph{list} >{\textbraceright}} applies 
          an existing one-parameter macro < \emph{cmd} > to each item in a list < \emph{list} > 
          in which terms are separated by commas.

          The package  \texttt{filesdo} provides the command \texttt{{\textbackslash}DoWithBasesExts} :

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}DoWithBasesExts} {\textbraceleft}< \emph{cmd} >{\textbraceright}{\textbraceleft}< \emph{bases} >{\textbraceright}{\textbraceleft}< \emph{exts} >{\textbraceright}

          which runs the single parameter command < \emph{cmd} > on each file whose base and extension 
          are respectively from the comma-separated lists < \emph{bases} > and < \emph{exts} >.

          These ‘loop’-like commands are (themselves) entirely expandable.

          The packages rely on packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/plainpkg}{plainpkg} , and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/catcodes}{stacklet}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/commado/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/commado/doc/commado.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./1242852012-commado.pdf|

\section[\texttt{comment} -- Selectively include/exclude portions of text]{\texttt{comment} -- Selectively include/exclude portions of text}\label{pkg:comment}
\index{Package!comment}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/comment}
\item[name] \texttt{comment}
\item[caption] Selectively include/exclude portions of text
\item[author] Eijkhout, Victor
\index{Author!Eijkhout, Victor}
\item[copyright] Victor Eijkhout (1998-2016)
\item[license] gpl2 = GNU General Public License, version 2 (free)
\index{License!gpl2}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 2}
\item[version] 3.8
\item[description] (no language specified) Selectively include/exclude pieces of text, allowing the user to define new, separately controlled, comment 
          versions. All text between  \texttt{{\textbackslash}comment ... {\textbackslash}endcomment} or \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}comment{\textbraceright} 
          ... {\textbackslash}end{\textbraceleft}comment{\textbraceright}} is discarded. 
          The opening and closing commands should appear on a line of their own. No starting spaces, nothing after 
          it. This environment should work with arbitrary amounts of comment, and the comment can be arbitrary 
          text.

          Other ‘comment’ environments are defined and selected/deselected with  \texttt{{\textbackslash}includecomment{\textbraceleft}versiona{\textbraceright}} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}excludecomment{\textbraceleft}versionb{\textbraceright}} These 
          environments are used as \texttt{{\textbackslash}versiona … {\textbackslash}endversiona} or \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}versiona{\textbraceright} 
          … {\textbackslash}end{\textbraceleft}versiona{\textbraceright}} with the opening 
          and closing commands again on a line of their own.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/comment/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/comment/comment.pdf}

\index{Year!2015}
\item[description] (no language specified) The author tells us: ''This is a small script written in Python to help you to automatically comment 
          and uncomment lines in your code. The program was sprung out of a need I myself had of turning on and 
          off certain environments in LaTeX. After digging around, trying to make this happen by using only LaTeX 
          code, I finally got fed up and just wrote this program instead.''

          Basically, you use the program by marking certain lines in your code with certain commands. The program 
          then detects these commands and comments or uncomments the whole line depending on which mode you’ve 
          set it to.
