\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.0.5-r1
\item[description] (no language specified) The package helps to keep track of formal ‘concepts’ for a specific field or document. This is particularly 
          useful for scientific papers (for example, in physics, mathematics or computer science), which may introduce 
          several concepts (with their own symbols). The package’s commands allow the user to define a concept 
          (typically, near its first use), and will ensure consistent use throughout the document.

          The package depends on several other packages; while these are fairly common packages, the user should 
          check the package’s README file for the complete list.

\section[\texttt{concrete} -- Concrete Roman fonts]{\texttt{concrete} -- Concrete Roman fonts}\label{pkg:concrete}
\index{Package!concrete}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/concrete}
\item[name] \texttt{concrete}
\item[caption] Concrete Roman fonts
\item[author] Knuth, Donald E.
\index{Author!Knuth, Donald E.}
\item[copyright] D. E. Knuth (null)
\item[license] knuth = Knuth License (free)
\index{License!knuth}
\index{License!Knuth License}
\item[description] (no language specified) Concrete Roman fonts, designed by Donald E. Knuth, originally for use with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsfonts}{Euler 
          mathematics fonts} . Alternative mathematics fonts, based on the concrete ‘parameter set’ are available 
          as the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/concmath-fonts}{concmath fonts} bundle.

          LaTeX support is offered by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beton}{beton} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/concmath}{concmath} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ccfonts}{ccfonts} packages.

\section[\texttt{conditext} -- Define and manage conditional content]{\texttt{conditext} -- Define and manage conditional content}\label{pkg:conditext}
\index{Package!conditext}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/conditext}
\item[name] \texttt{CondiTeXt}
\item[caption] Define and manage conditional content
\item[author] Brabant, Jean-Louis
\index{Author!Brabant, Jean-Louis}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.5 (2020-06-01)
\item[last changes] 2020-06-01
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides some commands to define and manage conditional content in a LaTeX source document.

          A conditional content, in the sense within this is understood in this package, is a text (including mathematical 
          or other formulas) and/or a graphical element (diagram, figure, image...) as substitutable forms, which, 
          according to a condition test, may or may not appear in the generated document.

          One of the most common forms of conditional content management is multilingual ; but it can also include 
          versioning, confidentiality levels, and so on.

          The philosophy of this package is based on the respective notions of condition field, condition property 
          and condition space.

          With this package, any substitutable form in a source document is identified by a condition field and 
          a condition property.

          The  \emph{condition field} is a functional theme that allows you to group together substitutable 
          forms for the same conditional management.

          The  \emph{condition property} is a functional characterization specific to each substitutable 
          form of a single condition domain.

          The  \emph{condition space} is used to designate the substitutable form(s) that must appear 
          in the generated document. A condition space is defined by specifying a condition domain and a condition 
          property to match with one or more substitutable forms.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/conditext/conditext.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3773134043-conditext.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/conditext/README.txt}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/conditext}
\item[on Mik\TeX] \texttt{conditext}
\item[on \TeX Live] \texttt{conditext}

\item[description] (no language specified) The module parses an ini-file and prints the contents with a user-defined layout. The entries of the 
          file may be sorted by up to three sort keys.

          The format of a simple ini-file would be:\\
          \begin{verbatim}
[key1]
symbol1 = value1
symbol2 = value2 
[key2]
symbol1 = value3
symbol2 = value4
          \end{verbatim}

          The module only works with ConTeXt MkIV, and uses Lua to help process the input.

\section[\texttt{context-vim} -- Generate ConTeXt syntax highlighting code from vim]{\texttt{context-vim} -- Generate ConTeXt syntax highlighting code from vim}\label{pkg:context-vim}
\index{Package!context-vim}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/context-vim}
\item[name] \texttt{context-vim}
\item[caption] Generate ConTeXt syntax highlighting code from vim
\item[author] Mahajan, Aditya
\index{Author!Mahajan, Aditya}
\item[author] Miklavec, Mojca
\index{Author!Miklavec, Mojca}
\item[license] bsd = BSD Style License (free)
\index{License!bsd}
\index{License!BSD Style License}
\item[version]  (2022-02-17)
\item[last changes] 2022-02-17
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) ConTeXt has excellent pretty printing capabilities for many languages. The code for pretty printing is 
          written in TeX, and due to catcode juggling, such verbatim typesetting is perhaps the trickiest part 
          of TeX. This makes it difficult for a ''normal'' user to define syntax highlighting rules for a new language. 
          This module takes the onus of defining syntax highlighting rules away from the user and uses ViM editor 
          to generate the syntax highlighting. There is a helper 2context.vim script to do the syntax parsing in 
          ViM.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package usage notes}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/context/contrib/context-vim/doc/context/third/vim/vim.txt}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/context/contrib/context-vim}

\index{Topic!synt-hlt}

\index{Topic!context}
\item[keyword] \texttt{ext-code} (run an external program from within a document)
\index{Topic!ext-code}
\item[see also] see section~\ref{pkg:context-filter} on page~\pageref{pkg:context-filter}: (\texttt{context-filter} -- Run external programs on the contents of a start-stop environment)

\item[description] (no language specified) This small package supports key-value syntax other than the standard LaTeX syntax of  \texttt{<key>=<value>} . 
          Using this package, create key-values of the form \texttt{<key>:<value>} or \texttt{<key>-><value>} , 
          for example.

          The package converts the new notation to  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} notation 
          and passes it on to \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} .

\section[\texttt{cool} -- COntent-Oriented LaTeX]{\texttt{cool} -- COntent-Oriented LaTeX}\label{pkg:cool}
\index{Package!cool}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cool}
\item[name] \texttt{cool}
\item[caption] COntent-Oriented LaTeX
\item[author] Setzer, Nick
\index{Author!Setzer, Nick}
\item[copyright] Nick Setzer (2005-2023)
\item[license] lgpl = GNU Lesser General Public License (free)

\item[version] 1.35 (2023-05-03)
\item[last changes] 2023-05-03
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package (COntent Oriented LaTeX) gives LaTeX the power to retain mathematical meaning of its expressions 
          in addition to the typsetting instructions; essentially separating style from the content of the math.

          One advantage of keeping mathematical meaning is that conversion of LaTeX documents to other executable 
          formats (such as Content MathML or Mathematica code) is greatly simplified.

          The package requires the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/coolstr}{coolstr} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/coollist}{coollist} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/forloop}{forloop} packages.

\section[\texttt{coop-writing} -- Support for Cooperative Writing and editorial comments]{\texttt{coop-writing} -- Support for Cooperative Writing and editorial comments}\label{pkg:coop-writing}
\index{Package!coop-writing}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/coop-writing}
\item[name] \texttt{coop-writing}
\item[caption] Support for Cooperative Writing and editorial comments
\item[author] Xexéo, Geraldo
\index{Author!Xexéo, Geraldo}
\item[copyright] Geraldo Xexéo (2022)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 1.2.4 (2022-01-13)
\item[last changes] 2022-01-13
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package for Cooperative Writing supports editorial comments and gives some extra support for writing 
          and submitting papers, such as anonymization commands for any document that involves more than one author 
          or editor.

          The general behavior of this package is to provide different ways of marking your text, for example with 
          comments or to-do-notes, suggestions to add, remove or change text that can be totally supressed from 
          the output when desired. Mostly, this can be easily done using one of the three main option states:  \texttt{editing} , \texttt{submit} , 
          and \texttt{publish} .

          Users should use the  \texttt{editing} state most of the time. In this state, all markings 
          will appear and anonymization will be off. When submitting, the submit state will provide a clean article, 
          without any markings, but anonymized. It is possible to use the options \texttt{submit} and \texttt{noanonymize} together. \texttt{Publish} will 
          never anonymize. The goal is to make the \texttt{submit} and \texttt{publish} documents 
          states minimally invasive, to avoid any clash with publishers’ styles.

          Commands were inspired from different packages that do not work together very well, such as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ed}{ed} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/todonotes}{todonotes} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/color-edits}{color-edits} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/coop-writing/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/coop-writing/coop-writing.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./5104648832-coop-writing.pdf|

\section[\texttt{corridx-obsolete} -- Add index entries to LaTeX document]{\texttt{corridx-obsolete} -- Add index entries to LaTeX document}\label{pkg:corridx-obsolete}
\index{Package!corridx-obsolete}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/corridx-obsolete}
\item[name] \texttt{corridx-obsolete}
\item[caption] Add index entries to LaTeX document
\item[author] Fink, Johannes K.
\index{Author!Fink, Johannes K.}
\item[license] noinfo = noinfo 
\index{License!noinfo}
\index{License!noinfo}
\item[version]  (2004-10-12)
\item[last changes] 2004-10-12
\item[year] 2004
\index{Year!2004}
\item[description] (no language specified) Corridx is a preprocessor which stands between your LaTeX run and  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/makeindex}{makeindex} . 
          It corrects index entries, in cases where the natural way to express an index item is bad for index sorting. 
          So, for example, it can simply transform an entry \texttt{{\textbackslash}index{\textbraceleft}1,2-ethanediol{\textbraceright}} to \texttt{{\textbackslash}index{\textbraceleft}ethanediol@1,2-ethanediol{\textbraceright}} , 
          which will be sorted as you might hope, rather than in amongst the numbers.

          The program is distributed as Pascal source, though a win32 executable is also available; the documentation 
          shows how to integrate it with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/winedt}{winedt} .

          The program has now been superseded by a  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/corridx-latex}{LaTeX

\item[last changes] 2026-04-03

\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) This is a simple package for generating exact wordcounts in LaTeX projects. It counts words, storing 
          the value in a standard LaTeX counter, which can then be printed in the normal way. Word counting can 
          be paused and resumed, so you can skip certain environments like mathematics, and multiple word counts 
          can happen in parallel (you could keep separate global and per-chapter counts, for example).

          The word counting engine itself is pulled from  \href{https://gist.github.com/phi-gamma/2622252}{https://gist.github.com/phi-gamma/2622252} .

\item[description] (no language specified) The package CoverPage was created to supplement scientific papers with a cover page containing bibliographical 
          information, a copyright notice, and/or some logos of the author's institution. The cover page is created 
          (almost) automatically; this is done by parsing BibTeX information corresponding to the main document 
          and reading a configuration file in which the author can set information like the affiliation he or she 
          is associated with.

          The cover page consists of header, body and footer; all three are macros which can be redefined using 
          \texttt{{\textbackslash}renewcommand} , thus allowing easy customization of the package. 
          Additionally, it should be stressed that the cover page layout is totally independent of the main document 
          and its page layout.

          This package requires four other packages ( \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/keyval}{keyval} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/url}{url} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/textcomp}{textcomp} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/verbatim}{verbatim} ), but all of them are standard packages 
          and should be part of every LaTeX installation.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Another sample}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/coverpage/ECCV06Sample.pdf}

          macro proof against verbatim in its argument; as, for example, \texttt{{\textbackslash}cprotect{\textbackslash}section{\textbraceleft}{\textbackslash}verb"foo"{\textbraceright}}

          an environment) sanitises the behavior of fragile environments.

\item[description] (no language specified) By default, when using cleveref’s  \texttt{{\textbackslash}cref} to reference theorem-like 
          environments, the names do not contain definite articles. In languages such as French, Italian, Portuguese, 
          Spanish, etc. this results in incorrect grammar. For this purpose, the current package offers \texttt{{\textbackslash}crefthe} , 
          which handles the definite articles properly (especially for the article contractions in many European 
          languages).

          designed by Sebastian Kosch.

          The Crimson family is for book production in the tradition of beautiful oldstyle typefaces, inspired 
          particularly by the work of people like Jan Tschichold (Sabon), Robert Slimbach (Arno, Minion), and Jonathan 
          Hoefler (Hoefler Text).

          Small caps and old-style numerals are mostly available, except old-style numerals are not supported in 
          Bold or Semibold.

\item[description] (no language specified) A package providing corner marks for camera alignment as well as for trimming paper stacks, and additional 
          page information on every page if required. Most macros are easily adaptable to personal preferences. 
          An option is provided for selectively suppressing graphics or text, which may be useful for printing 
          just colour graphics on a colour laser printer and the rest on a cheap mono laser printer. A page info 
          line contains the time and a new cropmarks index and is printed at the top of the page. A configuration 
          command is provided for the info line font. Options for better collaboration with dvips, pdfTeX and vtex 
          are provided.

\section[\texttt{crossrefenum} -- Smart typesetting of enumerated cross-references for various\ldots]{\texttt{crossrefenum} -- Smart typesetting of enumerated cross-references for various TeX formats}\label{pkg:crossrefenum}
\index{Package!crossrefenum}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/crossrefenum}
\item[name] \texttt{crossrefenum}
\item[caption] Smart typesetting of enumerated cross-references for various TeX formats
\item[author] Dumont, Bastien
\index{Author!Dumont, Bastien}
\item[copyright] Bastien Dumont (2022-2024)
\item[license] fdl = Free Documentation License (free)
\index{License!fdl}
\index{License!Free Documentation License}
\item[license] gpl3+ = GNU General Public License, version 3 or newer (free)
\index{License!gpl3+}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 3 or newer}
\item[version] 1.1 (2024-04-13)
\item[last changes] 2024-04-13
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) \emph{crossrefenum} lets TeX manage the formatting of bunches of cross-references for you. 
          It features:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Automatic collapsing of references;
          \item Support for references by various criteria, including page and note number, line number in ConTeXt and edpage and edline when used in conjunction with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/reledmac}{reledmac} 
          \item Handling of references combining two criteria (e.g. by page and note number)
          \item Extension mechanisms to add support to other types of references without modifying the internal macros.
          \end{itemize}
Note that sorting is not supported. I assume that users know in what order the labels they refer to appear 
          in their document.

          It is written in Plain TeX as much as possible in order to make it compatible with a wide array of formats. 
          For the moment, it works out of the box with ConTeXt and LaTeX.

\section[\texttt{crossword} -- Typeset crossword puzzles]{\texttt{crossword} -- Typeset crossword puzzles}\label{pkg:crossword}
\index{Package!crossword}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/crossword}
\item[name] \texttt{crossword}
\item[caption] Typeset crossword puzzles
\item[author] Neugebauer, Gerd
\index{Author!Neugebauer, Gerd}
\item[copyright] Gerd Neugebauer (1995-2026)
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version] 1.15 (2026-02-13)
\item[last changes] 2026-02-13
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) An extended grid-based puzzle package, designed to take all input (both grid and clues) from the same 
          file. The package can typeset grids with holes in them (for advertisements, or other sorts of stuff), 
          and can deal with several sorts of puzzle:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item The classical puzzle contains numbers for the words and clues for the words to be filled in.
          \item The numbered puzzle contains numbers in each cell where identical numbers represent identical letters. The goal is to find out which number corresponds to which letter.
          \item The fill-in type of puzzle consists of a grid and a list of words. The goal is to place all words in the grid.
          \item Sudoku and Kakuro puzzles involve filling in grids of numbers according to their own rules.
          \end{itemize}
Format may be block-separated, or separated by thick lines. Input to the package is somewhat redundant: 
          specification of the grid is separate from specification of the clues (if they are necessary). The author 
          considers this style both ‘natural’ and robust.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/gene/crossword/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/gene/crossword/cwpuzzle.pdf}

\section[\texttt{csplain} -- Plain TeX multilanguage support]{\texttt{csplain} -- Plain TeX multilanguage support}\label{pkg:csplain}
\index{Package!csplain}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/csplain}
\item[name] \texttt{csplain}
\item[caption] Plain TeX multilanguage support
\item[author] Olšák, Petr
\index{Author!Olšák, Petr}
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version] Mar. 2022
\item[description] (no language specified) CSplain is a small extension of basic Plain TeX macros, the formats csplain and pdfcsplain can be generated. 
          It supports:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item hyphenation of words for 50+ languages,
          \item simple and powerfull font loading system (various sizes of fonts),
          \item TeX, pdfTeX, XeTeX and LuaTeX engines,
          \item math fonts simply loaded with full amstex-like features,
          \item three internal encodings (IL2 for Czech/Slovak languages, T1 for many languages with latin alphabet and Unicode in new TeX engines),
          \item natural UTF-8 input in pdfTeX using encTeX without any active characters,
          \item Czech and Slovak special typesetting features.
          \end{itemize}
An important part of the package is OPmac, which implements most of LaTeX's features (sectioning, font 
          selection, color, hyper reference and urls, bibliography, index, toc, tables,etc.) by Plain TeX macros. 
          The OPmac macros can generate and bibliography without any external program.
\item[home page] \url{http://petr.olsak.net/csplain-e.html}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/cstex/base/csplain.tar.gz}

\section[\texttt{csquotes} -- Context sensitive quotation facilities]{\texttt{csquotes} -- Context sensitive quotation facilities}\label{pkg:csquotes}
\index{Package!csquotes}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/csquotes}
\item[name] \texttt{csquotes}
\item[caption] Context sensitive quotation facilities
\item[author] Wright, Joseph
\index{Author!Wright, Joseph}
\item[author] Lehman, Philipp
\index{Author!Lehman, Philipp}
\item[copyright] Philipp Lehman (2003-2011)
\item[copyright] Joseph Wright (2015-2019, 2021, 2022,2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 5.2o (2024-04-04)
\item[last changes] 2024-04-04
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides advanced facilities for inline and display quotations. It is designed for a wide 
          range of tasks ranging from the most simple applications to the more complex demands of formal quotations. 
          The facilities include commands, environments, and user-definable ‘smart quotes’ which dynamically adjust 
          to their context. Quotation marks are switched automatically if quotations are nested and they can be 
          adjusted to the current language if the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel} package 
          is available. There are additional facilities designed to cope with the more specific demands of academic 
          writing, especially in the humanities and the social sciences. All quote styles as well as the optional 
          active quotes are freely configurable.

          The package is dependent on e-TeX, and requires the author’s  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/etoolbox}{etoolbox} package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package README}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/csquotes/README.md}

\section[\texttt{csthm} -- Customized theorem environments for computer science documen\ldots]{\texttt{csthm} -- Customized theorem environments for computer science documents}\label{pkg:csthm}
\index{Package!csthm}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/csthm}
\item[name] \texttt{csthm}
\item[caption] Customized theorem environments for computer science documents
\item[author] Datta, Agni
\index{Author!Datta, Agni}
\item[copyright] Agni Datta (2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.3
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides customized theorem-like environments specifically designed for computer science 
          documents. It offers a set of pre-defined theorem styles and environments to streamline the creation 
          of theorems, definitions, remarks, and other common structures in computer science papers and documents.

          Features:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Predefined theorem styles tailored for computer science
          \item Environments for theorems, lemmas, definitions, examples, remarks, and more
          \item Special environments for cases and axioms
          \item Customizable accent color
          \item Optional cleveref support for enhanced cross-referencing
          \end{itemize}
The package requires the following packages to be installed:  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsmath}{amsmath} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsfonts}{amssymb} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsthm}{amsthm} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/enumitem}{enumitem} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/thmtools}{thmtools} . If using the \texttt{cleveref} option, \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cleveref}{cleveref} are 
          also required.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/csthm/README.md}

\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.24
\item[description] (no language specified) The csvtools package allows you to repeatedly perform a set of LaTeX commands on data in each row of 
          a comma separated variable (CSV) file (though substitution of the ‘comma’ is permitted). Such files may 
          be used as source for mail merging, generating tables etc. Examples are given in the documentation.

          The distribution also provides packages:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{csvsort} , that provides analagous commands to those in the main package, having first sorted the data (using the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xfor}{xfor} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/compare}{compare} packages); and
          \item  \texttt{csvpie} , for creating a pie-chart from a CSV file.
          \end{itemize}
The bundle has now been superseded by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datatool}{datatool} bundle.

\item[version] 0.01
\item[description] (no language specified) All CTAN packages are saved as bibdata with the entry type  \texttt{@manual} , which can 
          easily be changed by any editor via the replace function. For the old BibTeX program you have to define 
          your bibliography style file, eg \texttt{ctan.bst} . For \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/biber}{Biber} resp. \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/biblatex}{BibLaTeX} there 
          exists an own \texttt{ctan.bbx} file which uses the data fields:

          \texttt{title} , \texttt{subtitle} , \texttt{author} , \texttt{date} , \texttt{version} , \texttt{license} , \texttt{url} , \texttt{pkgurl} , \texttt{note} .

          \texttt{ctan.bbx} is based on \texttt{authortitle} which can be changed easily 
          in the file.

          The file  \texttt{ctan.bib} will be updated on a daily basis.

\item[name] \texttt{ctan-o-mat}
\item[caption] Upload or validate a package for CTAN
\item[author] Neugebauer, Gerd

\item[copyright] Gerd Neugebauer (2016-2017)
\item[license] bsd3 = 3-clause BSD License (free)
\index{License!bsd3}
\index{License!3-clause BSD License}
\item[version] 1.2
\item[description] (no language specified) This program can be used to automate the upload of a package to CTAN. The description of the package 
          is contained in a configuration file.

          The provided information is validated in any case. If the validation succeeds and not only the validation 
          is requested, then the provided archive file will be placed in the incoming area of the CTAN for further 
          processing by the CTAN team.

          In any case any finding during the validation is reported at the end of the processing. Note that the 
          validation is the default and an official submission has to be requested by an appropriate command line 
          option.

          \texttt{ctan-o-mat} requires an Internet connection to the CTAN server. Even the validation 
          retrieves the known attributes and the basic constraints from the server.

\index{Package!ctanify}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ctanify}
\item[name] \texttt{ctanify}
\item[caption] Prepare a package for upload to CTAN
\item[author] Pakin, Scott
\index{Author!Pakin, Scott}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.9.1
\item[description] (no language specified) Given a list of filenames, ctanify creates a tarball (a .tar.gz file) with the files laid out in CTAN’s 
          preferred structure.

          By default this tarball additionally contains a ZIP (.zip) file with copies of all files laid out in 
          the standard TeX Directory Structure (TDS), which may be used by those intending to install the package, 
          or by those who need to incorporate it in a distribution. (The TDS ZIP file will be installed in the 
          CTAN  \texttt{install/} tree.)

          Given that CTAN and TeX Live are not fond of .tds.zip files for small and/or otherwise straightforward 
          packages,  \texttt{ctanify} has now been provided with an option that prevents the creation 
          and inclusion of such a .tds.zip file.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ctanify/README}

\section[\texttt{currfile} -- Provide file name and path of input files]{\texttt{currfile} -- Provide file name and path of input files}\label{pkg:currfile}
\index{Package!currfile}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/currfile}
\item[name] \texttt{currfile}
\item[caption] Provide file name and path of input files
\item[author] Scharrer, Martin
\index{Author!Scharrer, Martin}
\item[copyright] Martin Scharrer (2010-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0 (2024-03-14)
\item[last changes] 2024-03-14
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides macros holding file name information (directory, base name, extension, full name 
          and full path) for files read by LaTeX  \texttt{{\textbackslash}input} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}include} macros; 
          it uses the file hooks provided by the author’s \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/filehook}{filehook} . 
          In particular, it restores the parent file name after the trailing \texttt{{\textbackslash}clearpage} of 
          an \texttt{{\textbackslash}include} d file; as a result, the macros may be usefully 
          employed in the page header and footer of the last printed page of such a file.

          The depth of inclusion is made available, together with the ''parent'' (including file) and ''parents'' 
          (all including files to the root of the tree).

          The package supersedes  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fink}{FiNK} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/currfile/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/currfile/currfile.pdf}

          provides a set of commands to create rubrics, entries in these rubrics etc. CurVe then format the CV 
          (possibly splitting it onto multiple pages, repeating the titles etc), which is usually the most painful 
          part of CV writing. Another nice feature of CurVe is its ability to manage different CV ‘flavours’ simultaneously. 
          It is often the case that you want to maintain slightly divergent versions of your CV at the same time, 
          in order to emphasize on different aspects of your background. CurVe also comes with support for use 
          with AUC-TeX.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/curve/README}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package draws curves in the standard LaTeX picture environment using parabolas between data points 
          with continuous slope at joins; for circles and arcs, it uses up to 16 parabolas. The package can also 
          draw symbols or dash patterns along curves.

          The package provides facilities equivalent to technical pens with compasses and French curves. Curves 
          consist of short secants drawn by overlapping disks or line-drawing  \texttt{{\textbackslash}special} commands 
          selected by package options.

\section[\texttt{cvss} -- Compute and display CVSS base scores]{\texttt{cvss} -- Compute and display CVSS base scores}\label{pkg:cvss}
\index{Package!cvss}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cvss}
\item[name] \texttt{cvss}
\item[caption] Compute and display CVSS base scores
\item[author] Vivegnis, Pierre
\index{Author!Vivegnis, Pierre}
\item[copyright] Pierre VIVEGNIS (2022)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.1.0 (2022-12-02)
\item[last changes] 2022-12-02
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) is an open framework for communicating the characteristics 
          and severity of software vulnerabilities. CVSS consists of three metric groups: Base, Temporal, and Environmental.

          This package allows the user to compute CVSS3.1 base scores and use them in documents, i.e. it only deals 
          with the Base score. Temporal and Environental scores will be part of a future release.

          More information can be found at  \href{https://www.first.org/cvss/specification-document}{https://www.first.org/cvss/specification-document} .

\section[\texttt{cweb} -- A Web system in C]{\texttt{cweb} -- A Web system in C}\label{pkg:cweb}
\index{Package!cweb}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cweb}
\item[name] \texttt{cweb}
\item[caption] A Web system in C
\item[author] Scherer, Andreas
\index{Author!Scherer, Andreas}
\item[author] Levy, Silvio
\index{Author!Levy, Silvio}
\item[author] Knuth, Donald E.
\index{Author!Knuth, Donald E.}
\item[copyright] Silvio Levy and Donald E. Knuth (null)
\item[license] knuth = Knuth License (free)
\index{License!knuth}
\index{License!Knuth License}
\item[version] 4.12.2
\item[description] (no language specified) The CWEB system is a system for literate programming, also known as structured software documentation, 
          with code written in the C and C++ languages.

          People have been accumulating several decades of experience with CWEB, and CTANGLE and CWEAVE are known 
          to work reasonably well on numerous platforms. In general those programs are now entirely stable: DEK 
          won't be changing them any more, because they've proved their value in extensive use. (Henceforth he 
          must devote full time to ''The Art of Computer Programming''!)

          However, further significant developments, including versions that DEK himself does not maintain, are 
          ongoing. All of the really current news about CWEB is, in fact, now to be found in the CWEB development 
          project, thanks to the tireless activities of Andreas Scherer.

          The first new release under his auspices incorporates the majority of material from his  \href{https://github.com/ascherer/cwebbin}{CWEBbin 
          project} , namely all the patches accumulated over many years, and all the changes for ANSI-C. What's 
          left in CWEBbin are a few extensions used in TeX Live:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item includes CTWILL and its utilities
          \item internationalization with the ''GNU gettext utilities''
          \item output is only written when different from the former run
          \item new options -l, -i, and -o for CWEAVE and CTWILL
          \item file lookup with the kpathsea library (TeX Live only)
          \end{itemize}
and it provides tools to bundle packages for various target systems.

\item[description] (no language specified) A highly portable and extended version of Levy/Knuth CWEB 3.64c for UNIX, Windows, Mac (and possibly 
          other operating systems). TeX macros, CWEB macros, and NLS catalogs are included for German, French (partially), 
          and Italian program documentation on any machine.

          Major features:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Thoroughly updated code base; several bug fixes; clean compilation (with both C and TeX) on at least four different architectures.
          \item Added CTWILL program with tools and utilities for brave users; including introductory manpage.
          \item Internationalization of CTANGLE, CWEAVE, and CTWILL with ''GNU gettext utilities''.
          \item New code base for CWEB in TeX Live 2019, incorporating all features of the TL 2018 version and adding new features from CWEBbin.
          \end{itemize}

          ''Controls in Contents'', and when you include this package, some notations of compliance are added to 
          section names as seen in the table of contents of the final document.

          It also makes your document more brittle in unexpected ways: for example, when you use  \texttt{cybercic} in 
          the same document as \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} , you cannot use 
          any formatting in your section titles. So don't use \texttt{cybercic} unless you need to.

\section[\texttt{cyklop} -- The Cyclop typeface]{\texttt{cyklop} -- The Cyclop typeface}\label{pkg:cyklop}
\index{Package!cyklop}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/cyklop}
\item[name] \texttt{cyklop}
\item[caption] The Cyclop typeface
\item[author] Nowacki, Janusz Marian
\index{Author!Nowacki, Janusz Marian}
\item[copyright] Janusz M. Nowacki (2008)
\item[license] gfl = The GUST Font License (GFL) (free)
\index{License!gfl}
\index{License!The GUST Font License (GFL)}
\item[version] 0.915
\item[description] (no language specified) The Cyclop typeface was designed in the 1920s at the workshop of Warsaw type foundry ''Odlewnia Czcionek 
          J. Idzkowski i S-ka''. This sans serif typeface has a highly modulated stroke so it has high typographic 
          contrast. The vertical stems are much heavier then horizontal ones. Most characters have thin rectangles 
          as additional counters giving the unique shape of the characters.

          The lead types of Cyclop typeface were produced in slanted variant at sizes 8-48 pt. It was heavily used 
          for heads in newspapers and accidents prints. Typesetters used Cyclop in the inter-war period, during 
          the occupation in the underground press. The typeface was used until the beginnings of the offset print 
          and computer typesetting era. Nowadays it is hard to find the metal types of this typeface.

          The font was generated using the Metatype1 package. Then the original set of characters was completed 
          by adding the full set of accented letters and characters of the modern Latin alphabets (including Vietnamese).

          The upright variant was generated and it was more complicated task than it appeared at the beginning. 
          11 upright letters of the Cyclop typeface were presented in the book by Filip Trzaska, ''Podstawy techniki 
          wydawniczej'' (''Foundation of the publishing techonology''), Warsaw 1967. But even the author of the 
          book does not know what was the source of the presented examples.

          The fonts are distributed in the Type1 and OpenType formats along with the files necessary for use these 
          fonts in TeX and LaTeX including encoding definition files: T1 (ec), T5 (Vietnamese), OT4, QX, texnansi 
          and nonstandard ones (IL2 for Czech fonts).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/cyklop/doc/fonts/cyklop/cyklop-info.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3029777410-cyklop-info.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/cyklop/README}

\section[\texttt{dancers} -- Font for Conan Doyle’s “The Dancing Men”]{\texttt{dancers} -- Font for Conan Doyle’s “The Dancing Men”}\label{pkg:dancers}
\index{Package!dancers}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/dancers}
\item[name] \texttt{dancers}
\item[caption] Font for Conan Doyle’s “The Dancing Men”
\item[author] Stanier, Alan
\index{Author!Stanier, Alan}
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version]  (1995-03-10)
\item[last changes] 1995-03-10
\item[year] 1995
\index{Year!1995}
\item[description] (no language specified) The (Sherlock Holmes) book contains a code which uses dancing men as glyphs.

          The alphabet as given is not complete, lacking f, j, k, q, u, w, x and z, so those letters in the font 
          are not due to Conan Doyle. The code required word endings to be marked by the dancing man representing 
          the last letter to be holding a flag: these are coded as A-Z. thaTiStOsaYsentenceSiNthEcodElooKlikEthiS. 
          In some cases, the man has no arms, making it impossible for him to hold a flag. In these cases, he is 
          wearing a flag on his hat in the ‘character’.

          The font is distributed as Metafont source; it works poorly in modern environments, and could do with 
          expert attention (if you are interested, please contact the CTAN team for details).
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/dancers}
\item[on Mik\TeX] \texttt{dancers}

\section[\texttt{dashrule} -- Draw dashed rules]{\texttt{dashrule} -- Draw dashed rules}\label{pkg:dashrule}
\index{Package!dashrule}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/dashrule}
\item[name] \texttt{dashrule}
\item[caption] Draw dashed rules
\item[author] Pakin, Scott
\index{Author!Pakin, Scott}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.3
\item[description] (no language specified) The dashrule package makes it easy to draw a huge variety of dashed rules (i.e., lines) in LaTeX. dashrule 
          provides a command,  \texttt{{\textbackslash}hdashrule} , which is a cross between 
          LaTeX's {\textbackslash}rule and PostScript's setdash command. \texttt{{\textbackslash}hdashrule} draws 
          horizontally dashed rules using the same syntax as \texttt{{\textbackslash}rule} , 
          but with an additional, setdash-like parameter that specifies the pattern of dash segments and the space 
          between those segments. Because dashrule's rules are constructed internally using \texttt{{\textbackslash}rule} (as 
          opposed to, e.g., PostScript \texttt{{\textbackslash}special} s) they are fully compatible 
          with every LaTeX back-end processor.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/dashrule/README}

\section[\texttt{datatool} -- Tools to load and manipulate data]{\texttt{datatool} -- Tools to load and manipulate data}\label{pkg:datatool}
\index{Package!datatool}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/datatool}
\item[name] \texttt{datatool}
\item[caption] Tools to load and manipulate data
\item[author] Talbot, Nicola
\index{Author!Talbot, Nicola}
\item[copyright] Nicola Talbot (2007-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 3.4 (2025-04-03)
\item[last changes] 2025-04-03
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The tools comprise the packages:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{datatool-base.sty} : the underlying base package used by all the other packages in this bundle;
          \item  \texttt{datatool.sty} : databases may be created using LaTeX commands or by importing external files; they may be sorted numerically or alphabetically; repetitive operations (such as mail merging) may be performed on each row of a database, subject to conditions to exclude particular rows; commands are provided to examine database elements, and to convert formats (for example, to convert a numeric element to a format compatible with l3fp or the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fp}{fp} package;
          \item  \texttt{datapie.sty} : a database may be represented as a pie chart; flexible options allow colouring of the chart, and annotation hooks are available;
          \item  \texttt{dataplot.sty} : a database may be represented as a 2-dimensional scatter or line plot; flexible options control of the plot's overall appearance, and of legends and other extra information;
          \item  \texttt{databar.sty} : a database may be represented as a bar chart; overall appearance, colouring and annotation are controllable;
          \item  \texttt{datagidx.sty} : provides a way of indexing or creating glossaries/lists of abbreviations that uses TeX to do the sorting and collating instead of using an external indexing application, such as \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xindy}{xindy} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/makeindex}{makeindex} (although you may prefer \texttt{{\textbackslash}printnoidxglossary} now provided by the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/glossaries}{glossaries} package);
          \item  \texttt{databib.sty} : a bibliography may be loaded into a datatool database, and manipulated there before being printed (this permits a LaTeX-based route to printing bibliographies in formats for which no BibTeX style is available, although \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/biblatex}{biblatex} is now the better route); and
          \item  \texttt{person.sty} : provides support for displaying a person’s name and pronoun in a document, thus avoiding cumbersome use of ''he/she'', etc.
          \end{itemize}
The drawing packages make use of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{PGF/TikZ} for their 
          output.

          Localisation support needs to be installed separately. See  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datatool-regions}{datatool-regions} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datatool-english}{datatool-english} .

          The bundle supersedes and replaces the author’s  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/csvtools}{csvtools} bundle.

\item[author] Talbot, Nicola

\item[version] 1.1 (2025-03-12)

\item[description] (no language specified) The datatool-english bundle provides English language support for the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datatool}{datatool} package 
          (v3.0+). The \texttt{*.ldf} files should all be placed somewhere on TeX's path.

          These files don't require any explicit loading. They will automatically be input by  \texttt{datatool-base.sty} (or 
          relevant supplementary package) if they are found and required by the tracklang localisation settings. 
          See the datatool v3.0+ and tracklang user manuals for further details.

          The English files provide encoding support for UTF-8 and ISO-8859-1 (Latin 1). Any other encoding will 
          be treated as US-ASCII.

          This bundle also includes limited support for Old English (Anglo-Saxon) mainly to provide an example 
          for a language that has multiple scripts (in this case, Latin and Runic) or for a language that has an 
          extended Latin or non-Latin script. The language codes are ang-Latn for Anglo-Saxon Latin Script and 
          ang-Runr for Anglo-Saxon Runic Script. There's only support for UTF-8 with the Anglo-Saxon files.

\section[\texttt{datepicker-pro} -- Create a popup datepicker using SWF]{\texttt{datepicker-pro} -- Create a popup datepicker using SWF}\label{pkg:datepicker-pro}
\index{Package!datepicker-pro}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/datepicker-pro}
\item[name] \texttt{datepicker-pro}
\item[caption] Create a popup datepicker using SWF
\item[author] Story, Donald P.
\index{Author!Story, Donald P.}
\item[copyright] D. P. Story (2013-2018)
\item[license] lppl1.2 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.2}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2}
\item[version] 1.4 (2020-08-07)
\item[last changes] 2020-08-07
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) One of the (many) deficiencies of Adobe Acrobat Reader/Adobe Acrobat is that they have never supported 
          a proper date picker. This package now supplies one. The  \texttt{{\textbackslash}datepicker} command 
          creates a readonly text field and a push button to its right. Pressing on the pushbutton brings forth 
          an SWF file displaying a calendar. The user then chooses a date from the calendar, and the date is transferred 
          to the text field.

          This is a ''pro'' application, which, in the jargon of AeB, means that Adobe Distiller is required as 
          the PDF creator. The only drivers supported, as a result, are dvips and dvipsone.

          As with all such special features, to experience the datepicker, Adobe Reader or Acrobat are needed. 
          Most other PDF readers do not support form field, rich media annotations, and JavaScript.

          This package has become obsolete as of December 2020. Since December 2020, Adobe no longer supports Flash 
          player (SWF, FLV). This package uses a custom SWF file ( \texttt{datepicker3.swf} , eg); 
          as a result this package will no longer function in Adobe Acrobat Reader DC. The package will continue 
          to produce PDFs as designed, but only if built using Acrobat XI (or a version of Acrobat prior to December 
          2020) and viewed in Adobe Acrobat Reader XI (or a version of Reader prior to December 2020).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/obsolete/macros/latex/contrib/datepicker-pro/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{PDF documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/obsolete/macros/latex/contrib/datepicker-pro/doc/datepickerpro_man.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./9666634699-datepickerpro_man.pdf|

\item[version] 1.3
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a macro,  \texttt{{\textbackslash}dateread} , that can be used 
          to parse date strings, either individually or recursively. The macro expects a human-readable syntax, 
          which it converts into an integer (a ''long date'') that can be more easily used for some types of computation. 
          A set of companion macros and token registers is also provided for converting long dates into human-readable 
          form.

\section[\texttt{datetime2} -- Formats for dates, times and time zones]{\texttt{datetime2} -- Formats for dates, times and time zones}\label{pkg:datetime2}
\index{Package!datetime2}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/datetime2}
\item[name] \texttt{datetime2}
\item[caption] Formats for dates, times and time zones
\item[author] Talbot, Nicola
\index{Author!Talbot, Nicola}
\item[copyright] Nicola Talbot (2015-2021)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.5.7 (2021-03-21)
\item[last changes] 2021-03-21
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides commands for formatting dates, times and time zones and redefines  \texttt{{\textbackslash}today} to 
          use the same formatting style. In addition to \texttt{{\textbackslash}today} , you 
          can also use \texttt{{\textbackslash}DTMcurrenttime} (current time) or \texttt{{\textbackslash}DTMnow} (current 
          date and time). Dates and times can be saved for later use.

          The accompanying  \texttt{datetime2-calc} package can be used to convert date-times to UTC+00:00.

          Language and regional support is provided by independently maintained and installed modules.

          The  \texttt{datetime2-calc} package uses the \texttt{pgfcalendar} package (part 
          of the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{PGF/TikZ} bundle).

          This package replaces  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datetime}{datetime.sty} which is now 
          obsolete.

\index{License!lppl1.3}

\item[version] 1.0 (2015-04-01)
\item[last changes] 2015-04-01
\item[year] 2015
\index{Year!2015}
\item[description] (no language specified) English date and time styles that use words for the numbers and ordinals.

          This package provides the following date and time styles: ''en-fulltext'', ''en-FullText'', ''en-FULLTEXT'', 
          and the additional time style ''en-Fulltext''. (The date equivalent can be obtained through commands 
          like  \texttt{{\textbackslash}Today} .)

          Unlike the base styles provided by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datetime2}{datetime2.sty} , 
          these styles aren't expandable styles. This means that you can't use the date or time in PDF bookmarks 
          or in the argument of certain commands, such as \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeUppercase} , 
          while these styles are in use.

\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.05 (2019-10-21)
\item[last changes] 2019-10-21
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) This module provides the following styles that can be set using  \texttt{{\textbackslash}DTMsetstyle} provided 
          by \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datetime2}{datetime2.sty} . The region not only determines 
          the date/time format but also the time zone abbreviations if the zone mapping setting is on.

          \begin{itemize}
          \item english (English – no region)
          \item en-GB (English – United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland)
          \item en-US (English – United States of America)
          \item en-CA (English – Canada)
          \item en-AU (English – Commonwealth of Australia)
          \item en-NZ (English – New Zealand)
          \item en-GG (English – Bailiwick of Guernsey)
          \item en-JE (English – Bailiwick of Jersey)
          \item en-IM (English – Isle of Man)
          \item en-MT (English – Republic of Malta)
          \item en-IE (English – Republic of Ireland)
          \end{itemize}

\item[description] (no language specified) De-macro is a Python script that helps authors who like to use private LaTeX macros (for example, as 
          abbreviations). A technical editor or a cooperating author may balk at such a manuscript; you can avoid 
          manuscript rejection misery by running de-macro on it.

          De-macro will expand macros defined in  \texttt{{\textbackslash}(re)newcommand} or \texttt{{\textbackslash}(re)newenvironment} commands,

\section[\texttt{decision-table} -- An easy way to create Decision Model and Notation decision t\ldots]{\texttt{decision-table} -- An easy way to create Decision Model and Notation decision tables}\label{pkg:decision-table}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/decision-table}
\item[name] \texttt{decision-table}
\item[caption] An easy way to create Decision Model and Notation decision tables
\item[author] Pantigny, François
\index{Author!Pantigny, François}
\item[author] Vandevelde, Simon
\index{Author!Vandevelde, Simon}
\item[copyright] Simon Vandevelde, Francois Pantigny (2020-2021)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.0.4 (2021-10-01)
\item[last changes] 2021-10-01
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) The decision-table package allows for an easy way to generate decision tables in the Decision Model and 
          Notation (DMN) format. This package ensures consistency in the tables (i.e. fontsize), and is thus a 
          better alternative to inserting tables via images.

          The decision-table package adds the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}dmntable} command, with 
          which tables can be created. This command expands into a tabular, so it can be used within a table or 
          figure environment. Furthermore, this allows labels and captions to be added seamlessly. It is also possible 
          to place multiple DMN tables in one table/figure environment.

          The package relies on  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/nicematrix}{nicematrix} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/l3keys2e}{l3keys2e} .

\item[author] Burleson, Neil

\index{License!noinfo}
\index{License!noinfo}
\item[version]  (1990-06-01)
\item[last changes] 1990-06-01
\item[year] 1990
\index{Year!1990}
\item[description] (no language specified) These macros provide a method of locally allocating registers without interference with previously allocated 
          registers; thus  \texttt{{\textbackslash}declarecount} allocates a count for local 
          use, in exactly the same way that \texttt{{\textbackslash}newcount} allocations one 
          for global use. The sequence

          \begin{verbatim}
{... \declarecount\foo ... \newcount\bar ...}
          \end{verbatim}
is of course a logical error; any  \texttt{{\textbackslash}new*} command should be 
          issued before the corresponding \texttt{{\textbackslash}declare*} command.

\section[\texttt{delig} -- Disable misplaced ligatures in LaTeX documents]{\texttt{delig} -- Disable misplaced ligatures in LaTeX documents}\label{pkg:delig}
\index{Package!delig}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/delig}
\item[name] \texttt{delig}
\item[caption] Disable misplaced ligatures in LaTeX documents
\item[author] Warner, Daniel
\index{Author!Warner, Daniel}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version]  (2008-03-12)
\item[last changes] 2008-03-12
\item[year] 2008
\index{Year!2008}
\item[description] (no language specified) DeLig disables misplaced ligatures in LaTeX documents, using a dictionary approach.

          With its original fonts, LaTeX always uses ligatures for the letter combinations ''ff'', ''fi'', ''fl'', 
          ''ffi'' and ''ffl''.

          This is not always correct in the German language, e.g., the word ''Auflage'' may not be printed with 
          an ''fl''-ligature, that is, the ''fl''-ligature in ''Auflage'' must be disabled.

          This may be accomplished by using the babel-package and the two symbols  \texttt{|"} : \texttt{Auf"lage} .

          The Java program DeLig does this job automatically for you, using a ligature word list. Please note that 
          DeLig is only as good as the ligature word list file DeLig.list it relies on.

          This version is intended for German language texts only.

          DeLig is partially based on the Perl script  \texttt{rmligs} by Björn Jacke, in particular 
          the wordlist data is based on his \texttt{igerman98} dictionary.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/delig/README}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/delig}

\index{Topic!typesetting}
\item[keyword] \texttt{german} (support for typesetting German)
\index{Topic!german}
\item[language(s)] no language specified
\index{Language in description/documentation!no language specified}

\section[\texttt{derivative} -- Nice and easy derivatives]{\texttt{derivative} -- Nice and easy derivatives}\label{pkg:derivative}
\index{Package!derivative}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/derivative}
\item[name] \texttt{derivative}
\item[caption] Nice and easy derivatives
\item[author] Jensen, Simon
\index{Author!Jensen, Simon}
\item[copyright] Simon Jensen (2019-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.4 (2024-02-08)
\item[last changes] 2024-02-08
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) Typesetting derivatives and differentials in a consistent way are clumsy and require care to ensure the 
          preferred formatting. Several packages have been developed for this purpose, each with its own features 
          and drawbacks, with the most ambitious one being diffcoeff. While this package is comparable to diffcoeff 
          in terms of features, it takes a different approach. One difference is this package provides more options 
          to tweak the format of the derivatives and differentials. However, the automatic calculation of the total 
          order isn't as developed as the one in diffcoeff.

          This package makes it easy to write derivatives and differentials consistently with its predefined commands. 
          It also provides a set of commands that can define custom derivatives and differential operators. The 
          options follow a consistent naming scheme making them easy to use and understand.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/derivative/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/derivative/derivative.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./5143224048-derivative.pdf|
\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{https://github.com/sjelatex/derivative}
\index{Contact!repository}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/derivative}

\item[version]  (1999-05-12)
\item[last changes] 1999-05-12
\item[year] 1999
\index{Year!1999}
\item[description] (no language specified) Detex is a program to remove TeX constructs from a text file. It recognizes the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}input} command.

          The program assumes it is dealing with LaTeX input if it sees the string  \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}document{\textbraceright}} in 
          the text. In this case, it also recognizes the \texttt{{\textbackslash}include} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}includeonly} commands.

          The author now considers this program to be ''retired'' and Piotr Kubowicz’s  \href{https://github.com/pkubowicz/opendetex/}{OpenDetex} as 
          its successor.

\item[last changes] 2018-07-22
\item[year] 2018
\index{Year!2018}
\item[description] (no language specified) Initally a logbook for me, a person with type one diabetes mellitus, this evolved over time into a TeX 
          project, making it prettier and/or easier to use. I’ve made it simple to use, while not forgoing the 
          document’s beauty or the speed of input. The logbook, with slight commenting out and editing, could be 
          used as a journal by anybody, although the template and graphing functionality are set up for people 
          using insulin injections and blood glucose teststrips, as well as counting/estimating carbs, protein, 
          and fat.

          Note: The names of the package’s files are not constructed using the long ''diabetes-logbook'', but the 
          acronym ''dmlb'' (for ''diabetes mellitus log book'').

\item[version] 1.1 (2015-05-20)
\item[last changes] 2015-05-20
\item[year] 2015
\index{Year!2015}
\item[description] (no language specified) The diadia package allows you to keep a diabetes diary. Usually, this means keeping record of certain 
          medical values like blood sugar, blood pressure, pulse or weight. It might also include other medical, 
          pharmaceutical or nutritional data (HbA1c, insulin doses, carbohydrate units). The diadia package supports 
          all of this plus more - simply by adding more columns to the data file! It is able to evaluate the data 
          file and typesets formatted tables and derived plots. Furthermore, it supports medication charts and 
          info boxes.

          Supported languages: English, German. Feel free to provide other translation files!

          available from the package home page.

          Books included are:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item ''LaTeX for Complete Novices'': an introductory guide to LaTeX.
          \item ''Using LaTeX to Write a PhD Thesis'': a follow-on from ''LaTeX for Complete Novices'' geared towards students who want to use LaTeX to write their PhD thesis.
          \item ''Creating a LaTeX minimal example'': describes how to create a minimal example, which can be used as a debugging aid when you encounter errors in your LaTeX documents.
          \end{itemize}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides macros and environments useful for writing teaching material. It provides more 
          semantic environments on top of the standard  \texttt{definition} , \texttt{theorem} , 
          and friends: for instance, \texttt{exercise} , \texttt{activity} and \texttt{question} . 
          These are suitably colour-coded when used with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer}{Beamer} . 
          They occur as ''normal'' text in handouts produced by \texttt{beamerarticle} (same style 
          as \texttt{definition} usually has).

          It also provides macros for typesetting code listings and output side by side.

          Finally, it modifies the appearance of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer}{beamer} ( \texttt{Berlin} -based 
          theme) and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/memoir}{memoir} (Tufte style layout), if loaded. 
          It is designed to be used with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer}{beamer} to produce 
          slides and \texttt{beamerarticle} with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/memoir}{memoir} to 
          produce notes and handouts from the same source.

\section[\texttt{diffcoeff} -- Write differential coefficients easily and consistently]{\texttt{diffcoeff} -- Write differential coefficients easily and consistently}\label{pkg:diffcoeff}
\index{Package!diffcoeff}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/diffcoeff}
\item[name] \texttt{diffcoeff}
\item[caption] Write differential coefficients easily and consistently
\item[author] Parsloe, Andrew
\index{Author!Parsloe, Andrew}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 5.6 (2025-12-19)
\item[last changes] 2025-12-19
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package allows the easy and consistent writing of ordinary, partial and other derivatives of arbitrary 
          (algebraic or numeric) order. For mixed partial derivatives, the total order of differentiation is calculated 
          by the package. Optional arguments allow specification of points of evaluation (ordinary derivatives), 
          or variables held constant (partial derivatives), and the placement of the differentiand (numerator or 
          appended).

          The package is built on  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xtemplate}{xtemplate} and the configurability 
          it enables, extending to differentials (including simple line elements) and jacobians.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/diffcoeff/diffcoeff.pdf}

\section[\texttt{dirtreex} -- Directory tree rendering for LaTeX with TikZ]{\texttt{dirtreex} -- Directory tree rendering for LaTeX with TikZ}\label{pkg:dirtreex}
\index{Package!dirtreex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/dirtreex}
\item[name] \texttt{dirtreex}
\item[caption] Directory tree rendering for LaTeX with TikZ
\item[author] CloudCauldron
\index{Author!CloudCauldron}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0 (2026-04-26)
\item[last changes] 2026-04-26
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a self-contained tool for rendering directory trees in an optionally breakable, 
          fully styleable frame. Built directly on TikZ and zref, it works natively without requiring tcolorbox, 
          dirtree, shell escape, or external scripts.

          Its main features include automatically tracked depth, so that  \texttt{{\textbackslash}dir} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}file} commands 
          can be nested naturally; breakable frames whose borders, background, and vertical connection lines continue 
          across page boundaries; extensive customization with per-tree and per-entry settings for line colors, 
          line widths, and elbow radii; and CJK-friendly operation with ctex and LuaTeX.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/dirtreex/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Examples of use}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/dirtreex/dirtreex_examples.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./6633203701-dirtreex_examples.pdf|

\item[description] (no language specified) This bundle, which provides a number of tools and libraries by Dirk Krause, is no longer available on 
          CTAN. It is now available only at  \href{https://sourceforge.net/project/dktools}{its SourceForge 
          project page} .

          The project does not contain any LaTeX packages, but source code to build executable programs. During 
          the last years, many programs unrelated to LaTeX have been added. Therefore, the CTAN is no longer a 
          suitable place to host the entire project.

          The programs related to LaTeX are:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{wxdkdraw} : Minimalistic drawing program for use with LaTeX
          \item  \texttt{wxd2lat} : Convert wxdkdraw drawings to PDF+TeX, EPS+TeX, TeX (PGF)
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bmpp}{bmpp} : Convert PNG, JPEG, TIFF to PDF, PS, EPS
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fig2lat}{fig2lat} : Convert *.fig to PS(+TeX), PDF(+TeX), PGF
          \item  \texttt{dk-t2l} : Convert plain text to LaTeX
          \item  \texttt{plpdftex} : Output driver for \texttt{octpgfpl} to produce PDF+TeX
          \end{itemize}
\item[home page] \url{https://sourceforge.net/projects/dktools/}

\item[last changes] 2010-03-04
\item[year] 2010
\index{Year!2010}
\item[description] (no language specified) The bundle contains various macros either used for creating the author’s book ''Introduktion til LaTeX'' 
          (in Danish), or presented in the book as code tips.

          The bundle comprises:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item dlfltxbcodetips: various macros helpful in typesetting mathematics;
          \item dlfltxbmarkup: provides macros used throughout, for registering macro names, packages etc. in the text, in the margin and in the index, all by using categorised keys (note, a configuration file may be used; a sample is included in the distribution);
          \item dlfltxbtocconfig: macros for the two tables of contents that the book has;
          \item dlfltxbmisc: various macros for typesetting LaTeX arguments, and the macro used in the bibliography that can wrap a URL up into a BibTeX entry.
          \end{itemize}
Interested parties may review the book itself on the web at  \href{http://www.imf.au.dk/system/latex/bog/}{the 
          author’s institution} (it is written in Danish).

          22 color-coded record type commands (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, TXT, SOA, PTR, SRV, CAA, DNSKEY, DS, RRSIG, 
          NSEC, NSEC3, TLSA, HTTPS, SVCB, SPF, DKIM, DMARC), seven environments for zone file tables, propagation

\section[\texttt{do-it-yourself-tex} -- Back to Plain XeTeX]{\texttt{do-it-yourself-tex} -- Back to Plain XeTeX}\label{pkg:do-it-yourself-tex}
\index{Package!do-it-yourself-tex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/do-it-yourself-tex}
\item[name] \texttt{do-it-yourself-tex}
\item[caption] Back to Plain XeTeX
\item[author] Herz-Fischler, Roger
\index{Author!Herz-Fischler, Roger}
\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[version] 1.3 (2019-03-17)
\item[last changes] 2019-03-17
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a collection of easily modifiable forms, macros and sample texts for use with plain 
          TeX/XeTeX.

          Plain TeX, as demonstrated by the myriad of articles and books dating from before the advent of LaTeX, 
          is capable of producing fine typography. It has the advantage of not being as obscure as far as macros, 
          font designation etc. are concerned, and this package is intended to be another contribution to the repertoire 
          in terms of macros, forms and examples.

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xetex}{XeTeX} , which works without the necessity of further 
          manipulation of classical TeX documents, has the further advantage of understanding Unicode, for which 
          many open source fonts are available. In additon, \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xetex}{XeTeX} ’s 
          immediate output is an extended variant of DVI format, which is ordinarily processed by a tightly bound 
          processor (called \texttt{xdvipdfmx} ) that produces PDF, i.e. if you type: \texttt{xetex 
          file\_01.tex} , you obtain: \texttt{file\_01.pdf} .

          This package provides easily modifiable forms and macros which illustrate how plain XeTeX can be used 
          to produce high quality texts with such features as precise font designations, imported images, marginal 
          notes, colour, right to left texts and syllabics. Real examples are provided in both the TeX and PDF 
          versions. A set of shell files, font tables, and an HTML page with links to font sources are also provided.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/xetex/plain/do-it-yourself-tex/do-it-yourself-tex.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./2348651553-do-it-yourself-tex.pdf|

\item[description] (no language specified) Domain coloring is a technique to visualize complex functions by assigning a color to each point of the 
          complex plane  \emph{z} = \emph{x} +i \emph{y} .

          This package calculates with the help of Lua any complex function to visualize its behaviour. The value 
          of the complex function( \emph{z} ) can be described by radius and angle which can be two 
          values of the hsv-color model, which then defines the color of each point in the complex plane \emph{z} = \emph{x} +i \emph{y} .

\section[\texttt{dosepsbin} -- Deal with DOS binary EPS files]{\texttt{dosepsbin} -- Deal with DOS binary EPS files}\label{pkg:dosepsbin}
\index{Package!dosepsbin}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/dosepsbin}
\item[name] \texttt{dosepsbin}
\item[caption] Deal with DOS binary EPS files
\item[author] Oberdiek, Heiko
\index{Author!Oberdiek, Heiko}
\item[copyright] Heiko Oberdiek (2011)
\item[license] artistic = Perl Artistic License (not free)
\index{License!artistic}
\index{License!Perl Artistic License}
\item[version] 1.2
\item[description] (no language specified) A Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) file may given in a special binary format to support the inclusion of 
          a thumbnail. This file format, commonly known as  \emph{DOS EPS} format starts with a binary 
          header that contains the positions of the possible sections:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item PostScript (PS);
          \item Windows Metafile Format (WMF); and
          \item Tag Image File Format (TIFF).
          \end{itemize}
The PS section must be present and either the WMF file or the TIFF file should be given.

          The package provides a Perl program that will extract any of the sections of such a file, in particular 
          providing a ‘text’-form EPS file for use with (La)TeX.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation (PDF format)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/dosepsbin/dosepsbin.pdf}

\section[\texttt{dot2tex} -- Convert graphs generated by Graphviz to LaTeX friendly forma\ldots]{\texttt{dot2tex} -- Convert graphs generated by Graphviz to LaTeX friendly formats}\label{pkg:dot2tex}
\index{Package!dot2tex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/dot2tex}
