\section[\texttt{latino-sine-flexione} -- LaTeX support for documents written in Peano’s Interlingua]{\texttt{latino-sine-flexione} -- LaTeX support for documents written in Peano’s Interlingua}\label{pkg:latino-sine-flexione}
\index{Package!latino-sine-flexione}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/latino-sine-flexione}
\item[name] \texttt{latino-sine-flexione}
\item[caption] LaTeX support for documents written in Peano’s Interlingua
\item[author] Leve, Victore
\index{Author!Leve, Victore}
\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[version] 1.2
\item[description] (no language specified) \textbf{Latino sine Flexione} (or Interlingua) is a language constructed by Giuseppe Peano 
          at the beginning of the last century. This simplified Latin is designed to be an instrument for international 
          cooperation, especially in the academic sphere. (Note that this ''Interlingua'' is different from the 
          ''Interlingua'' that was created a few decades after Peano’s work and which is supported by \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel-interlingua}{babel-interlingua} !)

          This package provides the necessary translations to use the language within a LaTeX document. It also 
          imports  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontenc}{fontenc} in order to be able to use ligatures 
          and quotation marks.

          Finally, it offers a text in Interlingua that can be used as a dummy text:  \emph{Fundamento de 
          intelligentia} . This article by H. Bijlsma was first published in \emph{Schola et Vita} Anno 
          I (1926).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/latino-sine-flexione/README.md}
\item[contact] \textit{support}: \url{http://reddit.com/r/LatinoSineFlexione/}
\index{Contact!support}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/latino-sine-flexione}
\item[on Mik\TeX] \texttt{latino-sine-flexione}
\item[on \TeX Live] \texttt{latino-sine-flexione}

\item[description] (no language specified) This little package serves the purpose of providing a uniform method to use lowercased small capitals 
          and spaced lowercased small capitals.

          It relies on the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/iftex}{iftex} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/textcase}{textcase} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/microtype}{microtype} packages and comes with four new 
          user macros: \texttt{{\textbackslash}textlcc} , the main feature: lowercased small 
          capitals; \texttt{{\textbackslash}spacedcaps} , a prefix to small capitals text commands 
          to slightly increase their spacing; \texttt{{\textbackslash}textslcc} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}textssc} , 
          which are shortcuts for \texttt{{\textbackslash}spacedcaps{\textbackslash}textlcc} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}spacedcaps{\textbackslash}textsc} (accordingly).

\section[\texttt{lcdf-typetools} -- A bundle of outline font manipulation tools]{\texttt{lcdf-typetools} -- A bundle of outline font manipulation tools}\label{pkg:lcdf-typetools}
\index{Package!lcdf-typetools}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lcdf-typetools}
\item[name] \texttt{LCDF-typetools}
\item[caption] A bundle of outline font manipulation tools
\item[author] Kohler, Eddie
\index{Author!Kohler, Eddie}
\item[copyright] Eddie Kohler (1997-2006)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[description] (no language specified) This bundle of tools comprises:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Cfftot1, which translates a Compact Font Format (CFF) font, or a PostScript-flavored OpenType font, into PostScript Type 1 format. It correctly handles subroutines and hints;
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mmafm}{Mmafm} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mmpfb}{mmpfb} , which create instances of multiple-master fonts (mmafm and mmpfb were previously distributed in their own package, mminstance);
          \item Otfinfo, which reports information about OpenType fonts, such as the features they support and the contents of their ‘size’ optical size features;
          \item Otftotfm, which creates TeX font metrics and encodings that correspond to a PostScript-flavored OpenType font. It will interpret glyph positionings, substitutions, and ligatures as far as it is able. You can say which OpenType features should be activated;
          \item T1dotlessj, creates a Type 1 font whose only character is a dotless j matching the input font’s design;
          \item T1lint, which checks a Type 1 font for correctness;
          \item T1reencode, which replaces a font’s internal encoding with one you specify; and
          \item T1testpage, which creates a PostScript proof for a Type 1 font. It is preliminary software.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/utilities/lcdf-typetools/README}
\item[home page] \url{http://www.lcdf.org/type/}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/utilities/lcdf-typetools}
\item[on Mik\TeX] \texttt{miktex-lcdf-typetools-bin-2.9}
\item[on \TeX Live] \texttt{lcdftypetools}

\section[\texttt{lecturer} -- On-screen presentations for (almost) all formats]{\texttt{lecturer} -- On-screen presentations for (almost) all formats}\label{pkg:lecturer}
\index{Package!lecturer}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lecturer}
\item[name] \texttt{lecturer}
\item[caption] On-screen presentations for (almost) all formats
\item[author] Isambert, Paul
\index{Author!Isambert, Paul}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version]  (2011-09-11)
\item[last changes] 2011-09-11
\item[year] 2011
\index{Year!2011}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package creates slides for on-screen presentations based on PDF features without manipulating TeX’s 
          typesetting process. The presentation flow relies on PDF’s abilities to display content step by step.

          Features include:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Free positioning of anything anywhere in painted areas on the slide, as well as in the main textblock;
          \item Numerous attributes to control the layout and the presentation flow, from TeX's primitive dimensions to the visibility of steps;
          \item Feature inheritance from global to local settings, with intermediate types;
          \item Basic drawing facilities to produce symbols, e.g., for list items or buttons;
          \item Colours, transparency, shades, and pictures;
          \item Navigation with links, pop-up menus, and customizable bookmarks;
          \item Easy switch between presentation and handout; and
          \item PDF transitions.
          \end{itemize}
Besides the traditional documentation, the distribution includes visual documentation and six demo presentations 
          ranging from geometric abstraction to classic style to silly video game.

          Lecturer is designed to work with all formats, but presently fails with ConTeXt MkIV (because of clashes 
          in management of PDF objects, probably), works only with pdfTeX and LuaTeX for the time being, and requires 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texapi}{texapi} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/yax}{yax} , 
          both v.1.02.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Visual package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/lecturer/doc/LecturerDemo-VisualDoc.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package is a LaTeX implementation of the business letter formatting that is used at Leiden University, 
          using the institute graphic identity as specified on  \href{https://www.leidenuniv.nl}{www.leidenuniv.nl} .

          The LEIletter class is an extension of the standard  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/koma-script}{KOMA-script} letter 
          class \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/scrlttr2}{scrlttr2} . It is intended to be used for 
          writing business letters. It is compliant to the house style and allows for using windowed envelopes 
          of the DL format, with right-aligned window.

          The class requires and uses the following packages that are part of most modern LaTeX distributions: 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphicx}{graphicx} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ifthen}{ifthen} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/array}{array} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ragged2e}{ragged2e} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/textcase}{textcase} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/microtype}{microtype} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/scrlayer-scrpage}{scrlayer-scrpage} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/geometry}{geometry} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/setspace}{setspace} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lipsum}{lipsum} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/minionpro}{minionpro} .

          The package relies on the Minion Pro fonts from Adobe, which are commercial but easily available.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/leiletter/LEIletter.pdf}

\section[\texttt{leporello} -- A simple LaTeX document class to create folded leaflets usin\ldots]{\texttt{leporello} -- A simple LaTeX document class to create folded leaflets using columns and boxes}\label{pkg:leporello}
\index{Package!leporello}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/leporello}
\item[name] \texttt{leporello}
\item[caption] A simple LaTeX document class to create folded leaflets using columns and boxes
\item[author] Habicht, Jasper
\index{Author!Habicht, Jasper}
\item[copyright] Jasper Habicht (2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0.3 (2025-09-15)
\item[last changes] 2025-09-15
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) A simple LaTeX document class to create folded leaflets with the following key features:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item The document layout consists of a specific number of pages that can have varying widths and are placed next to each other. Each page contains one frame to contain typeset material.
          \item Material is typeset in boxes, and boxes are positioned in columns which in turn are placed into the frames on the pages of the document.
          \item Columns are predefined and then placed into the frame of a page in the document layout. This way, columns can be used on pages with varying widths.
          \item Boxes can have padding (including bleed) and a background and are positioned inside a column.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/leporello/leporello-doc.pdf}

\section[\texttt{letgut} -- Class for the newsletter “La Lettre GUTenberg” of the French\ldots]{\texttt{letgut} -- Class for the newsletter “La Lettre GUTenberg” of the French TeX User Group GUTenberg}\label{pkg:letgut}
\index{Package!letgut}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/letgut}
\item[name] \texttt{letgut}
\item[caption] Class for the newsletter “La Lettre GUTenberg” of the French TeX User Group GUTenberg
\item[author] Association GUTenberg
\index{Author!Association GUTenberg}
\item[copyright] Association GUTenberg (1994-2026)
\item[copyright] Denis Bitouzé (2022)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.9.14 (2026-02-16)
\item[last changes] 2026-02-16
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) The French TeX User Group GUTenberg has been publishing ''The GUTenberg Letter'', its irregular newsletter, 
          since February 1993.

          For this purpose, a dedicated, in-house (La)TeX class was gradually created but, depending on new needs 
          and on the people who were publishing the Newsletter, its development was somewhat erratic; in particular, 
          it would not have been possible to publish its code as it was. In addition, its documentation was non-existent.

          The Board of Directors of the association, elected in November 2020, wished to provide a better structured, 
          more perennial and documented class, able to be published on the CTAN. This is now done with the present 
          ‘letgut’ class.

          \# French

          L’association GUTenberg publie ''La Lettre GUTenberg'', son bulletin irrégulomestriel, depuis février 
          1993.

          Pour ce faire, une classe (La)TeX dédiée, maison, a peu à peu vu le jour mais, au gré des nouveaux besoins 
          et des personnes qui ont assuré la publication de la Lettre, son développement a été quelque peu erratique 
          ; il n’aurait notamment pas été possible de publier son code en l’état. En outre, sa documentation était 
          inexistante.

          Le Conseil d’Administration de l’association, élu en novembre 2020, a souhaité fournir une classe mieux 
          structurée, davantage pérenne et documentée, à même d’être publiée sur le CTAN. C’est désormais chose 
          faite avec la présente classe  \texttt{letgut} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/letgut/README.md}

\section[\texttt{lh} -- Cyrillic fonts that support LaTeX standard encodings]{\texttt{lh} -- Cyrillic fonts that support LaTeX standard encodings}\label{pkg:lh}
\index{Package!lh}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lh}
\item[name] \texttt{lh}
\item[caption] Cyrillic fonts that support LaTeX standard encodings
\item[author] Khodulev, Andrey
\index{Author!Khodulev, Andrey}
\item[author] Lapko, Olga
\index{Author!Lapko, Olga}
\item[author] Berdnikov, Alexander
\index{Author!Berdnikov, Alexander}
\item[author] Volovich, Vladimir
\index{Author!Volovich, Vladimir}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 3.5g
\item[description] (no language specified) The LH fonts address the problem of the wide variety of alphabets that are written with Cyrillic-style 
          characters. The fonts are the original basis of the set of T2* and X2 encodings that are now used when 
          LaTeX users need to write in Cyrillic languages.

          Macro support in standard LaTeX encodings is offered through the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latex-cyrillic}{latex-cyrillic} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/t2}{t2} bundles, 
          and the package itself offers support for other (more traditional) encodings.

          The fonts, in the standard T2* and X2 encodings are available in Adobe Type 1 format, in the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cm-super}{CM-Super} family 
          of fonts.

          The package also offers its own LaTeX support for OT2 encoded fonts,  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cmbright}{CM 
          bright shaped fonts} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/concrete}{Concrete shaped fonts} .

\item[description] (no language specified) A collection of three LaTeX 2e styles intended for typesetting Russian and bilingual English-Russian 
          documents, using the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lh}{lh} fonts and without the benefit 
          of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel's} language-switching mechanisms.

          The packages (lhcyralt and lhcyrwin for use under  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/emtex}{emTeX} , 
          and lhcyrkoi for use under \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tetex}{teTeX} ) provide mappings 
          between the input encoding and the font encoding (which is described as OT1). The way this is done does \emph{not} match 
          the way \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/inputenc}{inputenc} would do the job, for output via \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontenc}{fontenc} to 
          one of the T2 series of font encodings.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides the Libertine and Biolinum fonts in both Type 1 and OTF styles, together with support 
          macros for their use. Monospaced and display fonts, and the ''keyboard'' set are also included, in OTF 
          style, only.

          The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mweights}{mweights} package is used to manage the selection 
          of font weights.

          The package supersedes both the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertineotf}{libertineotf} and 
          the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertine-legacy}{libertine-legacy} packages.

\section[\texttt{libertine-legacy} -- Linux Libertine fonts for (La)TeX and pdf(La)TeX users]{\texttt{libertine-legacy} -- Linux Libertine fonts for (La)TeX and pdf(La)TeX users}\label{pkg:libertine-legacy}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertine-legacy}
\item[name] \texttt{libertine-legacy}
\item[caption] Linux Libertine fonts for (La)TeX and pdf(La)TeX users
\item[author] Niedermair, Michael
\index{Author!Niedermair, Michael}
\item[author] Tennent, Bob
\index{Author!Tennent, Bob}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version]  (2011-12-30)
\item[last changes] 2011-12-30
\item[year] 2011
\index{Year!2011}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides support for (traditional-)TeX-based users of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertineotf}{libertine} bundle, 
          who were left isolated when that bundle switched to OTF-only form on 2012-12-11 (thus only, now, supporting 
          XeTeX and LuaTeX users).

          To prevent confusion with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertineotf}{libertine ‘original’} , 
          there are no OTF fonts in the present package.

          Note that the package is now deemed obsolete; the unified  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertine}{libertine} package 
          serves its purpose.

\section[\texttt{libertinus-fonts} -- The Libertinus font family]{\texttt{libertinus-fonts} -- The Libertinus font family}\label{pkg:libertinus-fonts}

\index{Author!Maclennan, Caleb}
\item[author] Hosny, Khaled
\index{Author!Hosny, Khaled}
\item[copyright] The Libertinus Project Authors (2012-2021)
\item[copyright] Philipp H. Poll (2003–2012)

\item[version] 7.051 (2024-09-27)
\item[last changes] 2024-09-27
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) This is a fork of the Linux Libertine and Linux Biolinum fonts that started as an OpenType math companion 
          of the Libertine font family, but grown as a full fork to address some of the bugs in the fonts.

          The family consists of:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Libertinus Serif: forked from Linux Libertine.
          \item Libertinus Sans: forked from Linux Biolinum.
          \item Libertinus Mono: forked from Linux Libertine Mono.
          \item Libertinus Math: an OpenType math font for use in OpenType math-capable applications like LuaTeX, XeTeX or MS Word 2007+.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Math font samples}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/libertinus-fonts/documentation/Math-Sample.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package allows LaTeX users (especially if using traditional LaTeX/pdfLaTeX) to set the Greek letters 
          in math mode using the glyphs from the Libertinus Serif or Sans font via the font support files provided 
          by Bob Tennent’s  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertinus-type1}{libertinus-type1} package. 
          All Greek letters are defined both in \texttt{{\textbackslash}…up} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}…it} variants. 
          The style (ISO, TeX, or French i.e. upright) can be modified midway in the document. A ''legacy'' mode 
          uses font support from the (obsolete) \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/libertine-legacy}{libertine-legacy} package 
          which maps to the Linux Libertine or Biolinum fonts.

          This package is for users who only want to customize Greek letters in math mode.

\section[\texttt{librarian} -- Tools to create bibliographies in TeX]{\texttt{librarian} -- Tools to create bibliographies in TeX}\label{pkg:librarian}
\index{Package!librarian}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/librarian}
\item[name] \texttt{librarian}
\item[caption] Tools to create bibliographies in TeX
\item[author] Isambert, Paul
\index{Author!Isambert, Paul}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The package extracts information in bib files, makes it available in the current document, and sorts 
          lists of entries according to that information and the user’s specifications. Citation and bibliography 
          styles can then be written directly in TeX, without any use of BibTeX. Creating references thus depends 
          entirely on the user's skill in TeX.

          The package works with all formats that use plain TeX’s basic syntactic sugar; the distribution includes 
          a third-party file for ConTeXt and a style file for LaTeX.

          As an example of use, an Author (Year) style is given in a separate file and explained in the documentation.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/librarian/README}

\section[\texttt{liederbuch} -- A LaTeX package for storing songs or other content, and repe\ldots]{\texttt{liederbuch} -- A LaTeX package for storing songs or other content, and repeated reuse in documents}\label{pkg:liederbuch}
\index{Package!liederbuch}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/liederbuch}
\item[name] \texttt{liederbuch}
\item[caption] A LaTeX package for storing songs or other content, and repeated reuse in documents
\item[author] Ruprecht, Gabriel
\index{Author!Ruprecht, Gabriel}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.1.0 (2025-01-20)
\item[last changes] 2025-01-20
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package is meant for content which you reuse regularly, like songs in small booklets. For example 
          the booklets used at church, weddings or similar events. It has two major parts:

          \begin{enumerate}
          \item You typeset your content once (most likely a song), garnish it with some meta data and put it into a sty-file. From there you can insert this content into your document with one single line. The inserted content can have header and footer that use the meta data (i.e. title, composer, lyricist).
          \item Inside these content fragments, you can use the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}notenzeile} (stave line) command to combine an image of a stave line with song lyrics. If correctly used, the lyrics are placed correctly below the notes and need most often no or only minor adjustments. With that you can combine any stave image with LaTeX fonts.
          \end{enumerate}
You can find resources and inspiration in a demo project.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/liederbuch/liederbuch-documentation.pdf}

\section[\texttt{light-latex-make} -- llmk: A build tool for LaTeX documents]{\texttt{light-latex-make} -- llmk: A build tool for LaTeX documents}\label{pkg:light-latex-make}
\index{Package!light-latex-make}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/light-latex-make}
\item[Alias] \texttt{llmk}
\index{Package!llmk (alias for light-latex-make)}
\index{Alias!llmk (for light-latex-make)}
\item[name] \texttt{Light LaTeX Make}
\item[caption] llmk: A build tool for LaTeX documents
\item[author] Asakura, Takuto
\index{Author!Asakura, Takuto}
\item[copyright] Takuto Asakura (2018-2023)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 1.2.0
\item[description] (no language specified) Light LaTeX Make (llmk) is yet another build tool specific for LaTeX documents. Its aim is to provide 
          a simple way to specify a workflow of processing LaTeX documents and encourage people to always explicitly 
          show the right workflow for each document.

          The main features of  \texttt{llmk} are all about the above purpose. First, you can describe 
          the workflows either in an external file \texttt{llmk.toml} or in a LaTeX document source 
          in the form of magic comments. Further, multiple magic comment formats can be used. Second, it is fully 
          cross-platform. The only requirement of the program is the \texttt{texlua} command; llmk 
          provides a uniform way to describe the workflows available for nearly all TeX environments. Third, it 
          behaves exactly the same in any environment. At this point, llmk intentionally does not provide any method 
          for user configuration. Therefore one can guarantee that for a LaTeX document with an \texttt{llmk} setup, 
          the process of typesetting the document will be reproduced in any TeX environment with the program.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/light-latex-make/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/light-latex-make/llmk.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package tries to prevent overflow lines in paragraphs or boxes. It changes LuaTeX’s  \texttt{{\textbackslash}linebreak} callback 
          and re-typesets the paragraph with increased values of \texttt{{\textbackslash}tolerance} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}emergencystretch} until 
          the overflow no longer happens. If that doesn’t help, it chooses the solution with the lowest badness.

\section[\texttt{linegoal} -- A “dimen” that returns the space left on the line]{\texttt{linegoal} -- A “dimen” that returns the space left on the line}\label{pkg:linegoal}
\index{Package!linegoal}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/linegoal}
\item[name] \texttt{linegoal}
\item[caption] A “dimen” that returns the space left on the line
\item[author] Chervet, Florent
\index{Author!Chervet, Florent}
\item[copyright] Florent Chervet (2010)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 2.9
\item[description] (no language specified) The linegoal package provides a macro  \texttt{{\textbackslash}linegoal} to be used 
          with \texttt{{\textbackslash}setlength} :\\ \texttt{{\textbackslash}setlength< \emph{some 
          dimen} >{\textbackslash}linegoal} \\will set < \emph{some dimen} > to 
          the horizontal length of the remainder of the line.

          This is achieved using the  \texttt{{\textbackslash}pdfsavepos} primitive of pdfTeX, 
          through the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/zref}{zref-savepos} package.

          Example:\\
          \begin{verbatim}
Some text: \begin{tabularx}\linegoal{|l|X|} \hline
one & two \\
three & four \\\hline
\end{tabularx}
          \end{verbatim}
will position the table after the initial text, and make the table fill the rest of the line.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/linegoal/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/linegoal/linegoal.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./9427531921-linegoal.pdf|

\item[description] (no language specified) This is an experimental bundle of packages that provide enhanced support for typesetting in linguistics. 
          It can be used as a single package, or the packages can be loaded independently for separate features. 
          Currently, it provides the following packages:

          \begin{enumerate}
          \item LinguisTiX-base: A base package used by other LinguisTiX siblings
          \item LinguisTiX-fixpex: Solves the compatibility bug between  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/expex}{expex} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/unicode-math}{unicode-math} 
          \item LinguisTiX-fonts: General text in the New Computer Modern font family
          \item LinguisTiX-ipa: IPA text in the New Computer Modern font family
          \item LinguisTiX-glossing: Accessible interlinear glossing
          \item LinguisTiX-leipzig: Leipzig-style glossing with tagging
          \item LinguisTiX-languages: Support for modern multilingual typesetting
          \item LinguisTiX-logos: For printing the logos of the LinguisTiX bundle
          \item LinguisTiX-nfss: Extra control over NFSS
          \end{enumerate}

\section[\texttt{linkedthm} -- Hyperlinked theorem–proof environments for LaTeX]{\texttt{linkedthm} -- Hyperlinked theorem–proof environments for LaTeX}\label{pkg:linkedthm}
\index{Package!linkedthm}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/linkedthm}
\item[name] \texttt{linkedthm}
\item[caption] Hyperlinked theorem–proof environments for LaTeX
\item[author] Ortega Andrés, Luis Antonio
\index{Author!Ortega Andrés, Luis Antonio}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0 (2025-07-21)
\item[last changes] 2025-07-21
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides lightweight infrastructure for bidirectional linking between theorem-like environments 
          and their corresponding proofs. It automatically adds a [Proof] hyperlink at the end of a theorem and 
          a restated version with a [Return] link inside the proof.

          You can declare any number of custom linked environments (e.g.,  \texttt{linkeddefinition} , \texttt{linkedexample} ) 
          using \texttt{{\textbackslash}DeclareLinkedTheorem} , and base them on any \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsthm}{amsthm} -compatible 
          environment.

          This is useful for mathematical writing and documentation, where proof navigation is essential.

          The package uses  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsthm}{amsthm} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xparse}{xparse} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} , and is compatible with all standard 
          LaTeX engines.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Example of use}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/linkedthm/linkedthm-example.pdf}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/listings}

\item[caption] Typeset source code listings using LaTeX
\item[author] Heinz, Carsten
\index{Author!Heinz, Carsten}
\item[author] Moses, Brooks
\index{Author!Moses, Brooks}
\item[author] Hoffmann, Jobst
\index{Author!Hoffmann, Jobst}
\item[copyright] Carsten Heinz (1996-2004)
\item[copyright] Jobst Hoffmann (2013-2025)
\item[copyright] Brooks Moses (2006-2007)

\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.11a
\item[description] (no language specified) The package enables the user to typeset programs (programming code) within LaTeX; the source code is 
          read directly by TeX—no front-end processor is needed. Keywords, comments and strings can be typeset 
          using different styles (default is bold for keywords, italic for comments and no special style for strings). 
          Support for  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} is provided.

          To use,  \texttt{{\textbackslash}usepackage{\textbraceleft}listings{\textbraceright}} , 
          identify the language of the object to typeset, using a construct like: \texttt{{\textbackslash}lstset{\textbraceleft}language=Python{\textbraceright}} , 
          then use environment \texttt{lstlisting} for inline code. External files may be formatted 
          using \texttt{{\textbackslash}lstinputlisting} to process a given file in the form 
          appropriate for the current language. Short (in-line) listings are also available, using either \texttt{{\textbackslash}lstinline|...|} or \texttt{|...|} (after 
          defining the \texttt{|} token with the \texttt{{\textbackslash}lstMakeShortInline} command).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/listings/README}

\section[\texttt{listofitems} -- Grab items in lists using user-specified sep char]{\texttt{listofitems} -- Grab items in lists using user-specified sep char}\label{pkg:listofitems}
\index{Package!listofitems}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/listofitems}
\item[name] \texttt{listofitems}
\item[caption] Grab items in lists using user-specified sep char
\item[author] Tellechea, Christian
\index{Author!Tellechea, Christian}
\item[copyright] Christian Tellechea (2016-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.65 (2024-03-09)
\item[last changes] 2024-03-09
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) This simple package is designed to read a list of items whose parsing character may be selected by the 
          user.

          Once the list is read, its items are stored in a structure that behaves as a dimensioned array. As such, 
          it becomes very easy to access an item in the list by its number.

          For example, if the list is stored in the macro  \texttt{{\textbackslash}foo} , the 
          item \#3 is designated by \texttt{{\textbackslash}foo[3]} .

          A component may, in turn, be a list with a parsing delimiter different from the parent list, paving the 
          way for nesting and employing a syntax reminiscent of an array of several dimensions of the type  \texttt{{\textbackslash}foo[3,2]} to 
          access the item \#2 of the list contained within the item \#3 of the top-tier list.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/listofitems/README}
\item[documentation] \textit{Package documentation (English)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/listofitems/listofitems-en.pdf}

\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.2
\item[description] (no language specified) Listofsymbols provides commands to automatically create a list of symbols (also called notation or nomenclature), 
          and to handle symbols logically, i.e. define a macro that is expanded to the desired output and use the 
          macro in the text rather than 'hardcoding' the output into the text. This helps to ensure consistency 
          throughout the text, especially if there is a chance that symbols will be changed at some stage.

          The package is more or less a combination of what the packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/nomencl}{nomencl} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/formula}{formula} do. 
          The concept of creating the list of symbols, though, is different from the way nomencl.sty does it.

          the Computer Modern fonts released into public domain by AMS (copyright © 1997 AMS). The lm font set 
          contains a lot of additional characters, mainly accented ones, but not exclusively. There is one set 
          of fonts, available both in Adobe Type 1 format (*.pfb) and in OpenType format (*.otf). There are five 
          sets of TeX Font Metric files, corresponding to: Cork encoding (cork-*.tfm); QX encoding (qx-*.tfm); 
          TeX’n’ANSI aka LY1 encoding (texnansi-*.tfm); T5 (Vietnamese) encoding (t5-*.tfm); and Text Companion

          environment to the user.

          The program lets the user choose which errors he cares to see. Furthermore LogFilter integrates with 
          your editor so that when pressing an error, your editor will open the TeX file and jump to the according 
          line. Some errors do not contain linenumbers in which case the program only opens the file where the 
          error has occoured.

\section[\texttt{logicproof} -- Box proofs for propositional and predicate logic]{\texttt{logicproof} -- Box proofs for propositional and predicate logic}\label{pkg:logicproof}
\index{Package!logicproof}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/logicproof}
\item[name] \texttt{logicproof}
\item[caption] Box proofs for propositional and predicate logic
\item[author] Davidson, Alan
\index{Author!Davidson, Alan}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version]  (2014-03-20)
\item[last changes] 2014-03-20
\item[year] 2014
\index{Year!2014}
\item[description] (no language specified) A common style of proof used in propositional and predicate logic is  \emph{Fitch proofs} , 
          in which each line of the proof has a statement and a justification, and subproofs within a larger proof 
          have boxes around them.

          The package provides environments for typesetting such proofs and boxes. It creates proofs in a style 
          similar to that used in ''Logic in Computer Science'' by Huth and Ryan.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/logicproof/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/logicproof/logicproof.pdf}

\index{License!lppl1.3}

\item[version] 2.5
\item[description] (no language specified) The package allows the user to typeset various logic puzzles. At the moment the following puzzles are 
          supported:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item 2D-Sudoku (aka Magiequadrat, Diagon, …),
          \item Battleship (aka Bimaru, Marinespiel, Batalla Naval, …),
          \item Bokkusu (aka Kakurasu, Feldersummenrätsel, …),
          \item Bridges (akak Brückenbau, Hashi, …),
          \item Chaos Sudoku,
          \item Four Winds (aka Eminent Domain, Lichtstrahl, …),
          \item Hakyuu (aka Seismic, Ripple Effect, …),
          \item Hitori,
          \item Kakuro,
          \item Kendoku (aka Mathdoku, Calcudoku, Basic, MiniPlu, Ken Ken, Square Wisdom, Sukendo, Caldoku, …,
          \item Killer Sudoku (aka Samunapure, Sum Number Place, Sumdoku, Gebietssummen, …),
          \item Laser Beam (aka Laserstrahl, …),
          \item Magic Labyrinth (aka Magic Spiral, Magisches Labyrinth, …),
          \item Magnets (aka Magnetplatte, Magnetfeld, …),
          \item Masyu (aka Mashi, {\textbraceleft}White|Black{\textbraceright} Pearls, …),
          \item Minesweeper (aka Minensuche, …),
          \item Nonogram (aka Griddlers, Hanjie, Tsunami, Logic Art, Logimage, …),
          \item Number Link (aka Alphabet Link, Arukone, Buchstabenbund, …),
          \item Resuko,
          \item Schatzsuche,
          \item Skyline (aka Skycrapers, Wolkenkratzer, Hochhäuser, …), including Skyline Sudoku and Skyline Sudoku (N*N) variants,
          \item Slitherlink (aka Fences, Number Line, Dotty Dilemma, Sli-Lin, Takegaki, Great Wall of China, Loop the Loop, Rundweg, Gartenzaun, …),
          \item Star Battle (aka Sternenschlacht, …),
          \item Stars and Arrows (aka Sternenhimmel, …),
          \item Sudoku,
          \item Sun and Moon (aka Sternenhaufen, Munraito, …),
          \item Tents and Trees (aka Zeltlager, Zeltplatz, Camping, …), and
          \item Tunnel.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/logicpuzzle/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/logicpuzzle/logicpuzzle.pdf}

\section[\texttt{logreq} -- Support for automation of the LaTeX workflow]{\texttt{logreq} -- Support for automation of the LaTeX workflow}\label{pkg:logreq}
\index{Package!logreq}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/logreq}
\item[name] \texttt{logreq}
\item[caption] Support for automation of the LaTeX workflow
\item[author] Lehman, Philipp
\index{Author!Lehman, Philipp}
\item[copyright] Philipp Lehman (2010)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The package helps to automate a typical LaTeX workflow that involves running LaTeX several times, running 
          tools such as BibTeX or makeindex, and so on. It will log requests like ''please rerun LaTeX'' or ''please 
          run BibTeX on file X'' to an external XML file which lists all open tasks in a machine-readable format. 
          Compiler scripts and integrated LaTeX editing environments may parse this file to determine the next 
          steps in the workflow in a way that is more efficient than parsing the main log file. In sum, the package 
          will do two things:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item enable package authors to use LaTeX commands to issue requests,
          \item collect all requests from all packages and write them to an external XML file at the end of the document.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/logreq/README}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/logreq}
\item[installation]\url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/install/macros/latex/contrib/logreq.tds.zip}
\item[on Mik\TeX] \texttt{logreq}
\item[on \TeX Live] \texttt{logreq}

\item[description] (no language specified) Lollipop is ''TeX made easy'' — it is a macro package that functions as a toolbox for writing TeX macros. 
          Its main aim is to make macro writing so easy that implementing a fully new layout in TeX would become 
          a matter of less than an hour for an average document. The aim is that such a task could be accomplished 
          by someone with only a very basic training in TeX programming.

          Thus, Lollipop aims to make structured text formatting available in environments where typical users 
          would switch to WYSIWYG packages for the freedom that such a mechanism offers.

          In addition, development of support for Lollipop documents written in RTL languages (such as Persian) 
          is underway.

\section[\texttt{longdivision} -- Typesets long division]{\texttt{longdivision} -- Typesets long division}\label{pkg:longdivision}
\index{Package!longdivision}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/longdivision}
\item[name] \texttt{longdivision}
\item[caption] Typesets long division
\item[author] Chatham, Hood
\index{Author!Chatham, Hood}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.2.2 (2023-10-21)
\item[last changes] 2023-10-21
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package executes the long division algorithm and typesets the solutions. The dividend must be a 
          positive decimal number and the divisor must be a positive integer. Repeating decimals is handled correctly, 
          putting a bar over the repeated part of the decimal. Dividends up to 20 digits long are handled gracefully 
          (though the typeset result will take up about a page), and dividends between 20 and 60 digits long slightly 
          less gracefully.

          The package defines two macros,  \texttt{{\textbackslash}longdivision} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}intlongdivision} . 
          Each takes two arguments, a dividend and a divisor. \texttt{{\textbackslash}longdivision} keeps 
          dividing until the remainder is zero, or it encounters a repeated remainder. \texttt{{\textbackslash}intlongdivision} stops 
          when the dividend stops (though the dividend doesn’t have to be an integer).

          This package depends on the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xparse}{xparse} package from 
          the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/l3packages}{l3packages} bundle.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/longdivision/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/longdivision/longdivision_manual.pdf}

\section[\texttt{longmath} -- Nested delimiter groups extending over multiple array cells \ldots]{\texttt{longmath} -- Nested delimiter groups extending over multiple array cells or lines}\label{pkg:longmath}
\index{Package!longmath}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/longmath}
\item[name] \texttt{longmath}
\item[caption] Nested delimiter groups extending over multiple array cells or lines
\item[author] Matschull, Hans-Jürgen
\index{Author!Matschull, Hans-Jürgen}
\item[copyright] Hans-Jürgen Matschull (2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.0 (2024-07-04)
\item[last changes] 2024-07-04
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides yet another solution to some well known typesetting problems solved in a variety 
          of ways: multi line formulas with paired and nested delimiters. It tackles the problem at the Lua level, 
          which has some advantages over solutions implemented in TeX. In particular, the TeX code need not be 
          executed multiple times, and there is no interference between TeX grouping and the nesting of delimiter 
          groups.

          As a byproduct, delimiters can be scaled in various ways, inner delimiters come in different flavours 
          like relational and binary operators, punctuation symbols etc., and outer delimiters can be selected 
          automatically according to the nesting level. Last but not least, delimiter groups can even extend across 
          several array cells or across the whole document.

          A special environment is provided as well, which allows multi line expressions to be placed inside a 
          displayed equation and make TeX do the line splitting and alignment.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/longmath/longmath-doc.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./2408400066-longmath-doc.pdf|

\item[description] (no language specified) Longtable allows you to write tables that continue to the next page. You can write captions within the 
          table (typically at the start of the table), and headers and trailers for pages of table. Longtable arranges 
          that the columns on successive pages have the same widths. This last contrasts with the superficially 
          similar  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/supertabular}{supertabular} package.

          Longtable (unlike supertabular) modifies the output routine, and consequently won’t work in a  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/multicol}{multicolumn} environment 
          (or in other circumstances where the output routine has been critically altered); it also fails in twocolumn 
          pages.

          This package is part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latex-tools}{latex-tools} bundle 
          in the LaTeX \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/required}{required} distribution.

          Just as with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xparse}{xparse} , it is possible to use a special 
          syntax consisting of single letters to express the arguments of a macro. However, \texttt{lparse} is 
          able to read arguments regardless of the macro system used — whether LaTeX, or ConTeXt, or even plain 
          TeX. Of course, LuaTeX must always be used as the engine.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package defines a convenient interface to put any LaTeX material on top of included graphics. The 
          LaTeX material may also be rotated and typeset on top of a white box overshadowing the graphics. The 
          coordinates of the LaTeX boxes are given relative to the original, unscaled graphics; when the graphics 
          is rescaled, the LaTeX annotations stay at their right places (unless you do something extreme). In a 
          draft mode, the package enables you to draw a coordinate grid over the picture for easy adjustment of 
          positions of the annotations.

\item[description] (no language specified) This package is similar to the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/msc}{msc} package in that 
          it provides macros for typesetting a variant of sequence diagrams, in this case the Live Sequence Charts

          verification and some of the Harel-extensions for the Play-In/Play-Out approach (cf. the manual).

\section[\texttt{lscape} -- Place selected parts of a document in landscape]{\texttt{lscape} -- Place selected parts of a document in landscape}\label{pkg:lscape}
\index{Package!lscape}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lscape}
\item[name] \texttt{lscape}
\item[caption] Place selected parts of a document in landscape
\item[author] The LaTeX Project Team
\index{Author!The LaTeX Project Team}
\item[author] Carlisle, David
\index{Author!Carlisle, David}
\item[copyright] David Carlisle, LaTeX3 Project (2000-2021)
\item[copyright] David Carlisle (1994, 1999-2000)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 3.02 (2020-05-28)
\item[last changes] 2020-05-28
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) Modifies the margins and rotates the page contents but not the page number. Useful, for example, with 
          large multipage tables, as it is compatible with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/longtable}{longtable} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/supertabular}{supertabular} .

          Note that the package makes no special provision for PDF output, where in principle a single page can 
          be shown at full landscape width; such an effect may be achieved using the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdflscape}{pdflscape} package 
          instead.

          The package is part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latex-graphics}{latex-graphics} bundle, 
          which is one of the collections in the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/required}{LaTeX ‘required’} set 
          of packages.
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/required/graphics}
\item[installation]\url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/install/macros/latex/required/latex-graphics.tds.zip}
\item[on Mik\TeX] \texttt{graphics}
\item[on \TeX Live] \texttt{graphics}
\item[keyword] \texttt{landscape} (print landscape orientation, manipulate landscape material)
\index{Topic!landscape}
\item[keyword] \texttt{layout} (layout of objects on the page)
\index{Topic!layout}
\item[see also] see section~\ref{pkg:rotating} on page~\pageref{pkg:rotating}: (\texttt{rotating} -- Rotation tools, including rotated full-page floats)
\item[language(s)] no language specified
\index{Language in description/documentation!no language specified}
\item[last access] 2025-02-07
\end{labeling}

          holds versions in  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-bulgarian}{Bulgarian} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-zh-cn}{Chinese} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-dutch}{Dutch} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-english}{English} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-finnish}{Finnish} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-french}{French} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-german}{German} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-italian}{Italian} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-japanese}{Japanese} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-korean}{Korean} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-mongol}{Mongolian} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-persian}{Persian} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-polish}{Polish} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-portuguese}{Portuguese} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lshort-portuguese-br}{Brazilian

\item[author] Bartholdi, Laurent
\index{Author!Bartholdi, Laurent}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.01
\item[description] (no language specified) This package implements a LaTeX command that converts an amsrefs bibliographical database ( \texttt{.ltb} ) 
          to a BibTeX bibliographical database ( \texttt{.bib} ).

          ltb2bib is the reverse of the "amsxport" option in amsrefs. Typical uses are:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item produce bib entries for some publishers which don't accept amsrefs (Taylor \& Francis, for example);
          \item import an ltb database in a database management program, e.g. for sorting;
          \item access one's ltb database within emacs's RefTeX mode.
          \end{itemize}

\item[description] (no language specified) Embed Mermaid diagrams in LaTeX. Diagram sources are written to disk, and the Mermaid CLI (mmdc) renders vector PDFs, which are then included using  \verb|\includegraphics| .

          \verb|mermaid.sty| is the implementation to be used with pdfLaTeX/XeLaTeX/upLaTeX/LuaLaTeX, etc. It invokes the Mermaid CLI via the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/shellesc}{shellesc} package (or directly via \verb|\write18| ). No Lua interpreter is required.

          \verb|ltmermaid.sty| is an implementation dedicated to LuaLaTeX that provides the same macros (the \verb|Renderer| option, \verb|\Mermaid...| macros, and the \verb|mermaid| environment) as \verb|mermaid.sty| . The CLI is invoked via Lua's \verb|os.execute| .

\section[\texttt{ltx-talk} -- A class for typesetting presentations]{\texttt{ltx-talk} -- A class for typesetting presentations}\label{pkg:ltx-talk}
\index{Package!ltx-talk}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ltx-talk}
\item[name] \texttt{ltx-talk}
\item[caption] A class for typesetting presentations
\item[author] Wright, Joseph
\index{Author!Wright, Joseph}
\item[copyright] Joseph Wright (2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.1.1 (2025-07-14)
\item[last changes] 2025-07-14
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This class is  \emph{highly} experimental, and changes may occur to almost all interfaces. 
          Development is focussed on tagging/functionality as the primary driver; as such, support for design aspects 
          is likely to be lower priority.

          It  \textbf{requires} LaTeX 2025-11-01: this is currently available as a pre-release by using \texttt{lualatex-dev} or \texttt{pdflatex-dev} .

          The  \texttt{ltx-talk} class is focused on producing (on-screen) presentations, along with 
          support material such as handouts and speaker notes. Content is created in a \texttt{frame} environment, 
          each of which can be divided up into a number of slides (actual output pages). A simple ‘overlay’ notation 
          is used to specify which material appears on each slide within a frame. The class supports a range of 
          environments to enable complex slide relationships to be constructed.

          The appearance of slides is controlled by a template system. Many of the elements of slides can be adjusted 
          by setting simple key-based values in the preamble. More complex changes can be implemented by altering 
          specific, targeted definitions without needing to rewrite entire blocks of code. This allows a variety 
          of visual appearances to be selected for the same content source.

          The  \texttt{ltx-talk} class has syntax similar to the popular \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer}{beamer} class, 
          although there are some (deliberate) differences. However, \texttt{ltx-talk} has been implemented 
          to support creation of tagged (accessible) PDF output as a core aim. As such, it is suited to creating 
          output for reuse in other formats, e.g. HTML conversions, without additional steps.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ltx-talk/ltx-talk.pdf}

          differ from the \texttt{multicols} environment of the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/multicol}{multicol} package

\section[\texttt{ltxkeys} -- A robust key parser for LaTeX]{\texttt{ltxkeys} -- A robust key parser for LaTeX}\label{pkg:ltxkeys}
\index{Package!ltxkeys}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ltxkeys}
\item[name] \texttt{ltxkeys}
\item[caption] A robust key parser for LaTeX
\item[author] Musa, Ahmed
\index{Author!Musa, Ahmed}
\item[copyright] Ahmed Musa (2011)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.0.3c
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides facilities for creating and managing keys in the sense of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/keyval}{keyval} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} packages, 
          but it is intended to be more robust and faster. Its robustness comes from its ability to preserve braces 
          in key values throughout parsing. The need to preserve braces in key values arises often in parsing keys 
          (for example, in the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xwatermark}{xwatermark} package). The 
          package is faster than \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} package because (among 
          other things) it avoids character-wise parsing of key values (called ''selective sanitization'' by the 
          xkeyval package).

          The package also provides functions for defining and managing keys.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ltxkeys/README}

          inside a longtable environment. The code of each such environment (with \texttt{X} specifiers 
          in its column layout) should be in a separate file, which is then included in your document by a command \texttt{{\textbackslash}LTXtable{\textbraceleft}<width>{\textbraceright}{\textbraceleft}<file 
          name>{\textbraceright}} 

          The  \texttt{{\textbackslash}multicolumn} command is suppressed in environments included 
          in this way.

          The package is distributed as part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/carlisle}{carlisle} bundle.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package looks at all hyphenation breaks in the document, comparing them against a white-list prepared 
          by the author. If a hyphenation break is found, for which there is no entry in the white-list, the package 
          flags the line where the break starts.

          The author may then either add the hyphenation to the white-list, or adjust the document to avoid the 
          break.

\item[caption] Draw properly occluded 3D parametric objects under perspective projection
\item[author] Nice, Jasper
\index{Author!Nice, Jasper}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)

\item[version] 1.1.0 (2025-09-04)
\item[last changes] 2025-09-04

\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This — currently experimental — package improves on existing 3D capabilities in Ti \emph{k} Z. 
          In particular, the package enables z-sorting of multiple triangulated parametric objects and uses elaborate 
          occlusion logic. The parametric objects are defined using \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgfkeys}{pgfkeys} , 
          and endeavor to enable user customization.

          All of the 3D math is handled in Lua, and the results are projected onto the 2D Ti \emph{k} Z 
          canvas. The user is enabled to use linear, affine and projective transformations on their parametric 
          objects.

          The current aim of the package is to enable parametric object clipping, and to improve on the occlusion 
          logic.

\section[\texttt{lua-uni-algos} -- Unicode algorithms for LuaTeX]{\texttt{lua-uni-algos} -- Unicode algorithms for LuaTeX}\label{pkg:lua-uni-algos}
\index{Package!lua-uni-algos}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lua-uni-algos}
\item[name] \texttt{lua-uni-algos}
\item[caption] Unicode algorithms for LuaTeX
\item[author] Krüger, Marcel
\index{Author!Krüger, Marcel}
\item[copyright] Marcel Krüger (2020-2022)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.4.1 (2022-02-26)
\item[last changes] 2022-02-26
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) Lua code working with Unicode data has to deal with quite some challenges. For example there are many 
          canonically equivalent sequences which should be treated in the same way, and even identifying a single 
          character becomes quite different once you have to deal with all kinds of combining characters, emoji 
          sequences and syllables in different scripts.

          Therefore  \texttt{lua-uni-algos} wants to build a collection of small libraries implementing 
          algorithms to deal with lots of the details in Unicode, such that authors of LuaTeX packages can focus 
          on their actual functionality instead of having to fight against the peculiarities of Unicode.

          Given that this package provides Lua modules, it is only useful in Lua(HB)TeX. Additionally, it expects 
          an up-to-date version of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/unicode-data}{unicode-data} package 
          to be present.

          This package is intended for package authors only; no user-level functionality provided.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/generic/lua-uni-algos/README.md}

\section[\texttt{lua-widow-control} -- Automatically remove widows and orphans from any document]{\texttt{lua-widow-control} -- Automatically remove widows and orphans from any document}\label{pkg:lua-widow-control}
\index{Package!lua-widow-control}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lua-widow-control}
\item[name] \texttt{lua-widow-control}
\item[caption] Automatically remove widows and orphans from any document
\item[author] Chernoff, Max
\index{Author!Chernoff, Max}
\item[copyright] gucci-on-fleek (2021-2022)
\item[license] cc-by-sa-4 = CC BY-SA 4.0 (free)
\index{License!cc-by-sa-4}
\index{License!CC BY-SA 4.0}
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version] 3.0.1 (2024-03-11)
\item[last changes] 2024-03-11
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) Unmodified TeX has very few ways of preventing widows and orphans. In documents with figures, section headings, and equations, TeX can stretch the vertical glue between items in order to prevent widows and orphans, but many documents have no figures or headings. TeX can also shorten the page by 1 line, but this will give each page a different length which can make a document look uneven. The typical solution is to strategically insert  \verb|\looseness=1| , but this requires manual editing every time that the document is edited. Lua-widow-control is essentially an automation of the \verb|\looseness| method: it uses Lua callbacks to find ''stretchy'' paragraphs, then it lengthens them to remove widows and orphans.

          Lua-widow-control is compatible with all LuaTeX and LuaMetaTeX-based formats. All that is required is 
          to load the package at the start of your document. To load:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Plain LuaTeX:  \verb|\input lua-widow-control| 
          \item LuaLaTeX:  \verb|\usepackage{lua-widow-control}| 
          \item ConTeXt:  \verb|\usemodule[lua-widow-control]| 
          \item OpTeX:  \verb|\load[lua-widow-control]| 
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{TUGboat article}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/generic/lua-widow-control/tb133chernoff-widows.pdf}

\item[author] Dales, Simon

\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.2
\item[description] (no language specified) The package extends the well-known C-like language autodoc tool,  \texttt{doxygen} , to read 
          and document \texttt{lua} code.

          In use, you edit and test your code and periodically run the autodoc tool to update the documentation, 
          which may be viewed via an html browser.

          Autodoc tools can read the code well enough to find  \texttt{function/...} declarations and 
          document them. If the code also contains appropriatly formatted ''magic comments'', the tool can use 
          them to supplement the documentation.

          The package is a first prototype of a planned  \texttt{TeX2DoX} tool (in development), which 
          will process joint (La)TeX/lua documents.

\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a portable computer algebra system capable of symbolic computation, written entirely 
          in Lua, designed for use in LuaLaTeX.

          Features include: arbitrary-precision integer and rational arithmetic, factoring of univariate polynomials 
          over the rationals and finite fields, number theoretic algorithms, symbolic differentiation and integration, 
          and more. The target audience for this package are mathematics students, instructors, and professionals 
          who would like some ability to perform basic symbolic computations within LaTeX without the need for 
          laborious and technical setup.

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/luagcd}
\item[name] \texttt{luagcd}
\item[caption] Computation of gcd of integers inside LaTeX using Lua
\item[author] Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar
\index{Author!Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.1
\item[description] (no language specified) Using Lua, the luagcd package is developped to find the greatest common divisor (gcd) of integers in 
          LaTeX. The package provides commands to obtain step-by-step computation of gcd of two integers by using 
          the Euclidean algorithm. In addition, the package has the command to express gcd of two integers as a 
          linear combination. The Bezout's Identity can be verified for any two integers using commands in the 
          package. No particular environment is required for the use of commands in the package. It is written 
          in Lua, and the TeX file has to be compiled with the LuaLaTeX engine.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/luagcd/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/luagcd/luagcd.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3752827129-luagcd.pdf|

\section[\texttt{luahyperbolic} -- Hyperbolic geometry in the Poincaré disk model]{\texttt{luahyperbolic} -- Hyperbolic geometry in the Poincaré disk model}\label{pkg:luahyperbolic}
\index{Package!luahyperbolic}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/luahyperbolic}
\item[name] \texttt{luahyperbolic}
\item[caption] Hyperbolic geometry in the Poincaré disk model
\item[author] Mégy, Damien
\index{Author!Mégy, Damien}
\item[license] cc0 = CC0 1.0 (free)
\index{License!cc0}
\index{License!CC0 1.0}
\item[version]  (2026-03-16)
\item[last changes] 2026-03-16
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package allows to draw pictures and do computations in plane hyperbolic geometry, in the Poincaré 
          disk model. Computations are done with Lua, and graphics are generated with TikZ. The package is written 
          in Lua and requires LuaLaTeX.

          Features:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Draw geodesic lines, segments, polygons, rays, circles, horocycles, hypercycles.
          \item Label and mark segments, angles
          \item Compute intersections of geodesics, circles, symmetries, reflections, exponential maps, automorphisms
          \item Draw hyperbolic triangle tilings with a simple LaTeX macro
          \end{itemize}
Example tiling :  \href{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmegy/luahyperbolic/refs/heads/main/triangle-tiling-2-4-5.png}{https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmegy/luahyperbolic/refs/heads/main/triangle-tiling-2-4-5.png}

\item[author] Roux, Élie

\item[author] Pégourié-Gonnard, Manuel
\index{Author!Pégourié-Gonnard, Manuel}
\item[copyright] Elie Roux (2009)
\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[version] 0.973
\item[description] (no language specified) LuaTeX operates by default in UTF-8 input; thus LaTeX documents that need 8-bit character-sets need special 
          treatment. (In fact, LaTeX documents using UTF-8 with ''traditional'' — 256-glyph — fonts also need support 
          from this package.)

          The package, therefore, replaces the LaTeX standard  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/inputenc}{inputenc} for 
          use under LuaTeX. With a current LuaTeX, the package has the same behaviour with LuaTeX as inputenc has 
          under pdfTeX.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/luainputenc/luainputenc.pdf}

\item[caption] A Lua module for parsing key-value options
\item[author] Friedrich, Josef
\index{Author!Friedrich, Josef}
\item[copyright] Josef Friedrich (2021-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}

\item[version] 0.17.0 (2025-07-19)
\item[last changes] 2025-07-19
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a Lua module that can parse key-value options like the TeX packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/keyval}{keyval} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/kvsetkeys}{kvsetkeys} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/kvoptions}{kvoptions} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgfkeys}{pgfkeys} etc. \texttt{luakeys} , 
          however, accomplishes this task entirely by using the Lua language and does not rely on TeX. Therefore 
          this package can only be used with the TeX engine \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/luatex}{LuaTeX} . 
          Since luakeys uses \href{http://www.inf.puc-rio.br/{\textasciitilde}roberto/lpeg/}{LPeg} , 
          the parsing mechanism should be pretty robust.

\section[\texttt{lualatex-platform} -- Load platform-specific code into LuaTeX]{\texttt{lualatex-platform} -- Load platform-specific code into LuaTeX}\label{pkg:lualatex-platform}
\index{Package!lualatex-platform}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lualatex-platform}
\item[name] \texttt{luaLaTeX-platform}
\item[caption] Load platform-specific code into LuaTeX
\item[author] Stephani, Philipp
\index{Author!Stephani, Philipp}
\item[copyright] Philipp Stephani (2011)
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version] 0.1
\item[description] (no language specified) While platform-specific problems can often be handled purely in Lua, it sometimes happens that access 
          to the native operating system API is required. For such tasks, Lua itself makes it possible to load 
          extension modules written in C (or other languages provided that they can produce a dynamic library that 
          exports a certain C-style function).

          The present package aims to provide such an extension module that is usable from both Lua and LuaTeX 
          and adds a small set of features not available otherwise. This release merely supports listing the fonts 
          known to the operating system (this feature could usefully be integrated into the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/luaotfload}{luaotfload} package).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/obsolete/systems/luatex/contrib/lualatex-platform/README}

\section[\texttt{lualinalg} -- A linear algebra package for LuaLaTeX]{\texttt{lualinalg} -- A linear algebra package for LuaLaTeX}\label{pkg:lualinalg}
\index{Package!lualinalg}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lualinalg}
\item[name] \texttt{lualinalg}
\item[caption] A linear algebra package for LuaLaTeX
\item[author] Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar
\index{Author!Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.9 (2023-11-17)
\item[last changes] 2023-11-17
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) The lualinalg package is developed to perform operations on vectors and matrices defined over the field 
          of real or complex numbers inside LaTeX documents. It provides flexible ways for defining and displaying 
          vectors and matrices. No particular environment of LaTeX is required to use commands in the package. 
          The package is written in Lua, and  \texttt{tex} file is to be compiled with the LuaLaTeX 
          engine.

          The time required for calculations is not an issue while compiling with LuaLaTeX. There is no need to 
          install Lua on the user's system as TeX distributions (TeX Live or MikTeX) come bundled with LuaLaTeX. 
          It may also save users' efforts to copy vectors and matrices from other software (which may not be in 
          LaTeX-compatible format) and to use them in a  \texttt{tex} file. The vectors and matrices 
          of reasonable size can be handled with ease. The package can be modified or extended by writing custom 
          Lua programs.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/lualinalg/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/lualinalg/lualinalg.pdf}

          and depending upon the choice of the engine, the drawing is done by MetaPost (with luamplib) or by TikZ.

\section[\texttt{luanumint} -- Numerical integration using Lua inside LaTeX documents]{\texttt{luanumint} -- Numerical integration using Lua inside LaTeX documents}\label{pkg:luanumint}
\index{Package!luanumint}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/luanumint}
\item[name] \texttt{luanumint}
\item[caption] Numerical integration using Lua inside LaTeX documents
\item[author] Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar
\index{Author!Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.2 (2023-11-17)
\item[last changes] 2023-11-17
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package uses Lua to calculate the numerical integral value of real-valued functions of a real variable 
          over closed and bounded intervals.

          The package provides commands to perform numerical integration using the mid-point, trapezoidal, and 
          Simpson’s one-third and three-eighth rules. The  \texttt{loadstring} command is used to load 
          and evaluate functions at different points in the mathematics environment of Lua. The package also provides 
          commands to perform numerical integration using step-by-step calculations.

          The package’s commands have an optional argument to round off the numbers to the desired number of decimal 
          places. The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/breqn}{breqn} package is loaded to display and 
          align step-by-step calculations properly. Advanced users can customize the code to achieve the desired 
          formatting of step-by-step computations.

          The package can assist in creating various problems on numerical integration with their solutions. The 
          results obtained using different methods of numerical integration can be compared. It can save users’ 
          efforts of doing computations involving numerical integration in external software and copying them inside 
          LaTeX documents.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/luanumint/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/luanumint/luanumint.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This LuaLaTeX package provides extensive support for handling  \emph{options} , on package 
          level and locally. It allows the declaration of sets of options, along with defaults, expected/allowed 
          values and limited type checking. These options can be enforced as package options, changed at any point 
          during a document, or overwritten locally by optional macro arguments. It is also possible to instantiate 
          an Options object as an independent Lua object, without linking it to a package. \texttt{Luaoptions} can 
          be used to enforce and prepopulate options, or it can be used to simply handle the parsing of optional \texttt{key=value} arguments 
          into proper Lua tables.
