\section[\texttt{luaplot} -- Plotting graphs using Lua]{\texttt{luaplot} -- Plotting graphs using Lua}\label{pkg:luaplot}
\index{Package!luaplot}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/luaplot}
\item[name] \texttt{luaplot}
\item[caption] Plotting graphs using Lua
\item[author] Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar
\index{Author!Chetan Shirore and Ajit Kumar}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.5 (2023-11-17)
\item[last changes] 2023-11-17
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package uses Lua to plot graphs of real-valued functions of a real variable in LaTeX. It furthermore 
          makes use of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/metapost}{MetaPost} system as well as the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/luamplib}{luamplib} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/luacode}{luacode} packages. 
          It provides an easy way for plotting graphs of standard mathematical functions.

          There is no particular environment in the package for plotting graphs. It also works inside LaTeX floating 
          environments, like tables and figures. The compilation time for plotting several graphs in LaTeX using 
          this package is significantly less with the LuaLaTeX engine.

          The package is based on the core idea of loading mathematical functions inside Lua and determining plot 
          points using different methods available in Lua. After determining plot points in Lua, two different 
          approaches are used:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Pass plot points to the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/metapost}{MetaPost} system via \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/luamplib}{luamplib} .
          \item Pass plot points to the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} package.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/luaplot/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/luaplot/luaplot.pdf}

\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.1
\item[description] (no language specified) The luaset package is developed to define finite sets and perform operations on them inside LaTeX documents. 
          There is no particular environment in the package for performing set operations. The package commands 
          can be used in any environment (including the mathematics environment). It is written in Lua, and the 
          \texttt{.tex} file is to be compiled with the LuaLaTeX engine. The time required for operations 
          on sets is not an issue while compiling with the LuaLaTeX engine. There is no need to install Lua on 
          the users system as TeX distributions (TeX Live or MikTeX) come bundled with LuaLaTeX.

          TrueType) fonts (for both text and mathematics).

\section[\texttt{luavlna} -- Prevent line breaks after single letter words, units, or aca\ldots]{\texttt{luavlna} -- Prevent line breaks after single letter words, units, or academic titles}\label{pkg:luavlna}
\index{Package!luavlna}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/luavlna}
\item[name] \texttt{luavlna}
\item[caption] Prevent line breaks after single letter words, units, or academic titles
\item[author] Hoftich, Michal
\index{Author!Hoftich, Michal}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.1n (2025-10-29)
\item[last changes] 2025-10-29
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) In some languages, like Czech or Polish, there should be no single letter words at the end of a line, 
          according to typographical norms. This package handles such situations using LuaTeX’s callback mechanism. 
          In doing this, the package can detect languages used in the text and insert spaces only in parts of the 
          document where languages requiring this feature are used.

          Another feature of this package is the inclusion of non-breakable space after initials (like in personal 
          names), after or before academic degrees, and between numbers and units.

          The package supports both plain LuaTeX and LuaLaTeX.

          BTW: ''vlna'' is the Czech word for ''wave'' or ''curl'' and also denotes the tilde which, in TeX, is 
          used for ''unbreakable spaces''.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/generic/luavlna/luavlna-doc.pdf}

\section[\texttt{lucold} -- Use old-style digits with Lucida fonts]{\texttt{lucold} -- Use old-style digits with Lucida fonts}\label{pkg:lucold}
\index{Package!lucold}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lucold}
\item[name] \texttt{lucold}
\item[caption] Use old-style digits with Lucida fonts
\item[author] Loreti, Maurizio
\index{Author!Loreti, Maurizio}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides the means to switch the rendering of all the digits of a document from ‘lining’ 
          to ‘old-style’ numbers, when using Lucida fonts. The switch affects all digits in text mode, or all digits 
          in text and math mode. It works both for normal weight and boldface text and math; since the boldface 
          old-style digits are in the Lucida Expert font set, you need it for the boldface digits. Includes a set 
          of AWK programs used to automatically build  \texttt{.fd} , \texttt{.tfm} , and \texttt{.vf} files 
          from the existing Lucida PSNFSS distribution, and that may easily changed for the generation of different 
          virtual files for whatever font.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/lucold/README}

\section[\texttt{lwarp} -- Converts LaTeX to HTML]{\texttt{lwarp} -- Converts LaTeX to HTML}\label{pkg:lwarp}
\index{Package!lwarp}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/lwarp}
\item[name] \texttt{lwarp}
\item[caption] Converts LaTeX to HTML
\item[author] Dunn, Brian
\index{Author!Dunn, Brian}
\item[copyright] Brian Dunn (2016-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.921 (2026-02-24)
\item[last changes] 2026-02-24
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package converts LaTeX to HTML by using LaTeX to process the user’s document and generate HTML tags. 
          External utility programs are only used for the final conversion of text and images. Math may be represented 
          by SVG files or MathJax. Hundreds of LaTeX packages are supported, and their load order is automatically 
          verified.

          Documents may be produced by LaTeX, LuaLaTeX, XeLaTeX, and by several CJK engines, classes, and packages. 
          A  \texttt{texlua} script automates compilation, index, glossary, and batch image processing, 
          and also supports \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latexmk}{latexmk} . Configuration is semi-automatic 
          at the first manual compile. Support files are self-generated. Print and HTML versions of each document 
          may coexist.

          Assistance is provided for HTML import into EPUB conversion software and word processors.

          Requirements include the commonly-available Poppler utilities, and Perl. Detailed installation instructions 
          are included for each of the major operating systems and TeX distributions. A quick-start tutorial is 
          provided.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/lwarp/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Quick-start tutorial}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/lwarp/lwarp_tutorial.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/lwarp/lwarp.pdf}

          of your documents, not their appearance. LyX lets you concentrate on writing, leaving details of visual 
          layout to the software.

          LyX produces its output using LaTeX in the background; LyX is far more than a front-end to LaTeX, however. 
          No knowledge of LaTeX is necessary to use LyX, but such knowledge sometimes helps explain the way LyX 
          is behaving.

          LyX is not provided on CTAN; potential users should go to the  \href{http://www.lyx.org}{LyX

          without \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/etex}{e-TeX} .

          The ConTeXt code is no longer distributed. The LaTeX wrapper has not been needed since LaTeX switched 
          to e-TeX 20 years ago.

          However a LaTeX  \texttt{m-pictex.sty} is available via the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latex-context-ppchtex}{latex-context-ppchtex} package.

          documents using \texttt{m-pictex} rather than \texttt{pictex} .

\section[\texttt{makecell} -- Tabular column heads and multilined cells]{\texttt{makecell} -- Tabular column heads and multilined cells}\label{pkg:makecell}
\index{Package!makecell}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/makecell}
\item[name] \texttt{makecell}
\item[caption] Tabular column heads and multilined cells
\item[author] Lapko, Olga
\index{Author!Lapko, Olga}
\item[copyright] Olga Lapko (2005-2007)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.1e
\item[description] (no language specified) This package supports common layouts for tabular column heads in whole documents, based on one-column 
          tabular environment. In addition, it can create multi-lined tabular cells.

          The Package also offers:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item a macro which changes the vertical space around all the cells in a tabular environment (similar to the function of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tabls}{tabls} package, but using the facilities of the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/array}{array} )
          \item macros for multirow cells, which use the facilities of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/multirow}{multirow} package;
          \item macros to number rows in tables, or to skip cells;
          \item diagonally divided cells;
          \item horizontal lines in tabular environments with defined thickness.
          \end{itemize}

\index{Package!makecookbook}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/makecookbook}
\item[name] \texttt{makecookbook}
\item[caption] Make a Cookbook
\item[author] Murphy, Terrence
\index{Author!Murphy, Terrence}
\item[author] D’Amico, Rosalie
\index{Author!D’Amico, Rosalie}
\item[copyright] Terrence P. Murphy and Rosalie D’Amico (2018)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.85
\item[description] (no language specified) The makecookbook bundle contains the files needed to create a nice quality family cookbook in a form 
          ready to submit to most print-on-demand companies. Modifiable choices have been made regarding standard 
          book features such as trim size, margins, headers/footers, chapter heading formatting, front matter (copyright 
          page, table of contents, etc.) and back matter (index). Commands and environments have been created to 
          format the food stories and recipes. The user will need to:

          \begin{enumerate}
          \item supply their own food stories and recipes(!), and
          \item install the needed fonts. We assume a LuaTeX compile.
          \end{enumerate}
Please note that no new document class or package is included here. Rather, we provide a modifiable preamble 
          and a small number of other files that, together, fully support creation of all of the  \emph{internal} pages 
          of a cookbook (i.e., everything except the cover art).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/makecookbook/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/makecookbook/makecookbook-doc.pdf}

\index{Package!makegobbler}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/makegobbler}
\item[name] \texttt{makegobbler}
\item[caption] Keep or drop some part of LaTeX source code
\item[author] Belaïche, Vincent
\index{Author!Belaïche, Vincent}
\item[copyright] Vincent Belaïche (2025-2026)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version] 0.3.2 (2026-02-15)
\item[last changes] 2026-02-15
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) The makegobbler package provides a mechanism to selectively drop (gobble) or keep (''ungobble'') portions 
          of LaTeX source code, either conditionally or unconditionally. The affected code is delimited by user-defined 
          control sequences that act as explicit markers.

          For example, you can define a conditional as follows:  \texttt{{\textbackslash}newif{\textbackslash}ifkeep} 

          You can then make a portion of the source conditional like this:  \texttt{{\textbackslash}keepfalse} 

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}MGBkeep*{\textbackslash}ifkeep{\textbackslash}SomeArbitraryDelimitingControlSequence} 

          Here, everything — including  \texttt{{\textbackslash}fi\#!{\textbraceleft}{\textbraceright}\_{\textasciicircum}\$} — 
          is dropped.

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}SomeArbitraryDelimitingControlSequence}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/makegobbler/README.md}

          but in common with Knuth's system, there is a separate program (makeprog) for producing code to run (equivalent 
          to Knuth's tangle). However, \texttt{makeprog} doesn't rearrange code in the way that tangle 
          does.

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/makerobust}
\item[name] \texttt{makerobust}
\item[caption] Making a macro robust (legacy package)
\item[author] Oberdiek, Heiko
\index{Author!Oberdiek, Heiko}
\item[copyright] Oberdiek Oberdiek Package Support Group (2019)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 2.0 (2019-11-12)
\item[last changes] 2019-11-12
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) Heiko Oberdiek’s  \texttt{makerobust} package defined a command with name \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeRobustCommand} that 
          could be used to make fragile commands robust.

          The LaTeX format has, since 2015, included a command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeRobust} with 
          the same syntax and behaviour. Also by 2019, almost all commands in LaTeX that may be used in a moving 
          argument are already robust.

          This package is now just a simple one-liner defining the name  \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeRobustCommand} as 
          an alias for \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeRobust} .

          This package should not be used in any new documents.
\item[documentation]  (English) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/makerobust/makerobust.pdf}

\section[\texttt{manjutex} -- Manju language support]{\texttt{manjutex} -- Manju language support}\label{pkg:manjutex}
\index{Package!manjutex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/manjutex}
\item[name] \texttt{manjutex}
\item[caption] Manju language support
\item[author] Corff, Oliver
\index{Author!Corff, Oliver}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[description] (no language specified) Manju is a language of North East Asia, belonging to the Tungusic branch of the Altaic languages. Though 
          it is virtually not spoken anymore, it survives in written form as Manju was the native language of the 
          rulers of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) in China. Large quantities of documents of the Imperial Archives 
          survive, as well as some of the finest dictionaries ever compiled in Asia, like the Pentaglot, a dictionary 
          comprising Manju, Tibetan, Mongolian, Uighur and Chinese.

          ManjuTeX was developed on the basis of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/montex}{MonTeX} , 
          and provides all necessary characters for writing standard Manju as well as transliterated Tibetan texts, 
          for which purpose a number of additional characters were created.

          This catalogue entry describes the ‘original’ ManjuTeX; its functionality has now been subsumed into 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/montex}{monTeX} , though the obsolete ManjuTeX remains on 
          the archive.

\section[\texttt{manyfoot} -- Adds footnote levels to standard LaTeX’s footnote mechanism]{\texttt{manyfoot} -- Adds footnote levels to standard LaTeX’s footnote mechanism}\label{pkg:manyfoot}
\index{Package!manyfoot}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/manyfoot}
\item[name] \texttt{manyfoot}
\item[caption] Adds footnote levels to standard LaTeX’s footnote mechanism
\item[author] Rozhenko, Alexander I.
\index{Author!Rozhenko, Alexander I.}
\item[copyright] Alexander I. Rozhenko (1998-2005)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.11 (2019-08-03)
\item[last changes] 2019-08-03
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) Implements a command,  \texttt{{\textbackslash}newfootnote} , that adds footnote levels 
          to standard LaTeX’s footnote mechanism. Footnotes of every additional level are automatically grouped 
          together on a LaTeX2e output page and are separated from other levels by special vertical spaces. The 
          command \texttt{{\textbackslash}newfootnote} allows customisation of the way foonotes 
          of additional level are represented in LaTeX2e documents. Two customisation styles are available now: 
          the \texttt{plain} style is the ordinary LaTeX style of footnote representation; the \texttt{para} style 
          causes footnotes to be typeset as a run-in paragraph.

          This package is part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ncctools}{ncctools} bundle.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ncctools/doc/manyfoot.pdf}

\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ncctools}

\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides the commands

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{{\textbackslash}showlostmarginals} , to output lost marginal notes at the left of the page,
          \item  \texttt{{\textbackslash}enlargefreelist} , to provide more free space for marginals and floats (see also \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/morefloats}{morefloats} ); and
          \item  \texttt{{\textbackslash}onesidemarginals} , to force all marginal notes onto the same side of the page, thus leaving space for twice as many notes.
          \end{itemize}
The package was formerly part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/sttools}{sttools} bundle 
          and has been withdrawn by the author in June 2015.

\section[\texttt{marginfix} -- Patch {\textbackslash}marginpar to avoid overfull margins]{\texttt{marginfix} -- Patch {\textbackslash}marginpar to avoid overfull margins}\label{pkg:marginfix}
\index{Package!marginfix}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/marginfix}
\item[name] \texttt{marginfix}
\item[caption] Patch {\textbackslash}marginpar to avoid overfull margins
\item[author] Hicks, Stephen
\index{Author!Hicks, Stephen}
\item[copyright] Stephen D. Hicks (2010-2020)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.2 (2020-05-06)
\item[last changes] 2020-05-06
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) Authors using LaTeX to typeset books with significant margin material often run into the problem of long 
          notes running off the bottom of the page. A typical workaround is to insert  \texttt{{\textbackslash}vshift} commands 
          by hand, but this is a tedious process that is invalidated when pagination changes. Another workaround 
          is \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/memoir}{memoir} ’s \texttt{{\textbackslash}sidebar} function, 
          but this can be unsatisfying for short textual notes, and standard marginpars cannot be mixed with sidebars. 
          This package implements a solution to make marginpars ''just work'' by keeping a list of floating inserts 
          and arranging them intelligently in the output routine.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/marginfix/marginfix.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3049636439-marginfix.pdf|

          and places it in the margin of a document. The position of the margin is assumed, rather than calculated, 
          so the package will not work with other than the author’s original paper size (presumably letter). A 
          command for writing a pale ''DRAFT'' diagonally across a page, is also provided.

          The package apparently relies on PostScript code from the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/psfig}{psfig} bundle.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package uses a text font (usually the document’s text font) for the letters of the Latin alphabet 
          needed when typesetting mathematics. (Optionally, other characters in the font may also be used). This 
          facility makes possible (for a document with simple mathematics) a far wider choice of text font, with 
          little worry that no specially designed accompanying maths fonts are available. The package also offers 
          a simple mechanism for using many different choices of (text hence, now, maths) font in the same document. 
          Of course, using one font for two purposes helps produce smaller PDF files.

\index{License!gpl2}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 2}
\item[version] 1.3.2
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides macros for typesetting math formulas in mixed horizontal and vertical mode, automatically 
          as best fit.

          It provides an environment  \texttt{mathpar} that behaves much as a loose centered paragraph 
          where words are math formulas, and spaces between them are larger and adjustable. It also provides a 
          macro \texttt{{\textbackslash}inferrule} for typeseting fractions where both the numerator 
          and denominator may be sequences of formulas that will be also typeset in a similar way. It can typically 
          be used for typeseting sets of type inference rules or typing derivations. A macro inferrule for typesetting 
          type inference rules.

\section[\texttt{mathpazo} -- Fonts to typeset mathematics to match Palatino]{\texttt{mathpazo} -- Fonts to typeset mathematics to match Palatino}\label{pkg:mathpazo}
\index{Package!mathpazo}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathpazo}
\item[name] \texttt{mathpazo}
\item[caption] Fonts to typeset mathematics to match Palatino
\item[author] Puga, Diego
\index{Author!Puga, Diego}
\item[copyright] Diego Puga (2000, 2002)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 1.003
\item[description] (no language specified) The Pazo Math fonts are a family of PostScript fonts suitable for typesetting mathematics in combination 
          with the Palatino family of text fonts. The Pazo Math family is made up of five fonts provided in Adobe 
          Type 1 format (PazoMath, PazoMath-Italic, PazoMath-Bold, PazoMath-BoldItalic, and PazoMathBlackboardBold). 
          These contain, in designs that match Palatino, glyphs that are usually not available in Palatino and 
          for which Computer Modern looks odd when combined with Palatino. These glyphs include the uppercase Greek 
          alphabet in upright and slanted shapes in regular and bold weights, the lowercase Greek alphabet in slanted 
          shape in regular and bold weights, several mathematical glyphs (partialdiff, summation, product, coproduct, 
          emptyset, infinity, and proportional) in regular and bold weights, other glyphs (Euro and dotlessj) in 
          upright and slanted shapes in regular and bold weights, and the uppercase letters commonly used to represent 
          various number sets (C, I, N, Q, R, and Z) in blackboard bold.

          LaTeX macro support (using package mathpazo.sty) is provided in  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/psnfss}{psnfss} (a 
          required part of any LaTeX distribution).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/mathpazo/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Font tables:}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/mathpazo/pazotest.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This LaTeX package provides both syntactic and semantic helpers to typeset mathematics in LaTeX. The 
          syntactic layer eases typesetting of formulae in general, while the semantic layer provides commands 
          like  \texttt{{\textbackslash}inner{\textbraceleft}x{\textbraceright}{\textbraceleft}y{\textbraceright}} to 
          unify typesetting of inner products. These not only unify typesetting of math formulae but also allow

\item[description] (no language specified) MathsPIC(Perl) is a development of the earlier MathsPIC(DOS) program, now implemented as a Perl script, 
          being much more portable than the earlier program. MathsPIC parses a plain text input file and generates 
          a plain text output-file containing commands for drawing a diagram. Version 1.0 produces output containing 
          PiCTeX and (La)TeX commands, which may then be processed by plain TeX or LaTeX in the usual way. MathsPIC 
          also outputs a comprehensive log-file. MathsPIC facilitates creating figures using PiCTeX by providing 
          an environment for manipulating named points and also allows the use of variables and maths (advance, 
          multiply, and divide)—in short—it takes the pain out of PiCTeX. Both the original DOS version and the 
          new Perl version are available.

\section[\texttt{mathtex} -- A CGI program to use LaTeX to put mathematics on the web]{\texttt{mathtex} -- A CGI program to use LaTeX to put mathematics on the web}\label{pkg:mathtex}
\index{Package!mathtex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathtex}
\item[name] \texttt{mathtex}
\item[caption] A CGI program to use LaTeX to put mathematics on the web
\item[author] Forkosh, John
\index{Author!Forkosh, John}
\item[copyright] John Forkosh Associates, Inc. (2007-2014)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 1.05 (2014-12-06)
\item[last changes] 2014-12-06
\item[year] 2014
\index{Year!2014}
\item[description] (no language specified) MathTeX is a CGI program, written in C, that uses LaTeX and either dvipng or dvips/convert to emit GIF 
          or PNG images of LaTeX mathematical expressions. Users can put mathematics directly in html pages with 
          an <img> tag of the form\\ \texttt{<img src="/cgi-bin/mathtex.cgi?f(x)={\textbackslash}int\_{\textbraceleft}-{\textbackslash}infty{\textbraceright}{\textasciicircum}xe{\textasciicircum}{\textbraceleft}-t{\textasciicircum}2{\textbraceright}dt">} \\(see 
          the package home page for a complete discussion).

          MathTeX is a successor of the author's earlier  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mimetex}{mimeTeX} ; 
          but mathTeX uses real LaTeX, where as mimeTeX uses its own built-in fonts, interpreter and rendering 
          engine. Users who have LaTeX available on their server can obtain higher quality images and full LaTeX 
          support with mathTeX. Users whose server doesn't offer LaTeX can continue to use mimeTeX. The two programs 
          are ''plug-compatible'', using the same <img> tag ''user interface'', so migration is trivial.

          The package home page carries extensive documentation of MathTeX.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/mathtex/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package manual (HTML)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/mathtex/mathtex.html}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/mathtex}

\index{Topic!cgi-latex}
\item[language(s)] no language specified
\index{Language in description/documentation!no language specified}
\item[last access] 2025-02-07

\item[author] The LaTeX Project Team
\index{Author!The LaTeX Project Team}
\item[author] Madsen, Lars
\index{Author!Madsen, Lars}
\item[author] Robertson, Will
\index{Author!Robertson, Will}
\item[author] Wright, Joseph
\index{Author!Wright, Joseph}
\item[copyright] Lars Madsen, The LaTeX3 Project (2020-2024)
\item[copyright] Morten Høgholm (2002-2011)
\item[copyright] Lars Madsen (2012-2019)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.31 (2024-10-04)
\item[last changes] 2024-10-04
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) Mathtools provides a series of packages designed to enhance the appearance of documents containing a 
          lot of mathematics. The main backbone is amsmath, so those unfamiliar with this required part of the 
          LaTeX system will probably not find the packages very useful.

          Mathtools provides many useful tools for mathematical typesetting. It is based on  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/amsmath}{amsmath} and 
          fixes various deficiencies of amsmath and standard LaTeX. It provides:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Extensible symbols, such as brackets, arrows, harpoons, etc.;
          \item Various symbols such as  \texttt{{\textbackslash}coloneqq} (:=);
          \item Easy creation of new tag forms;
          \item Showing equation numbers only for referenced equations;
          \item Extensible arrows, harpoons and hookarrows;
          \item Starred versions of the amsmath matrix environments for specifying the column alignment;
          \item More building blocks: multlined, cases-like environments, new gathered environments;
          \item Maths versions of  \texttt{{\textbackslash}makebox} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}llap} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}rlap} etc.;
          \item Cramped math styles; and more...
          \end{itemize}
Mathtools requires  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mhsetup}{mhsetup} .

\section[\texttt{mathtype} -- Evaluation version of a commercial equation editor]{\texttt{mathtype} -- Evaluation version of a commercial equation editor}\label{pkg:mathtype}
\index{Package!mathtype}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathtype}
\item[name] \texttt{MathType}
\item[caption] Evaluation version of a commercial equation editor
\item[author] Virga, Bruce
\index{Author!Virga, Bruce}
\item[author] Mathews, Bob
\index{Author!Mathews, Bob}
\item[license] other-nonfree = License that prevents distribution (not free)
\index{License!other-nonfree}
\index{License!License that prevents distribution}
\item[version] 7
\item[description] (no language specified) MathType is a point and click mathematical equation editor. While its mouse-centric user interface is 
          somewhat the opposite of TeX’s, it has a number of features that may be of interest to members of the 
          TeX community:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item It works with many Windows applications that TeX does not work directly with, such as word processors, presentation programs like PowerPoint, and many more. You can even place equations in flowcharts made with programs like Visio.
          \item It can produce TeX and LaTeX code from its equations. This can be helpful to someone learning TeX or just to take advantage of MathType’s ability to work directly in mathematical notation in order to get the nested braces right on a particularly gnarly equation.
          \item You can even type TeX language directly into the MathType window. This allows you to get the best of both the WYSIWYG editing and TeX worlds.
          \item MathType can also produce GIF files for websites and blogs and EPS files for desktop publishing chores.
          \end{itemize}
MathType does not require a product key for installation. Upon first launch, you will have an opportunity 
          to begin a 30-day trial or to enter a purchased product key. If you decide to purchase MathType, you 
          can use the Order MathType command within MathType itself to purchase a product key. You can also visit 
          the Wiris website to learn more about MathType. If you have questions, email them to  \texttt{support@wiris.com} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/mathtype/README.txt}

\section[\texttt{maybemath} -- Make math bold or italic according to context]{\texttt{maybemath} -- Make math bold or italic according to context}\label{pkg:maybemath}
\index{Package!maybemath}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/maybemath}
\item[name] \texttt{maybemath}
\item[caption] Make math bold or italic according to context
\item[author] Buckley, Andy
\index{Author!Buckley, Andy}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version]  (2005-02-22)
\item[last changes] 2005-02-22
\item[year] 2005
\index{Year!2005}
\item[description] (no language specified) The  \texttt{{\textbackslash}maybebm} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}maybeit} macros 
          can be used in maths expressions to make the arguments typeset as bold or italic respectively if the 
          surrounding context is appropriate. They are useful for writing user macros for use in general contexts.

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}maybebm} is especially appropriate when section titles contain 
          math expressions, since the title will appear bold but the header and table of contents usually replicate 
          the title in normal width. It uses the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bm}{bm} package to 
          make things bold

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}maybeit} performs a similar role to \texttt{{\textbackslash}mathrm{\textbraceleft}{\textbraceright}} but 
          the maths expression will be italicised if the surrounding text is. \texttt{{\textbackslash}maybeitsubscript} is 
          provided to shift subscripts to the left if the expression is italicised.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package README}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/maybemath/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/maybemath/maybemath.pdf}

\item[last changes] 2021-09-12

\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) This LaTeX package automatically randomly permutes the order of questions as well as the answer options 
          in different versions of a multiple choice exam/test.

          Next to the exam versions themselves, the package also allows printing a concept version of the exam, 
          a key table with the correct answers or points, and a document with solutions and explanations per exam 
          version.

          The package also allows writing an R code which processes the results of the exam and calculates the 
          grades.

          The following other LaTeX packages are required:  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/enumitem}{enumitem} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/environ}{environ} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/etoolbox}{etoolbox} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/longtable}{longtable} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/newfile}{newfile} , \texttt{pgffor} (from 
          the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{PGF/TikZ} bundle), \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xstring}{xstring} .

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}

\item[caption] Multimedia inclusion for the dvisvgm backend
\item[author] Grahn, Alexander
\index{Author!Grahn, Alexander}
\item[copyright] Alexander Grahn (2020-2022)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)

\item[version] 0.13 (2022-10-12)
\item[last changes] 2022-10-12
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package implements an interface for embedding video and audio files in SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) 
          output. SVG with embedded media is very portable, as it is supported by all modern Web browsers across 
          a variety of operating systems and platforms, including portable devices.

          All DVI producing TeX engines can be used. The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dvisvgm}{dvisvgm} utility, 
          which is part of all major TeX distributions, converts the intermediate DVI to SVG. By default, media 
          files are embedded into the SVG output to make self-sufficient SVG files.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides an interface to embed interactive Flash (SWF) and 3D objects (Adobe U3D \& PRC), 
          as well as video and sound files or streams in the popular MP4, FLV and MP3 formats into PDF documents 
          with Acrobat-9/X compatibility. Playback of multimedia files uses the built-in Flash Player of Adobe 
          Reader and does, therefore, not depend on external plug-ins. Flash Player supports the efficient H.264 
          codec for video compression.

          The package is based on the RichMedia Annotation, an Adobe addition to the PDF specification. It replaces 
          the now obsolete  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/movie15}{movie15} package.

          Permissible document ‘base’ font sizes range from 9 to 60pt. There is a range of page-styles and well 
          over a dozen chapter-styles to choose from, as well as methods for specifying your own layouts and designs. 
          The class also provides the functionality of over thirty of the more popular packages, thus simplifying 
          document sources.

          Users who wish to use the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} package, in 
          a document written with the memoir class, should also use the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/memhfixc}{memhfixc} package 
          (part of this bundle). Note, however, that any current version of hyperref actually loads the package 
          automatically if it detects that it is running under memoir.

\section[\texttt{memoize} -- Externalization of graphics and memoization of compilation r\ldots]{\texttt{memoize} -- Externalization of graphics and memoization of compilation results in general}\label{pkg:memoize}
\index{Package!memoize}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/memoize}
\item[name] \texttt{Memoize}
\item[caption] Externalization of graphics and memoization of compilation results in general
\item[author] Živanović, Sašo
\index{Author!Živanović, Sašo}
\item[copyright] Saso Zivanovic (2020-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.4.1 (2024-12-02)
\item[last changes] 2024-12-02
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) Memoize is a package for externalization of graphics and memoization of compilation results in general, 
          allowing the author to reuse the results of compilation-intensive code. Memoize (i) induces very little 
          overhead, as all externalized graphics is produced in a single compilation. It features (ii) automatic 
          recompilation upon the change of code or user-adjustable context, and (iii) automatic externalization 
          of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} pictures and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/forest}{Forest} trees, 
          easily extensible to other commands and environments. Furthermore, Memoize (iv) supports cross-referencing, \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} overlays 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer}{Beamer} , (v) works with all major engines and 
          formats, and (vi) is adaptable to any workflow.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/memoize/README.md}

\item[description] (no language specified) Automatic handling of additional kinds of material by or during memoization with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/memoize}{Memoize} . 
          Provides support for memoizing content in tagged PDFs and compatibility with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ltx-talk}{ltx-talk} . \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} pictures 
          tagged with \texttt{alt} , \texttt{actualtext} or \texttt{artifact} are 
          handled automatically. The package supports automatic detection of expl3 syntax zones, auto-replication 
          of expl3 functions without ‘weird’ arguments and auto-memoization of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/l3experimental}{l3draw} pictures. 
          The code is arranged into interdependent modules so activation may be customised at load time.

\section[\texttt{mensa-tex} -- Typeset simple school cafeteria menus]{\texttt{mensa-tex} -- Typeset simple school cafeteria menus}\label{pkg:mensa-tex}
\index{Package!mensa-tex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/mensa-tex}
\item[name] \texttt{mensa-tex}
\item[caption] Typeset simple school cafeteria menus
\item[author] Friedl, Sebastian
\index{Author!Friedl, Sebastian}
\item[copyright] Sebastian Friedl (2017)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version]  (2017-12-03)
\item[last changes] 2017-12-03
\item[year] 2017
\index{Year!2017}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a flexible LaTeX2e class for typesetting school cafeteria menus consisting of two 
          lunches (with dessert), and dinner.

          It supports two different layouts:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item The first layout is optimized for printing the menu on A4 paper.
          \item The second layout is optimized for smartphone screens and uses one (A6 sized) page per day.
          \end{itemize}
Supported localizations are English (GB/US) and German. A way of defining additional localizations is 
          described in the documentation.

          The package requires  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/array}{array} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/colortbl}{colortbl} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datetime2}{datetime2} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/datetime2}{datetime2-calc} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/geometry}{geometry} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphicx}{graphicx} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lm}{lmodern} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/textcomp}{textcomp} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xcolor}{xcolor} .

\section[\texttt{metacapture} -- A package for the capture of author-supplied metadata]{\texttt{metacapture} -- A package for the capture of author-supplied metadata}\label{pkg:metacapture}
\index{Package!metacapture}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/metacapture}
\item[name] \texttt{metacapture}
\item[caption] A package for the capture of author-supplied metadata
\item[author] McCurley, Kevin
\index{Author!McCurley, Kevin}
\item[copyright] Joppe W. Bos and Kevin S. McCurley (2026)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.9.1
\item[description] (no language specified) Curation and indexing of metadata is a crucial part of journal publishing. The  \texttt{metacapture} package 
          is one component in an open source workflow implementation that is designed to automate the production 
          and copy editing of journal articles. It is used by the iacrj document class for the journal \href{https://cic.iacr.org/}{IACR 
          CiC} , but can also be used for other journals. It is intended primarily for use by LaTeX document 
          class designers, but may also be useful for authors who may wish to change their document class in the 
          future.

          When a document that loads  \texttt{metacapture.sty} is compiled, it produces a YAML-like 
          text file containing all metadata from the document. The \texttt{metacapture} package accomplishes 
          this by providing replacements for the generic macros \texttt{{\textbackslash}title} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}author} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}maketitle} macros 
          that have traditionally been used by document classes. The \texttt{metacapture} package also 
          provides several implementations of the \texttt{{\textbackslash}maketitle} macro n 
          different styles, partly as a way to demonstrate how to separate metadata capture from styling of front 
          matter. Document class designers can also write their own implementation of \texttt{{\textbackslash}maketitle} with 
          their preferred styling using the dictionary-like data structures used to hold author metadata.

          The  \texttt{metacapture} package is part of a larger set of tools for implementing a journal 
          publishing workflow. There is also a companion open source implementation of a publishing workflow written 
          in Python that is used for this journal and provides a simplified workflow for copy editing and production. 
          Further information on this workflow can be found in two articles that were published by the authors:

          
          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.10424}{Lowering the Cost of Diamond Open Access Journals} ,
          \item  \href{https://tug.org/TUGboat/tb46-3/tb144bos-workflow.html}{A LaTeX publishing workflow} 
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/metacapture/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/metacapture/metacapture-doc.pdf}

\item[last changes] 2021-02-05
\item[year] 2021

\item[description] (no language specified) The program takes a programmatic specification of a font, and produces a bitmap font (whose properties 
          are defined by a set of parameters of the target device), and metrics for use by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex}{TeX} .

          The bitmap output may be converted into a format directly usable by a device driver, etc., by the tools 
          provided in the parallel  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mfware}{mfware} distribution. Third 
          parties have developed tools to convert the bitmap output to outline fonts.

          The distribution includes the source of Knuth’s  \emph{Metafont book} ; this source is there 
          to read, as an example of writing TeX — it should not be processed without Knuth’s direct permission.

          The mailing list  \texttt{tex-fonts@math.utah.edu} is the best for general discussion of 
          Metafont usage; the \texttt{tex-k@tug.org} list is best for bug reports about building the 
          software, etc.

\item[caption] Plot-manipulation macros for use in MetaPost
\item[author] Moses, Brooks
\index{Author!Moses, Brooks}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.91
\item[description] (no language specified) MetaPlot is a set of MetaPost macros for manipulating
    pre-generated plots (and similar objects), and formatting them for inclusion in a MetaPost figure. The 
          intent is that the plots can be generated by some outside program, in an abstract manner that does not 
          require making decisions about on-page sizing and layout, and then they can be imported into MetaPlot 
          and arranged using the full capabilities of MetaPost. Metaplot also includes a very flexible set of macros 
          for generating plot axes, which may be useful in other contexts as well.

          Presently, MetaPlot is in something of a pre-release beta state; it is quite functional, but the syntax 
          of the commands is still potentially in flux.

\section[\texttt{metapost-matlab} -- MetaPost data plotting in Matlab style]{\texttt{metapost-matlab} -- MetaPost data plotting in Matlab style}\label{pkg:metapost-matlab}
\index{Package!metapost-matlab}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/metapost-matlab}
\item[name] \texttt{metapost-matlab}
\item[caption] MetaPost data plotting in Matlab style
\item[author] Yang, Yang
\index{Author!Yang, Yang}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[description] (no language specified) Matlab has powerful data plotting ability, but one annoying problem prevents it from being perfect: when 
          you increase the linewidth, the dotted line size stays the same, so the plotted line no longer looks 
          like a dotted line.

          Another problem is Matlab's bugs: it often cuts away some curves and captions. And, of course, Matlab 
          is expensive. On the other hand, the free  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/gnuplot}{Gnuplot} doesn't 
          produce very satisfactory visual effects either.

          The author got accustomed to Matlab's easy interface, and wanted to integerate the powerful graphic functions 
          of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/metapost}{MetaPost} with the interface of Matlab. The 
          outcome was matlab.mp. It is based on graph.mp (part of the MetaPost distribution). The package collects 
          data into 2D arrays, and remembers the line styles, so it's easy to plot out legends. The package features:

          – All kinds of line colour, width, style (dotted/dashed, etc), and markers (the code may easily be expanded);\\– 
          Easy interface, very similar to Matlab;\\– The full power of LaTeX is available in captions and legends, 
          by using the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latexmp}{latexmp} package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package README}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/metapost/contrib/macros/matlab/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{User guide}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/metapost/contrib/macros/matlab/user_guide.pdf}

\section[\texttt{metre} -- Support for the work of classicists]{\texttt{metre} -- Support for the work of classicists}\label{pkg:metre}
\index{Package!metre}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/metre}
\item[name] \texttt{metre}
\item[caption] Support for the work of classicists
\item[author] Boggio-Togna, Gianfranco
\index{Author!Boggio-Togna, Gianfranco}
\item[copyright] Gianfranco Boggio-Togna (2000, 2001)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides classicists with some of the tools that are needed for typesetting scholarly publications 
          dealing with Greek and Latin texts, with special emphasis on Greek verse.

          As the package's name suggests, its core is a comprehensive set of commands for generating metrical schemes 
          and for placing prosodical marks on text set in the Latin or the Greek alphabet. The rest of the package 
          provides a miscellany of commands for symbols (most of them not directly related to metre) that are often 
          used in critical editions of classical texts.

          The package does not require any special font: all symbols are taken from the Computer Modern fonts (which 
          are included in all TeX distributions) and the package's commands are based on TeX primitives.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/metre/metre.pdf}

\section[\texttt{metsymb} -- The package provides dedicated TeX commands to generate (vec\ldots]{\texttt{metsymb} -- The package provides dedicated TeX commands to generate (vectorial) meteorological symbols}\label{pkg:metsymb}
\index{Package!metsymb}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/metsymb}
\item[name] \texttt{metsymb}
\item[caption] The package provides dedicated TeX commands to generate (vectorial) meteorological symbols
\item[author] Vogt, Frédéric P.A.
\index{Author!Vogt, Frédéric P.A.}
\item[copyright] MeteoSwiss (2021-2023)
\item[license] bsd3 = 3-clause BSD License (free)
\index{License!bsd3}
\index{License!3-clause BSD License}
\item[version] 1.2.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The metsymb package introduces commands to generate official meteorological symbols with vectorial quality. 
          These include: oktas ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}zerookta} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}oneokta} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}twooktas} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}ldots} ), 
          cloud genera ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}cirrus} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}cirrostratus} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}nimbostratus} , 
          ...), and C\_L / C\_M / C\_H cloud codes ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}clIII} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}cmVI} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}chIX} , 
          ...).

          Individual symbols are designed using  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} . They are 
          then bundled into a dedicated font with \href{https://fontforge.org/en-US/}{FontForge} , 
          and eventually tied to dedicted LaTeX commands. The metsymb \textbf{OpenType font} is a side-product 
          that can be used on its own. This package essentially introduces a new font in which each symbol is assigned 
          to a glyph, which can then be called individually from LaTeX documents via dedicated commands.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/metsymb/README.md}

\section[\texttt{mf-ps} -- Metafont-PostScript conversions]{\texttt{mf-ps} -- Metafont-PostScript conversions}\label{pkg:mf-ps}
\index{Package!mf-ps}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/mf-ps}
\item[name] \texttt{mf-ps}
\item[caption] Metafont-PostScript conversions
\item[author] Jackowski, Bogusław
\index{Author!Jackowski, Bogusław}
\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[description] (no language specified) A Metafont support package including:\\

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{epstomf} , a tiny AWK script for converting EPS files into Metafont;
          \item  \texttt{mftoeps} for generating (encapsulated) PostScript files readable, e.g., by CorelDRAW, Adobe Illustrator and Fontographer;
          \item a collection of routines (in folder  \texttt{progs} ) for converting Metafont-coded graphics into encapsulated PostScript; and
          \item  \texttt{roex.mf} , which provides Metafont macros for removing overlaps and expanding strokes.
          \end{itemize}
In  \texttt{mftoeps} , Metafont writes PostScript code to a log-file, from which it may be 
          extracted by either TeX or AWK.

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/mf2pt1}

\item[caption] Convert stylized Metafont to PostScript Type 1
\item[author] Pakin, Scott
\index{Author!Pakin, Scott}
\item[copyright] Scott Pakin (2005-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 2.8
\item[description] (no language specified) mf2pt1 is a Perl script that facilitates producing PostScript Type 1 fonts from a Metafont source file. 
          It is not, as the name may imply, an automatic converter of arbitrary Metafont fonts to Type 1 format. 
          mf2pt1 imposes a number of restrictions on the Metafont input. If these restrictions are met, mf2pt1 
          will produce valid Type 1 output with more accurate control points than can be reverse-engineered by 
          TeXtrace,  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mftrace}{mftrace} , and other programs which convert 
          bitmaps to outline fonts.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides commands  \texttt{{\textbackslash}makefirstuc} that uppercases 
          the first letter in its argument (with a check for a semantic markup command at the start of the argument), 
          and {\textbackslash}xmakefirstuc which expands the argument before uppercasing. It also provides \texttt{{\textbackslash}capitalisewords{\textbraceleft} \emph{phrase} {\textbraceright}} which 
          applies \texttt{{\textbackslash}makefirstuc} to each word in the \texttt{ \emph{phrase} } , 
          where the words are separated by regular spaces. (Exceptions can be made for words that shouldn't be 
          converted.)

\item[description] (no language specified) Mfpic is a scheme for producing pictures from (La)TeX commands. Commands  \texttt{{\textbackslash}mfpic} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}endmfpic} (in 
          LaTeX, the \texttt{mfpic} environment) enclose a group in which drawing commands may be placed.

          The commands generate a Meta-language file, which may be processed by MetaPost (or even Metafont). The 
          resulting image file will be read back in to the document to place the picture at the point where the 
          original (La)TeX commands appeared. Note that the ability to use MetaPost here means that the package 
          works equally well in LaTeX and pdfLaTeX.

\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 2.00
\item[description] (no language specified) ''Making Friends with LaTeX'' (MFwL) is a small presentation which the author uses to introduce LaTeX 
          to his students. It is made using the Prosper Package. The objective of MFwL is to introduce newcomers 
          to LaTeX and make them aware of various aspects of working with LaTeX. It covers:

          (i) LaTeX Advocacy\\(ii) LaTeX Document Structure\\(iii) Paragraph Mode and Math Mode\\(iv) 
          Structuring the document\\(v) Creating Tables, Graphics (in very short)\\(vi) BibTeX\\(vii) 
          Recommendations for a LaTeX system\\(viii) References for further reading

          Its objective is not to make a person expert in using LaTeX but to get the person interested in LaTeX 
          by making him understand the LaTeX way of working. The intention is that once the person is comfortable 
          with the idea s/he can then explore the wonders of LaTeX on his/her own pace.

          packages (no longer distributed as a bundle) comprise:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/breqn}{breqn} , which enables automatic line-breaking in displayed equations;
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/empheq}{empheq} , which provides various mechanisms for ‘visual markup’ of mathematical matter;
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/flexisym}{flexisym} , which converts symbol definitions to a form usable within \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/breqn}{breqn} ;
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathstyle}{mathstyle} , which takes advantage of LaTeX’s suppression of some of TeX’s maths operators, to improve the performance of sub- and superscripts, and other aspects of mathematical typesetting style, including the ever-tricky \texttt{{\textbackslash}mathchoice} operator;
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathtools}{mathtools} , providing a range of extensions to maths as a whole; and
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mhsetup}{mhsetup} , which provides various programming tools for other packages of the set.

          The first ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}ihack} ) uses an insert to build a margin-full

          The other macro ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}vhack} ) just \texttt{{\textbackslash}vadjust} s 
          each note to the horizontal position where it starts; this requires no change to the output routine,

          tagging equations therein. It supports sub-numbering of blocks of equations (like (1.2a), (1.2b), etc) 
          and references to each equation individually (1.2a) or to the whole block (1.2). The labels can be shown

\section[\texttt{microtype} -- Subliminal refinements towards typographical perfection]{\texttt{microtype} -- Subliminal refinements towards typographical perfection}\label{pkg:microtype}
\index{Package!microtype}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/microtype}
\item[name] \texttt{microtype}
\item[caption] Subliminal refinements towards typographical perfection
\item[author] Schlicht, Robert
\index{Author!Schlicht, Robert}
\item[copyright] Robert Schlicht (2004-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 3.2 (2024-12-12)
\item[last changes] 2024-12-12
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a LaTeX interface to the micro-typographic extensions that were introduced by pdfTeX 
          and have since also propagated to XeTeX and LuaTeX: most prominently, character protrusion and font expansion, 
          furthermore the adjustment of interword spacing and additional kerning, as well as hyphenatable letterspacing 
          (tracking) and the possibility to disable all or selected ligatures.

          These features may be applied to customisable sets of fonts, and all micro-typographic aspects of the 
          fonts can be configured in a straight-forward and flexible way. Settings for various fonts are provided.

          Note that character protrusion requires pdfTeX, LuaTeX, or XeTeX. Font expansion works with pdfTeX or 
          LuaTeX. The package will by default enable protrusion and expansion if they can safely be assumed to 
          work. Disabling ligatures requires pdfTeX or LuaTeX, while the adjustment of interword spacing and of 
          kerning only works with pdfTeX. Letterspacing is available with pdfTeX or LuaTeX.

          The alternative package ‘letterspace’, which also works with plain TeX, provides the user commands for 
          letterspacing only, omitting support for all other extensions.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package README}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/microtype/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{User manual}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/microtype/microtype.pdf}

\index{Package!miktex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/miktex}
\item[name] \texttt{miktex}
\item[caption] A free TeX distribution for MS-Windows
\item[author] Schenk, Christian
\index{Author!Schenk, Christian}
\item[license] other-free = Free license not otherwise listed (free)
\index{License!other-free}
\index{License!Free license not otherwise listed}
\item[version] 24.12
\item[description] (no language specified) A distribution of TeX and friends for Windows 2000, XP, Vista and Windows 7, as well as Windows Server 
          2003 and 2008. Features include easy installation and configuration, and full TeX, LaTeX and ConTeXt 
          support. MiKTeX includes a set of ''canned'' distributions, up to installation of ‘everything there is’. 
          Users may update their installation manually, or they can allow MiKTeX to install new stuff automatically 
          (as needed), from the net.

          A command-line utility, ‘texify’, simplifies the production of DVI (or PDF) documents by automatically 
          invoking LaTeX (pdfLaTeX), Makeindex, and BibTeX as many times as necessary to produce a DVI (PDF) file 
          with sorted indices and all cross-references resolved.

          A '' \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/miktex-portable}{portable} '' distribution is available, 
          for users to carry in their pocket…

          Users of MiKTeX commonly control their work with an editor/shell; many are available, such as the free 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texniccenter}{texniccenter} and the shareware \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/winedt}{winedt} .

\item[description] (no language specified) The milestonetimeline package provides a flexible way to create horizontal milestone timelines in LaTeX 
          documents with support for date-based positioning, label rotation, and per-milestone customization. Features:

          
          \begin{itemize}
          \item Date-based positioning (ISO format: YYYY-MM-DD)
          \item Automatic spacing (when no dates provided)
          \item Customizable label rotation (0, 45, 90 degrees)
          \item Per-milestone height control
          \item Highlighted milestones (different color/shape)
          \item Compact and vertical presets
          \item Date markers on timeline
          \end{itemize}

\section[\texttt{milog} -- A LaTeX class for fulfilling the documentation duties
    ac\ldots]{\texttt{milog} -- A LaTeX class for fulfilling the documentation duties
    according to the German minimum wage law MiLoG}\label{pkg:milog}
\index{Package!milog}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/milog}
\item[name] \texttt{milog}
\item[caption] A LaTeX class for fulfilling the documentation duties
    according to the German minimum wage law MiLoG
\item[author] Kleber, Josef
\index{Author!Kleber, Josef}
\item[copyright] Josef Kleber (2016)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) Seit dem 1. Januar 2015 gilt in Deutschland grundsätzlich für alle Arbeitnehmer ein flächendeckender 
          gesetzlicher Mindestlohn in Höhe von derzeit 8,50€ pro Stunde. Mit Wirkung ab 1. August 2015 wurden die 
          Dokumentations- und Aufzeichnungspflichten gelockert. Nach §17 MiLoG, muss Beginn, Ende und Dauer der 
          täglichen Arbeitszeit der in §22 MiLoG definierten Arbeitnehmern (formlos) aufgezeichnet werden. Zusätzlich 
          ermöglicht milog.cls aus praktischen Gründen die Aufzeichnug von unbezahlten Pausen und Bemerkungen (Ruhetag, 
          Urlaub, krank, …).

          Die Erfassung der Arbeitszeiten erfolgt in einer simplen CSV-Datei, aus der die Klasse automatisch einen 
          Arbeitszeitnachweis erstellt. Alternativ können die Daten auch durch einen CSV-Export – mit eventueller 
          Nachbearbeitung – einer geeigneteten App erhoben werden.

          The milog.cls class provides means to fulfill the documentation duties by the German minimum wage law 
          MiLoG. The recording of working hours is carried out in a simple CSV file from which the class will automatically 
          create a time sheet. Alternatively, data can also be collected by a CSV export of a suitable app.

\item[description] (no language specified) MimeTeX parses LaTeX mathematics expressions, emitting either gif images or mime xbitmaps of them, rather 
          than the usual TeX DVI files. MimeTeX images are therefore easily inserted directly into html documents 
          using a standard html img tag without intermediate dvi-to-gif conversion, and without storing lots of 
          little gif image files, one file for each converted expression. This makes your web site and html documents

\index{License!eupl}

\item[version] 2025/1.7
\item[description] (no language specified) This is a modern plain format for the LuaTeX engine, adding improved low-level support for many LuaTeX 
          extensions and newer PDF features. While it can be used as drop-in replacement for plain TeX, it probably 
          is most useful as a basis for your own formats.

          Most features included in the format are provided by separate packages that can be used on their own; see the packages 
          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/minim-mp}{minim-mp} for mplib (MetaPost) support
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/minim-math}{minim-math} for unicode mathematics
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/minim-pdf}{minim-pdf} for creating Tagged PDF
          \item  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/minim-xmp}{minim-xmp} for XMP (metadata) inclusion
          \end{itemize}

          This package contains only their shared lowest-level programming interface, along with their combined 
          format.

\item[description] (no language specified) This package offers you a LaTeX style file and two classes to typeset articles or books in a simple and 
          clear way. These classes currently have native support for English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese 
          (European and Brazilian), and Spanish typesetting. They compile with any major TeX engine.

          You may also wish to consider the packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/einfart}{einfart} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/simplivre}{simplivre} , 
          which are enhanced versions of the classes provided here. They have unicode support, thus can only be 
          used with either XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX. Currently they have native support for Chinese (both simplified 
          and traditional), English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese (European and Brazilian), Russian 
          and Spanish typesetting, and also use more beautiful fonts.

\section[\texttt{minionpro} -- LaTeX support for Adobe MinionPro fonts]{\texttt{minionpro} -- LaTeX support for Adobe MinionPro fonts}\label{pkg:minionpro}
\index{Package!minionpro}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/minionpro}
\item[name] \texttt{minionpro}
\item[caption] LaTeX support for Adobe MinionPro fonts
\item[author] Blumensath, Achim
\index{Author!Blumensath, Achim}
\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[version] 2.1
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides support for the Minion Pro fonts from Adobe. (Note that the font family itself 
          is only available under commercial terms from Adobe.)

          The package offers access to a wide range of encodings and variants, including greek, cyrillic, four 
          figure versions, and maths alphabets.

          The base font is the Open Type version of Minion Pro; scripts are provided to convert the Open Type to 
          Adobe Type 1 format. (Minion Pro is commercially available, and copies are bundled with Acrobat Reader.) 
          The font is  \emph{not} bundled with this package.

          By default, the package sets up Minion-based maths alphabets, and uses such symbols as are available 
          in Minion, in maths mode. A complementary set of symbols is provided by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mnsymbol}{MnSymbol} fonts 
          and package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/minionpro/README}

\section[\texttt{minitoc} -- Produce a table of contents for each chapter, part or sectio\ldots]{\texttt{minitoc} -- Produce a table of contents for each chapter, part or section}\label{pkg:minitoc}
\index{Package!minitoc}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/minitoc}
\item[name] \texttt{minitoc}
\item[caption] Produce a table of contents for each chapter, part or section
\item[author] Drucbert, Jean-Pierre
\index{Author!Drucbert, Jean-Pierre}
\item[copyright] Jean-Pierre F. Drucbert (1993-2008)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 62
\item[description] (no language specified) The minitoc package allows you to add mini-tables-of-contents (minitocs) at the beginning of every chapter, 
          part or section. There is also provision for mini-lists of figures and of tables. At the part level, 
          they are parttocs, partlofs and partlots. If the type of document does not use chapters, the basic provision 
          is section level secttocs, sectlofs and sectlots.

          The package has provision for language-specific configuration of its own ''fixed names'', using  \texttt{.mld} files 
          (analagous to \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel}  \texttt{.ldf} files 
          that do that job for LaTeX''s own fixed names).

\item[description] (no language specified) The package supports those who publish articles in peer-reviewed journals. In the final stages of the 
          review process, the authors typically have to provide an additional document (such as a letter to the 
          editors), in which they provide a list of modifications that they made to the manuscript. The package 
          automatically provides line numbers and quotations from the manuscript, for this letter.

          The package loads the package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lineno}{lineno} , so (in effect)

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Support of tasks (who, schedule, what, time of finishing;
          \item possibility of creating a list of open tasks;
          \item inclusion of open tasks from other minutes;
          \item Support for attachments;
          \item Support of schedule dates (in planning: support for the calendar package);

\section[\texttt{missaali} -- A late medieval OpenType textura font]{\texttt{missaali} -- A late medieval OpenType textura font}\label{pkg:missaali}
\index{Package!missaali}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/missaali}
\item[name] \texttt{missaali}
\item[caption] A late medieval OpenType textura font
\item[author] Syrjänen, Tommi
\index{Author!Syrjänen, Tommi}
\item[copyright] Tommi Syrjänen (2016)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[license] ofl = The SIL Open Font License (free)
\index{License!ofl}
\index{License!The SIL Open Font License}
\item[version] 2.0
\item[description] (no language specified) This package contains the free OpenType Textura font Missaali and a style file for using it with XeLaTeX.

          Textura is a typeface based on the textus quadratus form of the textualis formata that late medieval 
          scribes used for the most valuable manuscripts. The font Missaali is based on Textura that German printer 
          Bartholomew Ghotan used for printing missals and psalters in the 1480s.

          This font has two intended use cases:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item as a Gothic display font; and
          \item for emulating late-medieval manuscripts.
          \end{itemize}
In addition to the basic textura letters, the font contains a large number of abbreviation sigla as well 
          as a set of Lombardic initials.

          As modern typesetting algorithms are not intended for creating 15th century style layout, the package 
          contains a XeLaTeX style file that makes it easier to achieve the classic incunabula look.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/missaali/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/missaali/missaali.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3934544473-missaali.pdf|

\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[version] 1.4
\item[description] (no language specified) MnSymbol is a symbol font family, designed to be used in conjunction with Adobe Minion Pro (via the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/minionpro}{MinionPro} package). 
          Almost all of LaTeX and AMS mathematical symbols are provided; remaining coverage is available from the 
          MinionPro font with the MinionPro package.

          The fonts are available both as Metafont source and as Adobe Type 1 format, and a comprehensive support 
          package is provided.

          While the fonts were designed to fit with Minon Pro, the design should fit well with other renaissance 
          or baroque faces: indeed, it will probably work with most fonts that are neither too wide nor too thin, 
          for example Palatino or Times; it is known to look good with Sabon. There is no package designed to configure 
          its use with any font other than Minion Pro, but (for example) simply loading mnsymbol after  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathpazo}{mathpazo} will 
          probably do what is needed.
