\section[\texttt{oops} -- A framework for making definitions, typically mathematical, \ldots]{\texttt{oops} -- A framework for making definitions, typically mathematical, inline}\label{pkg:oops}
\index{Package!oops}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/oops}
\item[name] \texttt{oops}
\item[caption] A framework for making definitions, typically mathematical, inline
\item[author] Rogard, Erwann
\index{Author!Rogard, Erwann}
\item[copyright] Erwann Rogard (2020)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) oops is a package for LaTeX (hence "scribe") that organizes (typically mathematical) definitions along 
          two dimensions: functions and objects, hence"OO".

          Such definitions are made inline thanks to a minimalist interface built upon xparse. To make a definition, 
          use {\textbackslash}OopsNew{\textbraceleft}<tl1>{\textbraceright}, where <tl1> identifies 
          an object, fol- lowed by input that alternates between "text" and instructions. The latter create and 
          expand definitions using rules that can be modified at the package level or themselves inline. This framework 
          is suitable for instance where <tl1> is either of ModelA and ModelB, and each requires its own definition 
          of, say, a space. In this case, they would be encoded respectively as {\textbackslash}Space{\textbraceleft}ModelA{\textbraceright} 
          and {\textbackslash}Space{\textbraceleft}ModelB{\textbraceright}. However, this would 
          be verbose if most functions applied to just one object, so the package provides a generic one that is 
          set by default to Math. For example, {\textbackslash}OopsNew{\textbraceleft}Math{\textbraceright}[Let{\textasciitilde}]{\textbraceleft}Space={\textbackslash}Omega{\textbraceright}[{\textasciitilde}denote 
          the sample space]{\textbraceleft}{\textbraceright}, followed by \${\textbackslash}Space\$, 
          expand to: "Let Omega denote the sample space" and "Omega".

          Other features automate repetitive formatting tasks. Altogether, "practical".

          As of April 2020, this package has been superseded by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ccool}{ccool} package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/obsolete/macros/latex/contrib/oops/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/obsolete/macros/latex/contrib/oops/oops.pdf}

\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.1
\item[description] (no language specified) This package addresses the problem of expressing citations in a style that is natural for humanities 
          studies, yet does not interfere with the flow of text (as author-year styles do).

          The package differs from  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/footbib}{footbib} in that it uses \emph{real} footnotes, 
          potentially in the same series as any of the document’s other footnotes. Opcit also, as its name implies, 
          avoids repetition of full citations, achieving this, to a large extent, automatically.

\item[name] \texttt{optidef}
\item[caption] Environments for writing optimization problems
\item[author] Lago Garcia, Jesus
\index{Author!Lago Garcia, Jesus}
\item[copyright] Jesus Lago Garcia (2016-2018)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 3.1 (2019-04-23)
\item[last changes] 2019-04-23
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) This small library provides a standard set of environments for writing optimization problems.

          It automatically aligns the problems in three points with an optional fourth:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Beginning of the words ''minimize/argmin'' and ''subject to''
          \item The objective function and the longest left hand side of the constraints.
          \item The  \texttt{\$= | > | <\$} signs of the constraints.
          \item Optionally, the user can add manually a double align character  \texttt{\&\&} to align some common constraints feature. A clear example could be the constraints names, e.g. (boundary constraint) alignment with (dynamic constraint).
          \end{itemize}
Furthermore, it provides an easy interface to define optimization problem for three different reference 
          situations:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Where no equation is referenced/numbered.
          \item Where the problem is referenced with a single number.
          \item Where each equation has an individual reference.
          \end{itemize}
Finally, it also allows a definition of any optimization problem without a limitless number of constraints.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/optidef/optidef.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package automatically places a copyright notice as an un-numbered footnote on the title page of 
          a document that calls  \texttt{{\textbackslash}maketitle} , indicating the information 
          on the workshop where the paper was presented, along with additional information on the host conference, 
          the license under which the document is published, and a link to the corresponding web page of the paper. 
          The generated copyright notice contains a logo of the workshop, and a QR code that points to the paper’s 
          web page (to lead to further material). For cases when the copyright notice is not automatically set 
          in the title page’s footnote, the copyright notice can be set manually as well.

\section[\texttt{pagecolor} -- Interrogate page color]{\texttt{pagecolor} -- Interrogate page color}\label{pkg:pagecolor}
\index{Package!pagecolor}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pagecolor}
\item[name] \texttt{pagecolor}
\item[caption] Interrogate page color
\item[author] Münch, Hans-Martin
\index{Author!Münch, Hans-Martin}
\item[copyright] H.-Martin Münch (2011-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.2d (2025-01-28)
\item[last changes] 2025-01-28
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides the command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}thepagecolor} , which gives 
          the current page (background) color, i. e. the argument used with the most recent call of \texttt{{\textbackslash}pagecolor{\textbraceleft}...{\textbraceright}} . 
          The command \texttt{{\textbackslash}thepagecolornone} gives the same color as \texttt{{\textbackslash}thepagecolor} , 
          except when the page background color is ''none'' (e.g., as a result of using the \texttt{{\textbackslash}nopagecolor} command). 
          In that case \texttt{{\textbackslash}thepagecolor} is ''white'' and \texttt{{\textbackslash}thepagecolornone} is 
          ''none''.

          When  \texttt{{\textbackslash}nopagecolor} is unknown or broken (crop package), this 
          package provides a replacement. Similar to \texttt{{\textbackslash}newgeometry} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}restoregeometry} of 
          the geometry package \texttt{{\textbackslash}newpagecolor{\textbraceleft}...{\textbraceright}} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}restorepagecolor} are 
          provided. For use with the crop package \texttt{{\textbackslash}backgroundpagecolor{\textbraceleft}...{\textbraceright}} as 
          well as \texttt{{\textbackslash}newbackgroundpagecolor{\textbraceleft}...{\textbraceright}} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}restorebackgroundpagecolor} are 
          provided.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pagecolor/pagecolor.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pagelayout} -- Layout graphic rich documents]{\texttt{pagelayout} -- Layout graphic rich documents}\label{pkg:pagelayout}
\index{Package!pagelayout}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pagelayout}
\item[Alias] \texttt{xput}
\index{Package!xput (alias for pagelayout)}
\index{Alias!xput (for pagelayout)}
\item[name] \texttt{pagelayout}
\item[caption] Layout graphic rich documents
\item[author] Bartels, Friedemann
\index{Author!Bartels, Friedemann}
\item[copyright] Friedemann Bartels (2022-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.1.1 (2024-07-31)
\item[last changes] 2024-07-31
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) The pagelayout class enables you to layout pages declaratively using simple macros for pages, covers, 
          grids, templates, text, and graphics to create graphic rich, perfectly typeset, and print ready PDFs.

          The integration of  \href{https://inkscape.org}{Inkscape} allows you to create box shadows.

          The integration of  \href{https://imagemagick.org}{ImageMagick} allows you to configure 
          compression and sharpening for bitmap graphics to export web, print or preview versions of your document. 
          Parallelized image optimization, caching, and a draft mode enable fast PDF creation and a responsive 
          workflow, even for large documents with lots of photos and graphics.

          The pagelayout class also integrates the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{PGF/TikZ} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tcolorbox}{tcolorbox} LaTeX 
          packages.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pagelayout/doc/pagelayout-manual.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pageslts} -- Variants of last page labels]{\texttt{pageslts} -- Variants of last page labels}\label{pkg:pageslts}
\index{Package!pageslts}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pageslts}
\item[name] \texttt{pagesLTS}
\item[caption] Variants of last page labels
\item[author] Münch, Hans-Martin
\index{Author!Münch, Hans-Martin}
\item[copyright] H.-Martin Münch (2010-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 2.0e (2025-06-05)
\item[last changes] 2025-06-05
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package was designed as an extension of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lastpage}{lastpage} package 
          — as well as that package’s \texttt{LastPage} label (created in hook \texttt{enddocument/afterlastpage} , 
          formerly \texttt{{\textbackslash}AtEndDocument} ) it adds a \texttt{VeryLastPage} (created 
          in the same hook, but formerly \texttt{{\textbackslash}AfterLastShipout} ).

          When more than one page numbering scheme is in operation (as in a  \texttt{book} class document 
          with frontmatter), the labels above do not give the total number of pages, so the package also provides 
          labels \texttt{pagesLTS.< \emph{numbering scheme} >} , where the \emph{numbering 
          scheme} is \texttt{arabic} , \texttt{roman} , etc.

          The package relies on the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/undolabl}{undolabl} package.

          Note: The ''LTS'' of the package name stands for: ''L'' = number of  \textbf{L} ast page, 
          ''T'' = \textbf{T} otal number of pages, ''S'' = page numbering \textbf{S} chemes 
          (roman, arabic, ...)
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pageslts/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package examples}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pageslts/pageslts-example.pdf}

          and the other deals with symbols; the implementation is quite similar.

          palettes based on this theme with specific color values for each of the theme's color slots. The active 
          palette for each theme can be swapped in to make experimenting with colors easier or give users choices 
          as to which theme they pick.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package offers LaTeX support for the fonts PT Sans, PT Serif and PT Mono developed by ParaType for 
          the project ''Public Types of Russian Federation'', and released under an open user license.

\item[version] 2.4
\item[description] (no language specified) Patgen takes a list of hyphenated words and generates a set of patterns that can be used by the TeX 82 
          hyphenation algorithm.

          Patgen was originally written by Frank M. Liang as part of his Stanford Ph.D. work, and has always been 
          distributed alongside the other programs coming from the Stanford TeX project. It was updated in 1991 
          by Peter Breitenlohner for the new 8-bit features of TeX version 3. (These updates related to input/output 
          and programming overhead; the actual pattern generation algorithms were not changed.)

          Patgen is currently maintained as part of TeX Live.

\section[\texttt{pax} -- Extract and reinsert PDF annotations with pdfTeX]{\texttt{pax} -- Extract and reinsert PDF annotations with pdfTeX}\label{pkg:pax}
\index{Package!pax}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pax}
\item[name] \texttt{pax}
\item[caption] Extract and reinsert PDF annotations with pdfTeX
\item[author] Roucariès, Bastien
\index{Author!Roucariès, Bastien}
\item[author] Oberdiek, Heiko
\index{Author!Oberdiek, Heiko}
\item[copyright] Bastien Roucariès (2020)
\item[copyright] Heiko Oberdiek (2006-2012)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version]  (2022-06-07)
\item[last changes] 2022-06-07
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) If PDF files are included using  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftex}{pdfTeX} , PDF annotations 
          are stripped. The pax project offers a solution without altering pdfTeX. A Java program (pax.jar) parses 
          the PDF file that will later be included. The program then writes the data of the annotations into a 
          file that can be read by TeX.

          The LaTeX package pax extends the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphics}{graphics} package 
          to support the scheme: if a PDF file is included, the package looks for the file with the annotation 
          data, reads them and puts the annotations in the right place.

          Project status: experimental
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package README}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pax/README}

\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides LaTeX support for using Caslon Open Face.

          Caslon Open Face font was desgined by Barnhart Brothers and Spindler in 1915. It was initially called 
          College Oldstyle and based on Le Moreau de Jeune from G. Peignot foundry. Its relation to the classical 
          Caslon font family is rather distant. Nevertheless it is a nice titling and display font.

          Adobe sells an OpenType version of this font, but other versions, including Adobe Type 1 are still available 
          from other vendors, including  \href{http://www.fonts.com}{fonts.com} . Note that there 
          are many ''free'' variants of this font available on the web; the package addresses the commercial product(s).

\section[\texttt{pdbf-toolkit} -- A Toolkit for Creating Janiform Data Documents]{\texttt{pdbf-toolkit} -- A Toolkit for Creating Janiform Data Documents}\label{pkg:pdbf-toolkit}
\index{Package!pdbf-toolkit}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdbf-toolkit}
\item[name] \texttt{pdbf-toolkit}
\item[caption] A Toolkit for Creating Janiform Data Documents
\item[author] Bender, Patrick
\index{Author!Bender, Patrick}
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 1.2.5
\item[description] (no language specified) PDBF documents are a hybrid format. They are a valid PDF and a valid HTML page at the same time. You 
          can now optionally add an VirtualBox OVA file with a complete operating system to the PDBF document. 
          This means that the resulting file is a valid PDF, HTML, and OVA file at the same time.

          If you change the file extension to PDF and open it with an PDF viewer, you can see the static part of 
          the document. If you change the file extension to HTML and open it with a Browser (currently Chrome, 
          Firefox, Safari, and IE 10 are supported), you can see the dynamic part of the document. And if an ova 
          file is attached you can also change the file extension to OVA and install and run the attached operating 
          system.

          The difference between the PDF and the HTML version is that the PDF version contains a static version 
          of all PDBF elements, whereas the HTML version is dynamic. For example you can zoom into graphs, temporarily 
          remove dataseries from the graph, inspect and change the underling query of the PDBF element and see 
          the result of the change directly in the browser. This approach works completely offline. No internet 
          connection is required, neither at compile time, nor at viewing time.

          The toolkit is licensed under the MIT License.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/pdbf-toolkit/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation (HTML)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/pdbf-toolkit/pdbf-doc.html}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{PDBF Documentation (HTML)}: \url{http://uds-datalab.github.io/PDBF/pdbf-doc.html}
\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{http://uds-datalab.github.io/PDBF}

\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/pdbf-toolkit}

\section[\texttt{pdfbook2} -- Create booklets from PDF files]{\texttt{pdfbook2} -- Create booklets from PDF files}\label{pkg:pdfbook2}
\index{Package!pdfbook2}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdfbook2}
\item[name] \texttt{pdfbook2}
\item[caption] Create booklets from PDF files
\item[author] Neumann, Johannes
\index{Author!Neumann, Johannes}
\item[copyright] Johannes Neumann (2015-2020)
\item[license] gpl3 = GNU General Public License, version 3 (free)
\index{License!gpl3}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 3}
\item[version] 1.4
\item[description] (no language specified) This python program creates print-ready PDF files from some input PDF files for booklet printing. The 
          resulting files need to be printed in landscape/long edge double sided printing. The default paper format 
          depends on the locale and is chosen by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xypic}{pdfjam} . It 
          can be chosen using the \texttt{--paper} option.

          Before the pdf is composed, the input file is cropped to the relevant area in order to discard unnecessary 
          white spaces. In this process, all pages are cropped to the same dimensions. Extra margins can be defined 
          at the edges of the booklet and in the middle where the binding occurs.

          The output is written to INPUT-book.pdf. Existing files will be overwritten. All input files are processed 
          seperately.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/pdfbook2/README}

\section[\texttt{pdfcolmk} -- Improved colour support under pdfTeX (legacy stub)]{\texttt{pdfcolmk} -- Improved colour support under pdfTeX (legacy stub)}\label{pkg:pdfcolmk}
\index{Package!pdfcolmk}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdfcolmk}
\item[name] \texttt{pdfcolmk}
\item[caption] Improved colour support under pdfTeX (legacy stub)
\item[author] Oberdiek, Heiko
\index{Author!Oberdiek, Heiko}
\item[copyright] Oberdiek Package Support Group (2019)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 2.0 (2019-11-24)
\item[last changes] 2019-11-24
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package used to provide macros that emulated the ‘colour stack’ functionality of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dvips}{dvips} . 
          The colour stack deals with colour manipulations when asynchronous events (like page-breaking) occur. 
          At the time the package was written, \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftex}{pdfTeX} did not 
          (yet) have such a stack, though \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dvips}{dvips} had had one 
          for a long time.

          This package was an experimental solution to the problem, and worked best with pdfeTeX.

          For current releases of pdfTeX (later than version 1.40.0, released in 2007), this package is not needed, 
          since ''real'' colour stacks are available. The present  \texttt{pdfcolmk} is therefore just 
          an empty stub that does nothing at all, just in case there are still documents that reference it.

          The documented source of the original package is still available at the  \href{https://github.com/ho-tex/old-source}{github 
          repository} .
\item[contact] \textit{bugs}: \url{https://github.com/ho-tex/pdfcolmk/issues}
\index{Contact!bugs}
\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{https://github.com/ho-tex/pdfcolmk}
\index{Contact!repository}

\index{Package!pdfcomment}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdfcomment}

\item[caption] A user-friendly interface to pdf annotations
\item[author] Kleber, Josef

\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 2.4a
\item[description] (no language specified) For a long time pdfLaTeX has offered the command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}pdfannot} for 
          inserting arbitrary PDF annotations. However, the command is presented in a form where additional knowledge 
          of the definition of the PDF format is indispensable. This package is an answer to the – occasional – 
          questions in newsgroups, about how one could use the comment function of Adobe Reader. At least for the 
          writer of LaTeX code, the package offers a convenient and user-friendly means of using \texttt{{\textbackslash}pdfannot} to 
          provide comments in PDF files. Since version v1.1, pdfcomment.sty also supports LaTeX → dvips → ps2pdf, 
          LaTeX → dvipdfmx, XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX.

          Unfortunately, support of PDF annotations by PDF viewers may vary. The reference viewer for the development 
          of this package is Adobe Reader.

\section[\texttt{pdfoverlay} -- A LaTeX style for overlaying text on a PDF]{\texttt{pdfoverlay} -- A LaTeX style for overlaying text on a PDF}\label{pkg:pdfoverlay}
\index{Package!pdfoverlay}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdfoverlay}
\item[name] \texttt{pdfoverlay}
\item[caption] A LaTeX style for overlaying text on a PDF
\item[author] Purton, David
\index{Author!Purton, David}
\item[copyright] David Purton (2018-2022)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.3 (2022-08-27)
\item[last changes] 2022-08-27
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) It is often desirable to take an exisiting PDF and easily add annotations or text overlaying the PDF. 
          This might arise if you wish to add comments to a PDF, fill in a PDF form, or add text to a PDF where 
          space has been left for notes.

          This package provides a simple interface to do this without having to resort to inserting one page at 
          a time. Some or all of the pages of the PDF can be included and not all pages of the PDF need have overlayed 
          text. It is also possible to include text  \emph{between} pages of the PDF.

          Another advantage of this package is that the overlayed text can be set as normal flowing from one page 
          to another or with manual page breaks if you wish. It is also possible to use any standard method to 
          position text at arbitrary places on a given page.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pdfoverlay/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pdfoverlay/pdfoverlay.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pdfreview} -- Annotate PDF files with margin notes]{\texttt{pdfreview} -- Annotate PDF files with margin notes}\label{pkg:pdfreview}
\index{Package!pdfreview}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdfreview}
\item[name] \texttt{pdfreview}
\item[caption] Annotate PDF files with margin notes
\item[author] Palmer, Michael
\index{Author!Palmer, Michael}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.2 (2019-02-22)
\item[last changes] 2019-02-22
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package lets you add comments in the page margins of PDF files, e.g. when reviewing manuscripts 
          or grading reports. The PDF file to be annotated is included, one page at a time, as graphics, in a manner 
          similar to the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdfpages}{pdfpages} package. Notes are placed 
          in the margin next to the included graphics using a grid of help lines. Alternatively, only numbers are 
          placed in the page margins, and the notes are collected into a numbered list at the end of the document.

          Note that this package is  \emph{not} intended for adding notes directly to the LaTeX source 
          of the document that is being reviewed; instead, the document undergoing review is already in PDF format 
          and remains unchanged. Also note that this package does not produce the usual PDF ''sticky notes'' that 
          must be opened by clicking on them; instead, the notes are simply shown as text.

          This package depends on the following other LaTeX package:  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/adjustbox}{adjustbox} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/calc}{calc} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/geometry}{geometry} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphicx}{graphicx} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/grffile}{grffile} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ifthen}{ifthen} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/kvoptions}{kvoptions} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{tikz} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ulem}{ulem} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xstring}{xstring} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pdfreview/pdfreview.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) pdfToolbox is a toolbox of various ''subpackages'' intended for programming and creating beautiful plain-pdfTeX 
          documents.

          It is an amalgamation of the following ''subpackages'' (in the future there will be an ability to access 
          each one by itself):

          \begin{enumerate}
          \item pdfData — for storing and manipulating data;
          \item pdfDstruct — for managing the layout and structure of your document;
          \item pdfGraphics — for adding some color and illustrations to your document.
          \end{enumerate}
pdfToolbox currently only works with pdfTeX. It is not compatible with any form of LaTeX, and currently 
          does not work with XeTeX or LuaTeX (though hopefully LuaTeX support will be added in the future).

\section[\texttt{pdftricks} -- Support for PSTricks in pdfTeX]{\texttt{pdftricks} -- Support for PSTricks in pdfTeX}\label{pkg:pdftricks}
\index{Package!pdftricks}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftricks}
\item[name] \texttt{pdftricks}
\item[caption] Support for PSTricks in pdfTeX
\item[author] Radhakrishnan, C. V.
\index{Author!Radhakrishnan, C. V.}
\item[author] Rajagopal, C. V.
\index{Author!Rajagopal, C. V.}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 1.16
\item[description] (no language specified) The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} macros cannot be used (directly) 
          with pdfTeX, since PSTricks uses PostScript arithmetic, which isn't part of PDF. This package circumvents 
          this limitation so that the extensive facilities offered by the powerful PSTricks package can be made 
          use of in a pdfTeX document. This is done using the shell escape function available in current TeX implementations.

          The package may also be used in support of other ‘PostScript-output-only’ packages, such as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/psfrag}{PSfrag} .

          For alternatives, users may care to review the discussion in the PSTricks  \href{https://tug.org/PSTricks/main.cgi?file=pdf/pdfoutput}{online 
          documentation} .

          bounding box of (some of) the pages of the document, and then uses \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftex}{pdflatex} (with

          document.

          tiles. It currently supports the kite/dart, rhombus, and pentagon tile sets. There are two main methods 
          for their placement: one that automatically generates a tiling, and one that allows for ''by hand'' placement. 
          Furthermore, the tiles themselves can be deformed and will still (hopefully!) fit together in the correct 
          fashion.

          This package is now superseded by package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tilings}{tilings} , 
          which deals with more extensive tiles than just the Penrose tile sets.

\section[\texttt{perfectcut} -- Nested delimiters that consistently grow regardless of the c\ldots]{\texttt{perfectcut} -- Nested delimiters that consistently grow regardless of the contents}\label{pkg:perfectcut}
\index{Package!perfectcut}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/perfectcut}
\item[name] \texttt{perfectcut}
\item[caption] Nested delimiters that consistently grow regardless of the contents
\item[author] Munch-Maccagnoni, Guillaume
\index{Author!Munch-Maccagnoni, Guillaume}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 2.3
\item[description] (no language specified) This package defines the command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}perfectcut\#1\#2} which 
          displays a bracket \texttt{<\#1||\#2>} . Various other delimiters are similarly defined 
          (parentheses, square brackets ...). The effect of these commands is to let the delimiters grow according 
          to the number of nested \texttt{{\textbackslash}perfectcommands} (regardless of the 
          size of the contents).

          The package was originally intended for solving a notational issue for direct-style continuation calculi 
          in proof theory. For general use, the package also defines commands for defining other sorts of delimiters 
          which will behave in the same way (see example in the documentation). The package also offers a robust 
          reimplementation of {\textbackslash}big, {\textbackslash}bigg, etc.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/perfectcut/perfectcut.pdf}

\item[author] Pakin, Scott
\index{Author!Pakin, Scott}
\item[copyright] Scott Pakin (2003-2024)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 2.3
\item[description] (no language specified) PerlTeX is a combination Perl script (perltex.pl) and LaTeX2e package (perltex.sty) that, together, give 
          the user the ability to define LaTeX macros in terms of Perl code. Once defined, a Perl macro becomes 
          indistinguishable from any other LaTeX macro. PerlTeX thereby combines LaTeX's typesetting power with 
          Perl's programmability. PerlTeX will make use of persistent named pipes, and thereby run more efficiently, 
          on operating systems that offer them (mostly Unix-like systems).

          Also provided is a switch to generate a PerlTeX-free, document-specific, noperltex.sty that is useful 
          when distributing a document to places where PerlTeX is not available.

\item[author] Kastrup, David
\index{Author!Kastrup, David}
\item[license] gpl2 = GNU General Public License, version 2 (free)
\index{License!gpl2}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 2}
\item[version] 1.12
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a mechanism to reset counters per page and/or keep their occurences sorted in order 
          of appearance on the page.

          The package also defines a command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakePerPage} that designates 
          a counter to be reset per page. For example \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakePerPage[2]{\textbraceleft}footnote{\textbraceright}} will 
          cause footnote numbers to start at 2 at the start of every page (the optional argument defaults to 1). 
          The machanism may require multiple passes to work; LaTeX gives the usual changed label warning if this 
          is necessary.

          The package is distributed as part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bigfoot}{bigfoot} bundle.

          By default  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{pgf} used to support only RGB shadings. The 
          package attempts to produce shadings consistent with the currently selected \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xcolor}{xcolor} colour

          models from the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xcolor}{xcolor} package are supported.

          \textbf{Note:} This package has been deprecated since \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{pgf 
          version 3.1.3} , since CMYK and grayscale shadings are now directly supported.

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}

\item[caption] Create custom periodic tables of elements
\item[author] Gomes, Hugo

\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)

\item[version] 2.1.5 (2025-02-10)
\item[last changes] 2025-02-10
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The purpose of this package is to provide the Periodic Table of Elements in a simple way. It relies on 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{PGF/TikZ} to offer a full or partial periodic table 
          with a variety of options and displaying the desired data for all the 118 elements. It can be done in 
          different languages: English, French, German, Portuguese (from Portugal and from Brazil), Spanish, Italian 
          and translations provided by user contributions -- currently in Dutch and Chinese.

\section[\texttt{pgf-spectra} -- Draw continuous or discrete spectra using PGF/TikZ]{\texttt{pgf-spectra} -- Draw continuous or discrete spectra using PGF/TikZ}\label{pkg:pgf-spectra}
\index{Package!pgf-spectra}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf-spectra}
\item[name] \texttt{pgf-spectra}
\item[caption] Draw continuous or discrete spectra using PGF/TikZ
\item[author] Gomes, Hugo
\index{Author!Gomes, Hugo}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 3.0.2 (2025-06-16)
\item[last changes] 2025-06-16
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The purpose of this package is to draw the spectrum of elements in a simple way. It relies on  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{PGF/TikZ} to 
          draw the desired spectrum, continuous or discrete.

          Data for the spectra of 98 elements and their ions are available (from the NASA database and from NIST). 
          Lines data ranges from Extreme UV to Near IR (from 10 to 4000 nanometers).

          It also allows the user to draw spectra using their own data.

          It is possible to redshift the lines of a spectrum, by directly entering the redshift value or the velocity 
          and the angle to compute the redshift value.

          Spectral lines data can be presented in a table or exported to a file.

          The package also provides color conversion (correlated color temperature), shadings for use with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} and/or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgfplots}{pgfplots} and 
          color maps for use with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgfplots}{pgfplots} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/pgf-spectra/pgf-spectraManual.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pgfmath-xfp} -- Define pgfmath functions using xfp]{\texttt{pgfmath-xfp} -- Define pgfmath functions using xfp}\label{pkg:pgfmath-xfp}
\index{Package!pgfmath-xfp}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgfmath-xfp}
\item[name] \texttt{pgfmath-xfp}
\item[caption] Define pgfmath functions using xfp
\item[author] Spratte, Jonathan P.
\index{Author!Spratte, Jonathan P.}
\item[copyright] Jonathan P. Spratte (2020-2021)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0a (2025-01-11)
\item[last changes] 2025-01-11
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package allows to define  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{pgfmath} functions that 
          use the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xfp}{xfp} fpu for their calculations.

          The input arguments are parsed with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{pgfmath} (while 
          the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{pgf} -fpu is locally active), and the results are 
          forwarded to \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xfp}{xfp} ’s fpu for the function evaluation. 
          The result of that calculation is then parsed by pgfmath again (with the surrounding settings of pgfmath). 
          This way the functions should be usable in every pgfmath context, though there is some overhead to this 
          approach.

          The package is only meant as a temporary stopgap until a more dedicated solution is available to use 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xfp}{xfp} in \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{pgf} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pgfmath-xfp/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pgfmath-xfp/pgfmath-xfp.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./9315654265-pgfmath-xfp.pdf|
\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{https://github.com/Skillmon/ltx_pgfmath-xfp}
\index{Contact!repository}

          for Chinese traditional motifs and patterns. The command \texttt{{\textbackslash}pgfornamenthan} takes 
          the same options as \texttt{{\textbackslash}pgfornament} from the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgfornament}{pgfornament} package, 
          but renders Chinese traditional motifs instead. The list of supported motifs, as well as some examples, 
          can be found in the accompanying documentation.

          This bundle also provides three beamer themes incorporating these motifs; sample  \texttt{.tex} files 
          for creating beamer presentations and posters are included.

\item[description] (no language specified) The pgothic and allpgoth packages provide Metafont fonts based on the Gothic Textura Prescisus vel sine 
          pedibus manuscript book-hand used from the 13th century AD. The font consists of majuscules, minuscules, 
          and digits, with some appropriate period punctuation marks and ligatures. Both normal and bold versions 
          are provided.

          to the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/docmfp}{docmfp} package is desirable but not essential 
          to compile the package documentation.

\index{License!lppl}

\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) A font that contains all the symbols of the famous  \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaistos\_Disc}{Disc 
          of Phaistos} , together with a LaTeX package. The disc was ‘printed’ by stamping the wet clay with 
          some sort of punches, probably around 1700 BCE. The font is available in Adobe Type 1 and OpenType formats 
          (the latter using the Unicode positions for the symbols).

          There are those who believe that this Cretan script was used to ‘write’ Greek (it is known, for example, 
          that the rather later Cretan  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/linearb}{Linear B} script was 
          used to write Greek), but arguments for other languages have been presented.

A convenient syntax enables you to mark text additions (e.g., '' \verb|... \phf{I'm adding this text} ...| '' or '' \verb|... \phf I'm adding this text\endphf ...| ''), an in-line comment (e.g., '' \verb|... \section[\texttt{phfextendedabstract} -- Typeset extended abstracts for conferences, such as often en\ldots]{\texttt{phfextendedabstract} -- Typeset extended abstracts for conferences, such as often encountered in quantum information theory}\label{pkg:phfextendedabstract}
\index{Package!phfextendedabstract}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/phfextendedabstract}
\item[name] \texttt{phfextendedabstract}
\item[caption] Typeset extended abstracts for conferences, such as often encountered in quantum information theory
\item[author] Faist, Philippe
\index{Author!Faist, Philippe}
\item[copyright] Philippe Faist, philippe.faist@bluewin.ch (2021)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.0 (2021-09-08)
\item[last changes] 2021-09-08
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) Several conferences in various fields (such as quantum information theory) require the submission of 
          \emph{extended abstracts} . An extended abstract is a summary of a scientific result, presented 
          at a high level, and consisting of at most a small handful of pages.

          The  \texttt{phfextendedabstract} LaTeX class provides a simple style for such abstracts. 
          There are only two sectioning levels, sections and paragraphs, and the style is optimized to save space 
          as well as to guide the reader's eye through the overall structure of the document. An option will try 
          to compress all vertical space to save some space, in case you need to satisfy page constraints. The 
          style builds upon the powerful \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/revtex}{RevTeX} class, so you 
          can use all of RevTeX's features such as author affiliations, etc.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/phfextendedabstract/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/phfextendedabstract/phfextendedabstract.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./4554604012-phfextendedabstract.pdf|

\section[\texttt{physconst} -- Macros for commonly used physical constants]{\texttt{physconst} -- Macros for commonly used physical constants}\label{pkg:physconst}
\index{Package!physconst}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/physconst}
\item[name] \texttt{physconst}
\item[caption] Macros for commonly used physical constants
\item[author] Mulligan, Brian W.
\index{Author!Mulligan, Brian W.}
\item[copyright] Brian W. Mulligan (2020)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.1.2 (2021-03-26)
\item[last changes] 2021-03-26
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package consists of several macros that are shorthand for a variety of physical constants, e.g. 
          the speed of light. The package developed out of physics and astronomy classes that the author has taught 
          and wanted to ensure that he had correct values for each constant and did not wish to retype them every 
          time he uses them.

          The constants can be used in two forms, the most accurate available values, or versions that are rounded 
          to 3 significant digits for use in typical classroom settings, homework assignments, etc.

          Most constants are taken from CODATA 2018, with the exception of the astronomical objects, whose values 
          are taken from International Astronomical Union specified values. Constants that are derived from true 
          constants, e.g. the fine structure constant, have been calculated using the accepted values of the fundamental 
          constants.

          You can load modules separately after loading \texttt{physics2} .

          \begin{itemize}

          \item Dirac bra-ket notation;

\index{Package!pi}

\item[caption] Calculate pi
\item[author] Roegel, Denis B.
\index{Author!Roegel, Denis B.}
\item[license] noinfo = noinfo 
\index{License!noinfo}
\index{License!noinfo}
\item[version] 0.993
\item[description] (no language specified) Generates pi, using the formula: 
          \begin{verbatim}
Pi=16*arctan(1/5)-4*arctan(1/239)
          \end{verbatim}
and leaves the result in an array \texttt{{\textbackslash}xr} , printing what is calculated as it goes along.

          The number of digits you can compute depends on your implementation of TeX. The last digit may be wrong, 
          and if it's 0 or 9, the penultimate digit may also be wrong.
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/plain/contrib/misc/pi.tex}

\item[author] Niepraschk, Rolf
\index{Author!Niepraschk, Rolf}
\item[author] Tkadlec, Josef
\index{Author!Tkadlec, Josef}
\item[author] Gäßlein, Hubert
\index{Author!Gäßlein, Hubert}
\item[copyright] Rolf Niepraschk, Hubert Gaesslein, Josef Tkadlec (2003-2020)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}

\item[version] 0.4b (2020-09-30)
\item[last changes] 2020-09-30
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package was described in the 2nd edition of ‘LaTeX: A Document Preparation System’, but the LaTeX 
          project team declined to produce the package. For a long time, LaTeX included a ‘pict2e package’ that 
          merely produced an apologetic error message.

          The new package extends the existing LaTeX picture environment, using the familiar technique (cf. the 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphics}{graphics} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/color}{color} packages) 
          of driver files (at present, drivers for \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dvips}{dvips} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftex}{pdfTeX} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/luatex}{LuaTeX} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xetex}{XeTeX} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/vtex-free}{VTeX} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dvipdfm}{dvipdfm} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dvipdfmx}{dvipdfmx} are available). The package documentation 
          has a fair number of examples of use, showing where things are improved by comparison with the LaTeX 
          picture environment.

\index{Package!pkbbox}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pkbbox}
\item[name] \texttt{pkbbox}

\item[author] Walsh, Norman
\index{Author!Walsh, Norman}
\item[license] noinfo = noinfo 
\index{License!noinfo}
\index{License!noinfo}
\item[version]  (1992-11-30)
\item[last changes] 1992-11-30
\item[year] 1992
\index{Year!1992}
\item[description] (no language specified) The author found that AFM files generated by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pfm2afm}{pfm2afm} lacked 
          glyph bounding box information, so that they are not much use for generating TFM files. This package 
          proceeds by generating a PK file from the Type 1 font by use of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ps2pk}{ps2pk} , 
          and then using information from that to generate a more nearly valid AFM file from the original.

\section[\texttt{pkfix-helper} -- Make PostScript files accessible to pkfix]{\texttt{pkfix-helper} -- Make PostScript files accessible to pkfix}\label{pkg:pkfix-helper}
\index{Package!pkfix-helper}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pkfix-helper}
\item[name] \texttt{pkfix-helper}
\item[caption] Make PostScript files accessible to pkfix
\item[author] Pakin, Scott
\index{Author!Pakin, Scott}
\item[copyright] Scott Pakin (2009-2020)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.6 (2020-08-06)
\item[last changes] 2020-08-06
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pkfix}{Pkfix} is a useful utility for replacing resolution-dependent 
          bitmapped fonts in a dvips-produced PostScript file with the corresponding resolution-independent vector 
          fonts. Unfortunately, pkfix needs to parse certain PostScript comments that appear only in files produced 
          by dvips versions later than 5.58 (ca. 1996); it fails to work on PostScript files produced by older 
          versions of dvips.

          Pkfix-helper is a program that attempts to insert newer-dvips comments into an older-dvips PostScript 
          file, thereby making the file suitable for processing by pkfix. pkfix-helper can sometimes process documents 
          fully autonomously but does require the user to verify and, if needed, correct its decisions.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Encoding tables and how to use them}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/pkfix-helper/encoding-samples.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./5110654189-encoding-samples.pdf|

\item[-- local file] \verb|./4687195301-pkfix-helper.pdf|

\section[\texttt{plain-ltx} -- Make plain TeX files LaTeXable]{\texttt{plain-ltx} -- Make plain TeX files LaTeXable}\label{pkg:plain-ltx}
\index{Package!plain-ltx}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/plain-ltx}
\item[name] \texttt{plain-ltx}
\item[caption] Make plain TeX files LaTeXable
\item[author] Carlisle, David
\index{Author!Carlisle, David}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package plain.sty defines a LaTeX environment which can process a document written to use Knuth's 
          basic  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/plain}{Plain TeX} macros.

          Inside the environment, not everything is as Knuth intended (some Plain commands are suppressed, some 
          are faked, and some basic mechanisms—such as font selection and the output routine—remain as in LaTeX). 
          Thus ''simple'' documents will run, but elaborate macros defined in the document have a chance of failing.

          The package is distributed as part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/carlisle}{carlisle} bundle.
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/carlisle/plain.sty}

\index{Package!plautopatch}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/plautopatch}
\item[name] \texttt{plautopatch}
\item[caption] Automated patches for pLaTeX/upLaTeX
\item[author] Yamashita, Hironobu
\index{Author!Yamashita, Hironobu}
\item[copyright] Hironobu Yamashita (2018-2021)
\item[license] bsd3 = 3-clause BSD License (free)
\index{License!bsd3}
\index{License!3-clause BSD License}
\item[version] 0.9q (2021-12-07)
\item[last changes] 2021-12-07
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) Japanese pLaTeX/upLaTeX formats and packages often conflict with other LaTeX packages which are unaware 
          of pLaTeX/upLaTeX. In the worst case, such packages throw a fatal error or end up with a wrong output.

          The goal of this package is that there should be no need to worry about such incompatibilities, because 
          specific patches are loaded automatically whenever necessary. This helps not only to simplify source 
          files, but also to make the appearance of working pLaTeX/upLaTeX sources similar to those of ordinary 
          LaTeX ones.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation (English)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/jptex/latex/plautopatch/plautopatch.pdf}

\item[last changes] 2022-09-28
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides the PlayFairDisplay family of fonts, designed by Claus Eggers Sørensen, for use 
          with LaTeX, pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX.

          PlayFairDisplay is well suited for titling and headlines. It has an extra large x-height and short descenders. 
          It can be set with no leading if space is tight, for instance in news headlines, or for stylistic effect 
          in titles. Capitals are extra short, and only very slightly heavier than the lowercase characters. This 
          helps achieve a more even typographical colour when typesetting proper nouns and initialisms.

\section[\texttt{pmdb} -- Create a DB (PDF) document for selecting content for inclusi\ldots]{\texttt{pmdb} -- Create a DB (PDF) document for selecting content for inclusion in another documents}\label{pkg:pmdb}
\index{Package!pmdb}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pmdb}
\item[name] \texttt{pmdb}
\item[caption] Create a DB (PDF) document for selecting content for inclusion in another documents
\item[author] Story, Donald P.
\index{Author!Story, Donald P.}
\item[copyright] D. P. Story (2019-2021)
\item[license] lppl1.2 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.2}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2}
\item[version]  (2021-06-07)
\item[last changes] 2021-06-07
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) The ''poor man's database'' (pmdb) package promotes a workflow for building exams, homework, and other 
          content. The package supports the creation of a PDF document, which is a database of problems (or content) 
          to be included in a target document.

          The package inserts checkboxes into the margins of the DB document. The instructor can select which which 
          of the problems are to be included in the target document by checking one ore more of the checkboxes. 
          By clicking the special  \texttt{{\textbackslash}displayChoices} control, the selected 
          content is copied into the AR/AA console window in the form of \texttt{{\textbackslash}input} statements 
          ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}input{\textbraceleft}prob1.tex{\textbraceright}} , 
          eg), which is then be copied and pasted into the target document. By pressing \texttt{Ctrl+Click} while 
          hovering over a checkbox, the associated content is loaded into the default application, possibly a LaTeX 
          editor. For the \texttt{Ctrl+Click} feature to work, the file \texttt{aeb-reader.js} needs 
          to be installed. As the filename suggests, this file will work for Adobe Acrobat Reader (DC), as well 
          as for the magnificent Adobe Acrobat itself.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pmdb/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pmdb/docs/pmdb.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./8243879219-pmdb.pdf|

\section[\texttt{polexpr} -- A parser for polynomial expressions]{\texttt{polexpr} -- A parser for polynomial expressions}\label{pkg:polexpr}
\index{Package!polexpr}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/polexpr}
\item[name] \texttt{polexpr}
\item[caption] A parser for polynomial expressions
\item[author] Burnol, Jean-François
\index{Author!Burnol, Jean-François}
\item[copyright] Jean-François Burnol (2018-2022)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.8.7a (2022-05-19)
\item[last changes] 2022-05-19
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a parser  \texttt{{\textbackslash}poldef} of algebraic polynomial 
          expressions. As it is based on \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xint}{xintexpr} , the coefficients 
          are allowed to be arbitrary rational numbers.

          Once defined, a polynomial is usable by its name either as a numerical function in  \texttt{{\textbackslash}xintexpr} / \texttt{{\textbackslash}xinteval} , 
          or for additional polynomial definitions, or as argument to the package macros. The localization of real 
          roots to arbitrary precision as well as the determination of all rational roots is implemented via such 
          macros.

          Since release 0.8, polexpr extends the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xint}{xintexpr} syntax 
          to recognize polynomials as a new variable type (and not only as functions). Functionality which previously 
          was implemented via macros such as the computation of a greatest common divisor is now available directly 
          in \texttt{{\textbackslash}xintexpr} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}xinteval} or \texttt{{\textbackslash}poldef} via 
          infix or functional syntax.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Examples of use}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/polexpr/polexpr-examples.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./1512175399-polexpr-examples.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation (HTML)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/polexpr/polexpr.html}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/polexpr/README.md}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/polexpr}

\index{Package!polski}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/polski}
\item[name] \texttt{polski}
\item[caption] Typeset Polish documents with LaTeX and Polish fonts
\item[author] Woliński, Marcin
\index{Author!Woliński, Marcin}
\item[author] Olko, Mariusz
\index{Author!Olko, Mariusz}
\item[copyright] Marcin Woliński (2000, 2002, 2003, 2007, 2017, 2021)
\item[copyright] Mariusz Olko and Marcin Woliński (1997, 1998)
\item[copyright] Mariusz Olko (1994)
\item[license] lppl1.2 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.2}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2}
\item[version] 1.3.6 (2021-08-25)
\item[last changes] 2021-08-25
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) Tools to typeset monolingual Polish documents in LaTeX2ε without  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/polyglossia}{polyglossia} . 
          The package

          \begin{itemize}
          \item loads Polish hyphenation patterns,
          \item ensures that a font encoding suitable for Polish is used; in particular it enables Polish adaptation of Computer Modern fonts (the so-called PL fonts),
          \item provides translations of  \texttt{{\textbackslash}today} and names like ''Bibliography'' or ''Chapter'',
          \item redefines math symbols according to Polish typographical tradition,
          \item provides macros for dashes according to Polish orthography,
          \item provides a historical input method for ''Polish characters'',
          \item works with traditional TeX as well as with Unicode aware variants.
          \end{itemize}
(This package was previously known as platex, but has been renamed to resolve a name clash.)

\section[\texttt{poltawski} -- Antykwa Półtawskiego Family of Fonts]{\texttt{poltawski} -- Antykwa Półtawskiego Family of Fonts}\label{pkg:poltawski}
\index{Package!poltawski}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/poltawski}
\item[name] \texttt{poltawski}
\item[caption] Antykwa Półtawskiego Family of Fonts
\item[author] Nowacki, Janusz Marian
\index{Author!Nowacki, Janusz Marian}
\item[author] Jackowski, Bogusław
\index{Author!Jackowski, Bogusław}
\item[copyright] Bogusław Jackowski, Janusz M. Nowacki and P. Strzelczyk (1999-2010)
\item[license] gfl = The GUST Font License (GFL) (free)
\index{License!gfl}
\index{License!The GUST Font License (GFL)}
\item[version] 1.101
\item[description] (no language specified) The package contains the Antykwa Półtawskiego family of fonts in the PostScript Type 1 and OpenType formats. 
          The original font was designed in the twenties of the XX century by the Polish typographer Adam Półtawski(1881-1952).

          Following the route set out by the Latin Modern and TeX Gyre projects ( \href{https://www.gust.org.pl/projects/e-foundry}{https://www.gust.org.pl/projects/e-foundry} ), 
          the Antykwa Półtawskiego digitisation project aims at providing a rich collection of diacritical characters 
          in the attempt to cover as many Latin-based scripts as possible. To our knowledge, the repertoire of 
          characters covers all European languages as well as some other Latin-based alphabets such as Vietnamese 
          and Navajo; at the request of users, recent extensions (following the enhancement of the Latin Modern 
          collection) provide glyphs sufficient for typesetting of romanized transliterations of Arabic and Sanskrit 
          scripts.

          The Antykwa Półtawskiego family consists of 4 weights (light, normal, medium, bold), each having upright 
          and italic forms and one of 5 design sizes: 6, 8, 10, 12 and 17pt. Altogether, the collection comprises 
          40 font files, containing the same repertoire of 1126 characters.

          The preliminary version of Antykwa Półtawskiego ( \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/antp}{antp} package) 
          released in 2000 is rendered obsolete by this package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{README}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/poltawski/README}

\section[\texttt{poormanlog} -- Logarithms and powers with (almost) 9 digits]{\texttt{poormanlog} -- Logarithms and powers with (almost) 9 digits}\label{pkg:poormanlog}
\index{Package!poormanlog}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/poormanlog}
\item[name] \texttt{poormanlog}
\item[caption] Logarithms and powers with (almost) 9 digits
\item[author] Burnol, Jean-François
\index{Author!Burnol, Jean-François}
\item[copyright] Jean-François Burnol (2019-2022)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.07 (2022-05-25)
\item[last changes] 2022-05-25
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) This small package (usable with Plain e-TeX, LaTeX, or others) with no dependencies provides two fast 
          expandable macros computing logarithms in base 10 and fractional powers of 10.

          They handle arguments of 9 digit tokens which stand for either  \texttt{1 <= d.dddddddd < 10} (for 
          the log) or \texttt{0.xxxxxxxxx} (for powers of 10). They achieve a precision of 1ulp for 
          the logarithm and 2ulp for fractional powers of ten.

          Extension to other numerical ranges has to be done by user, via own macros or some math engine.

          The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xint}{xintexpr} package (at 1.3f) imports the poormanlog 
          macros as core constituents of its log10(), pow10(), log(), exp() and pow() functions.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/generic/poormanlog/README}

\item[description] (no language specified) The package offers macros for making posters and banners with TeX. It is compatible with most TeX macro 
          formats, including Plain TeX, LaTeX, AmSTeX, and AmS-LaTeX. The package creates a poster as huge box, 
          which is then distributed over as many printer pages as necessary.

          The only special requirement is that your printer not be bothered by text that lies off the page. This 
          is true of most printers, including laser printers and PostScript printers.

\item[version] 0.5.1 (2024-12-05)
\item[last changes] 2024-12-05
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) This is an endnotes package for LaTeX. Its user interface provides means to print multiple sections of 
          notes along the document, and to subdivide them either automatically — by chapter, by section — or at 
          manually specified places, thus being able to easily handle both numbered and unnumbered headings. The 
          package also provides infrastructure for setting up contextual running headers for printed notes. The 
          default is a simple but useful one, in the form ''Notes to pages N-M'', but more elaborate ones can be 
          built. When  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} is loaded, \texttt{postnotes} provides 
          hyperlinked notes, including back links.

\section[\texttt{ppmcheckpdf} -- Convert PDF to PNG and compare PNG files after l3build]{\texttt{ppmcheckpdf} -- Convert PDF to PNG and compare PNG files after l3build}\label{pkg:ppmcheckpdf}
\index{Package!ppmcheckpdf}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ppmcheckpdf}
\item[name] \texttt{ppmcheckpdf}
\item[caption] Convert PDF to PNG and compare PNG files after l3build
\item[author] Lyu, Jianrui
\index{Author!Lyu, Jianrui}
\item[copyright] Jianrui Lyu (2024-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 2025A (2025-02-20)
\item[last changes] 2025-02-20
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The build system  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/l3build}{l3build} normally writes the contents 
          of some boxes from \texttt{.lvt} files into corresponding \texttt{.tlg} files. 
          Sometimes a dependent package adds e.g. the command \texttt{{\textbackslash}kern0pt} , 
          so that test files fail, even if the PDF files look the same as before and are still correct.

          The ppmcheckpdf tool offers an alternative option for regression testing: instead of printing the contents 
          of boxes in  \texttt{.lvt} files, PDF files are converted to PNG files and you can compare 
          the PNG files after l3build has finished its work.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ppmcheckpdf/README.txt}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ppmcheckpdf/ppmcheckpdf.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./4982601788-ppmcheckpdf.pdf|

\index{Contact!repository}

\section[\texttt{prettyref} -- Make label references "self-identify"]{\texttt{prettyref} -- Make label references "self-identify"}\label{pkg:prettyref}
\index{Package!prettyref}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/prettyref}
\item[name] \texttt{prettyref}
\item[caption] Make label references "self-identify"
\item[author] Ruland, Kevin
\index{Author!Ruland, Kevin}
\item[copyright] Kevin Ruland (1995, 1998)
\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[version] 3.0
\item[description] (no language specified) Prettyref provides a command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}newrefformat} , which specifies 
          the way in which a reference is typeset, according to a label ''identification''. The identification 
          is set in the \texttt{{\textbackslash}label} command, by using prefixed label names; 
          so instead of \texttt{{\textbackslash}label{\textbraceleft}mysection{\textbraceright}} , 
          one uses \texttt{{\textbackslash}label{\textbraceleft}sec:mysection{\textbraceright}} , 
          and prettyref interprets the '' \texttt{sec:} '' part. The package is compatible with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/hyperref}{hyperref} and 
          with other packages.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/prettyref/prettyref.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./1047310279-prettyref.pdf|

          the value of a LaTeX length in the units specified by \texttt{{\textbackslash}uselengthunit{\textbraceleft}unit{\textbraceright}} (‘unit’ 
          may be any TeX length unit except for scaled point, viz., any of: \texttt{pt} , \texttt{pc} , \texttt{in} , \texttt{mm} , \texttt{cm} , \texttt{bp} , \texttt{dd} or \texttt{cc} ). 
          When the unit is \texttt{pt} , the printed length value will include any stretch or shrink; 
          otherwise these are not printed. The ‘unit’ argument may also be \texttt{PT} , in which case 
          length values will be printed in point units but without any stretch or shrink values.

\section[\texttt{probsoln} -- Generate problem sheets and their solution sheets]{\texttt{probsoln} -- Generate problem sheets and their solution sheets}\label{pkg:probsoln}
\index{Package!probsoln}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/probsoln}
\item[name] \texttt{probsoln}
\item[caption] Generate problem sheets and their solution sheets
\item[author] Talbot, Nicola
\index{Author!Talbot, Nicola}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 3.05 (2017-07-10)
\item[last changes] 2017-07-10
\item[year] 2017
\index{Year!2017}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package is designed for lecturers who have to generate new problem sheets for their students on a 
          regular basis (e.g. yearly) by randomly selecting a specified number of problems defined in another file.

          The package allows you easily to generate a new problem sheet that is different from the previous year, 
          thus alleviating the temptation of students to seek out the previous year's students and checking out 
          their answers. The solutions to the problems can be defined along with the problem, making it easy to 
          generate the solution sheet from the same source code; problems may be reused within a document, so that 
          solutions may appear in a different section of the same document as the problems they cover.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Example of use}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/probsoln/samples/sample.pdf}

\section[\texttt{proofread} -- Commands for inserting annotations]{\texttt{proofread} -- Commands for inserting annotations}\label{pkg:proofread}
\index{Package!proofread}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/proofread}
\item[name] \texttt{proofread}
\item[caption] Commands for inserting annotations
\item[author] Dekker, Wybo H.
\index{Author!Dekker, Wybo H.}
\item[copyright] Wybo Dekker (2017)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.04 (2019-04-25)
\item[last changes] 2019-04-25
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package defines a few LaTeX commands that may be useful when you proofread a LaTeX document. They 
          allow you to easily highlight text and add comments in the margin. Vim escape sequences are provided 
          for inserting or removing these LaTeX commands in the source.

          Options are provided for displaying the document with extra line spacing, and for displaying it in either 
          corrected or uncorrected state, both without margin notes.

          The package is based on code for a text highlighting command that was published by Antal Spector-Zabusky 
          on  \href{https://tex.stackexchange.com/questions/5959}{https://tex.stackexchange.com/questions/5959} .

          The main file,  \texttt{proofread.dtx} , is self-extracting, so you can generate the style 
          file by compiling \texttt{proofread.dtx} with pdfLaTeX.

          This package is based on the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/soul}{soul} package; so if you 
          plan to highlight non-ASCII characters, you must compile your source with either XeTeX- or LuaTeX-based 
          compilers.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/proofread/README}

\section[\texttt{prooftrees} -- Forest-based proof trees (symbolic logic)]{\texttt{prooftrees} -- Forest-based proof trees (symbolic logic)}\label{pkg:prooftrees}
\index{Package!prooftrees}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/prooftrees}
\item[name] \texttt{prooftrees}
\item[caption] Forest-based proof trees (symbolic logic)
\item[author] Rees, Clea F.
\index{Author!Rees, Clea F.}
\item[copyright] Clea F. Rees (2016-2026)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.9.3 (2026-02-21)
\item[last changes] 2026-02-21
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package supports drawing proof trees of the kind often used in introductory logic classes, especially 
          those aimed at students without strong mathematical backgrounds. Hodges (1991) is one example of a text 
          which uses this system. When teaching such a system it is especially useful to annotate the tree with 
          line numbers, justifications and explanations of branch closures.

          \texttt{prooftrees} provides a single environment, \texttt{prooftree} , and 
          a variety of tools for annotating, customising and highlighting such trees. A cross-referencing system 
          is provided for trees which cite line numbers in justifications for proof lines or branch closures.

          prooftrees is based on  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/forest}{forest} and, hence, \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} . 
          The package requires version 2.1+ of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/forest}{forest} for expected 
          results. It will not work with versions prior to 2.1.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{User manual}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/prooftrees/prooftrees-doc.pdf}

\section[\texttt{ps2eps} -- Produce Encapsulated PostScript from PostScript]{\texttt{ps2eps} -- Produce Encapsulated PostScript from PostScript}\label{pkg:ps2eps}
\index{Package!ps2eps}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ps2eps}
\item[name] \texttt{ps2eps}
\item[caption] Produce Encapsulated PostScript from PostScript
\item[author] Bless, Roland
\index{Author!Bless, Roland}
\item[copyright] Roland Bless (1999-2020)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 1.70
\item[description] (no language specified) Produce Encapsulated PostScript Files (EPS/EPSF) from a one-page PostScript document, or any PostScript 
          document. A correct Bounding Box is calculated for the EPS files and some PostScript command sequences 
          that can produce errorneous results on printers are filtered. The input is cropped to include just the 
          image contained in the PostScript file. The EPS files can then be included into TeX documents.

          Other programs like  \texttt{ps2epsi} (a script distributed with \texttt{ghostscript} ) 
          don’t always calculate the correct bounding box (because the values are put on the PostScript stack which 
          may get corrupted by bad PostScript code) or they round it off, resulting in clipping the image. Therefore \texttt{ps2eps} uses 
          a resolution of 144 dpi to get the correct bounding box. The bundle includes binaries for Linux, Solaris, 
          Digital Unix or Windows 2000/9x/NT; for other platforms, the user needs \texttt{perl} , \texttt{ghostscript} and 
          an ANSI-C compiler.

          Included in the distribution is the  \texttt{bbox} program, an application to produce Bounding 
          Box values for \texttt{rawppm} or \texttt{rawpbm} format files.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Bbox documentation (PDF)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ps2eps/doc/bbox.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./8735137828-bbox.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Ps2eps documentation (HTML)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ps2eps/doc/ps2eps.html}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ps2eps/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Ps2eps documentation (PDF)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ps2eps/doc/ps2eps.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./2884381703-ps2eps.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Bbox documentation (HTML)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/ps2eps/doc/bbox.html}
