\section[\texttt{psfragx} -- A psfrag eXtension]{\texttt{psfragx} -- A psfrag eXtension}\label{pkg:psfragx}
\index{Package!psfragx}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/psfragx}
\item[name] \texttt{psfragx}
\item[caption] A psfrag eXtension
\item[author] Kockaert, Pascal
\index{Author!Kockaert, Pascal}
\item[copyright] Pascal Kockaert (2003-2012)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.1
\item[description] (no language specified) PSfragX offers a mechanism to embed  \texttt{{\textbackslash}psfrag} commands, as provided 
          by the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/psfrag}{psfrag} package, into the EPS file itself. 
          Each time a graphic is included, the EPS file is scanned. If some tagged lines are found, they are used 
          to define the psfrag replacements that should be performed automatically. In addition, a similar mechanism 
          holds for \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/overpic}{overpic} objects. These are picture objects 
          superimposed on the included graphic.

          A similar mechanism is implemented in psfrag itself (but deprecated in the documentation), but psfragx 
          offers much more flexibility. For example, if  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel} is 
          used, it is possible to define different replacements corresponding to different languages. The replacements 
          to take into account will be selected on the basis of the current language of the document.

          A Matlab script (LaPrint) is provided, to export an EPS file with psfragx annotations ready embedded.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{LaPrint documentation:}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/psfragx/laprint-3.16/laprintdoc.ps}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/psfragx/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Psfragx documentation:}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/psfragx/Pre-Compiled-Files/psfragx.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pslatex} -- Use PostScript fonts by default]{\texttt{pslatex} -- Use PostScript fonts by default}\label{pkg:pslatex}
\index{Package!pslatex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pslatex}
\item[name] \texttt{pslatex}
\item[caption] Use PostScript fonts by default
\item[author] Carlisle, David
\index{Author!Carlisle, David}
\item[copyright] David Carlisle (1994, 1996, 2021, 2023)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.3 (2023-06-24)
\item[last changes] 2023-06-24
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) A small package that makes LaTeX default to ‘standard’ PostScript fonts. It is basically a merger of 
          the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/times}{times} and the (obsolete) \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathptm}{mathptm} packages 
          from the psnfss suite. You must have installed standard LaTeX and the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/psnfss}{psnfss} PostScript 
          fonts to use this package. The main novel feature is that the pslatex package tries to compensate for 
          the visual differences between the Adobe fonts by scaling Helvetica by 90\%, and ‘condensing’ Courier 
          (i.e. scaling horizontally) by 85\%. The package is supplied with a (unix) shell file for a ‘pslatex‘ 
          command that allows standard LaTeX documents to be processed, without needing to edit the file.

          Note that current  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/psnfss}{psnfss} uses a different technique 
          for scaling Helvetica, and treats Courier as a lost cause (there are better free fixed-width available 
          now, than there were when pslatex was designed). As a result, pslatex is widely considered obsolete.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pslatex/README.txt}
\item[contact] \textit{bugs}: \url{https://github.com/davidcarlisle/dpctex/issues}
\index{Contact!bugs}

\index{Contact!repository}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pslatex}

\section[\texttt{psnfss} -- Font support for common PostScript fonts]{\texttt{psnfss} -- Font support for common PostScript fonts}\label{pkg:psnfss}
\index{Package!psnfss}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/psnfss}
\item[name] \texttt{psnfss}
\item[caption] Font support for common PostScript fonts
\item[author] Rahtz, Sebastian
\index{Author!Rahtz, Sebastian}
\item[author] Schmidt, Walter A.
\index{Author!Schmidt, Walter A.}
\item[author] The LaTeX Project Team
\index{Author!The LaTeX Project Team}
\item[author] Harcombe, Keiran
\index{Author!Harcombe, Keiran}
\item[copyright] Sebastian Rahtz, Walter Schmidt (1995-2020)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 9.3
\item[description] (no language specified) Font definition files, macros and font metrics for freely-available Adobe Type 1 fonts. The font set 
          consists of the ‘LaserWriter 35’ set (originally ‘freely available’ because embedded in PostScript printers), 
          and a variety of other free fonts, together with some additions. Note that while many of the fonts are 
          available in PostScript (and other) printers, most publishers require fonts  \emph{embedded} in 
          documents, which requires that you have the fonts in your TeX system. Fortunately, there are free versions 
          of the fonts from URW (available in the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/urw-base35}{URW base5} bundle).

          The base set of text fonts covered by PSNFSS are: AvantGarde, Bookman, Courier, Helvetica, New Century 
          Schoolbook, Palatino, Symbol, Times Roman and Zapf Dingbats. In addition, the fonts  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/charter}{Bitstream 
          Charter} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/utopia}{Adobe Utopia} are covered (those 
          fonts were contributed to the Public Domain by their commercial foundries).

          Separate packages are provided to load each font for use as main text font. The packages  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/helvet}{helvet} (which 
          allows Helvetica to be loaded with its size scaled to something more nearly appropriate for its use as 
          a Sans-Serif font to match Times) and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pifont}{pifont} (which 
          provides the means to select single glyphs from symbol fonts) are tailored to special requirements of 
          their fonts.

          Mathematics are covered by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathptmx}{mathptmx} package, 
          which constructs passable mathematics from a combination of Times Roman, Symbol and some glyphs from 
          Computer Modern, and by \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mathpazo}{Pazo Math} (optionally extended 
          with the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fpl}{fpl} small-caps and old-style figures fonts) 
          which uses Palatino as base font, with the mathpazo fonts.

          The bundle as a whole is part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/required}{LaTeX ‘required’} set 
          of packages.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/required/psnfss/psnfss2e.pdf}

          \begin{itemize}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides LaTeX support for the  \texttt{8r} encoding, which is how Adobe Standard 
          Encoding Type 1 fonts are represented within a TeX system. Normally, 8r encoding is merely the base encoding 
          of virtual fonts that specify OT1 or T1 encoding, but when virtual fonts are undesirable (for speed reasons) 
          or unavailable, this package will serve.

\section[\texttt{pst-cox} -- Drawing regular complex polytopes with PSTricks]{\texttt{pst-cox} -- Drawing regular complex polytopes with PSTricks}\label{pkg:pst-cox}
\index{Package!pst-cox}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-cox}
\item[name] \texttt{pst-cox}
\item[caption] Drawing regular complex polytopes with PSTricks
\item[author] Luque, Jean-Gabriel
\index{Author!Luque, Jean-Gabriel}
\item[license] lgpl = GNU Lesser General Public License (free)
\index{License!lgpl}
\index{License!GNU Lesser General Public License}
\item[version] 0.98 Beta
\item[description] (no language specified) Pst-cox is a  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} package for drawing 
          2-dimensional projections of complex regular polytopes (after the work of Coxeter).

          The package consists of a macro library for drawing the projections. The complex polytopes appear in 
          the study of the root systems and play a crucial role in many domains related to mathematics and physics. 
          These polytopes have been completely described by Coxeter in his book ''Regular Complex Polytopes''.

          There exist only a finite numbers of exceptional regular complex polytopes (for example the icosahedron) 
          and some infinite series (for example, one can construct a multi-dimensional analogue of the hypercube 
          in any  \emph{finite} dimension).

          The library contains two packages. The first, pst-coxcoor, is devoted to the exceptional complex regular 
          polytopes whose coordinates have been pre-computed. The second, pst-coxeterp, is devoted to the infinite 
          series.
\item[documentation]  (English) \textit{Documentation for pst-coxcoor}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/contrib/pst-cox/doc/pst-coxcoor/pst-coxcoor_doc.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./5611178701-pst-coxcoor_doc.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (English) \textit{Documentation for pst-coxeterp}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/contrib/pst-cox/doc/pst-coxeterp/pst-coxeterp_doc.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./5161817640-pst-coxeterp_doc.pdf|

\index{License!lppl}

\item[version] 2.06a
\item[description] (no language specified) The package enables the user to draw (using  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} ) 
          the diffraction patterns for different geometric forms of apertures for monochromatic light (using \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} ). 
          The aperture stops can have rectangular, circular or triangular openings. The view of the diffraction 
          may be planar, or three-dimensional.

          Options available are the dimensions of the aperture under consideration and of the particular optical 
          setting, e.g. the radius in case of an circular opening. Moreover one can choose the wavelength of the 
          light (the associated color will be calculated by the package).

\section[\texttt{pst-func} -- PSTricks package for plotting mathematical functions]{\texttt{pst-func} -- PSTricks package for plotting mathematical functions}\label{pkg:pst-func}
\index{Package!pst-func}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-func}
\item[name] \texttt{pst-func}
\item[caption] PSTricks package for plotting mathematical functions
\item[author] Voß, Herbert
\index{Author!Voß, Herbert}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.02a (2024-03-31)
\item[last changes] 2024-03-31
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package is built for use with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} . 
          It provides macros for plotting and manipulating various mathematical functions:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item polynomials and their derivatives  \emph{f(x)=an*x{\textasciicircum}n+an-1*x{\textasciicircum}(n-1)+...+a0} defined by the coefficients \emph{a0 a1 a2 ...} and the derivative order;
          \item the Fourier sum  \emph{f(x) = a0/2+a1cos(omega x)+...+b1sin(omega x)+...} defined by the coefficients \emph{a0 a1 a2 ... b1 b2 b3 ...} ;
          \item the Bessel function defined by its order;
          \item the Gauss function defined by  \emph{sigma} and \emph{mu} ;
          \item Bézier curves from order 1 (two control points) to order 9 (10 control points);
          \item the superellipse function (the Lamé curve);
          \item Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kind;
          \item the Thomae (or popcorn) function;
          \item the Weierstrass function;
          \item various integration-derived functions;
          \item normal, binomial, poisson, gamma, chi-squared, student’s t, F, beta, Cauchy and Weibull distribution functions and the Lorenz curve;
          \item the zeroes of a function, or the intermediate point of two functions;
          \item the  \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasicek\_model}{Vasicek function} for describing the evolution of interest rates; and
          \item implicit functions.
          \end{itemize}
The plots may be generated as volumes of rotation about the X-axis, as well.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/contrib/pst-func/doc/pst-func-doc.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pst-geo} -- Geographical Projections]{\texttt{pst-geo} -- Geographical Projections}\label{pkg:pst-geo}
\index{Package!pst-geo}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-geo}
\item[name] \texttt{pst-geo}
\item[caption] Geographical Projections
\item[author] Matarazzo, Giuseppe
\index{Author!Matarazzo, Giuseppe}
\item[author] Voß, Herbert
\index{Author!Voß, Herbert}
\item[author] Luque, Manuel
\index{Author!Luque, Manuel}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.09
\item[description] (no language specified) The package offers a set of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} related 
          packages for various cartographic projections of the terrestrial sphere. The package \texttt{pst-map2d} provides 
          conventional projections such as Mercator, Lambert, cylindrical, etc.

          The package  \texttt{pst-map3d} treats representation in three dimensions of the terrestrial 
          sphere. Packages \texttt{pst-map2dII} and \texttt{pst-map3dII} allow use of the \href{http://www.evl.uic.edu/pape/data/WDB/}{CIA 
          World DataBank II} . Various parameters of the packages allow for choice of the level of the detail 
          and the layouts possible (cities, borders, rivers etc).

          Substantial data files are provided, in an (internally) compressed format. Decompression happens on-the-fly 
          as a document using the data is displayed, printed or converted to PDF format. A Perl script is provided 
          for the user to do the decompression, if the need should arise.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/contrib/pst-geo/doc/pst-geo-doc.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pst-math} -- Enhancement of PostScript math operators to use with PSTrick\ldots]{\texttt{pst-math} -- Enhancement of PostScript math operators to use with PSTricks}\label{pkg:pst-math}
\index{Package!pst-math}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-math}
\item[name] \texttt{pst-math}
\item[caption] Enhancement of PostScript math operators to use with PSTricks
\item[author] Jorssen, Christophe
\index{Author!Jorssen, Christophe}
\item[author] Voß, Herbert
\index{Author!Voß, Herbert}
\item[copyright] Herbert Voss (2023)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.67 (2023-07-03)
\item[last changes] 2023-07-03
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) PostScript lacks a lot of basic operators such as tan, acos, asin, cosh, sinh, tanh, acosh, asinh, atanh, 
          exp (with e base). Also (oddly) cos and sin use arguments in degrees.

          Pst-math provides all those operators in a header file  \texttt{pst-math.pro} with wrappers \texttt{pst-math.sty} and \texttt{pst-math.tex} .

          In addition, sinc, gauss, gammaln and bessel are implemented (only partially for the latter). The package 
          is designed essentially to work with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-plot}{pst-plot} but 
          can be used in whatever PS code (such as PSTricks \texttt{SpecialCoor "!"} , which is useful 
          for placing labels).

          The package also provides a routine SIMPSON for numerical integration and a solver of linear equation 
          systems.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/contrib/pst-math/doc/pst-math-doc.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./2169789233-pst-math-doc.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/contrib/pst-math/README}

\section[\texttt{pst-ode} -- Solving initial value problems for sets of Ordinary Differen\ldots]{\texttt{pst-ode} -- Solving initial value problems for sets of Ordinary Differential Equations}\label{pkg:pst-ode}
\index{Package!pst-ode}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-ode}
\item[name] \texttt{pst-ode}
\item[caption] Solving initial value problems for sets of Ordinary Differential Equations
\item[author] Grahn, Alexander
\index{Author!Grahn, Alexander}
\item[copyright] Alexander Grahn (2012-2024)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 0.19 (2024-01-04)
\item[last changes] 2024-01-04
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package defines  \texttt{{\textbackslash}pstODEsolve} for solving initial value 
          problems for sets of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODE) using the Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg (RKF45) method 
          with automatic step size adjustment.

          The result is stored as a PostScript object and may be plotted later using macros from other PSTricks 
          packages, such as  \texttt{{\textbackslash}listplot} ( \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-plot}{pst-plot} ) 
          and \texttt{{\textbackslash}listplotThreeD} ( \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-3dplot}{pst-3dplot} ), 
          or may be further processed by user-defined PostScript procedures. Optionally, the computed state vectors 
          can be written as a table to a text file.

          As in building a bibliography with BibTeX, additional external programmes are invoked. In this case they 
          are used to create a PDF file ( \texttt{{\textbackslash}PDFcontainer} ) that will contain 
          all the graphics material. In the final document these contents will be inserted instead of the original 
          PostScript code.

          a recent version of the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/preview}{preview} package.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package offers a collection of useful macros for disciplines related to signal processing. It defines 
          macros for plotting a sequence of numbers, drawing the pole-zero diagram of a system, shading the region 
          of convergence, creating an adder or a multiplier node, placing a framed node at a given coordinate, 
          creating an up-sampler or a down-sampler node, drawing the block diagram of a system, drawing adaptive 
          systems, sequentially connecting a list of nodes, and connecting a list of nodes using any node-connecting 
          macro.

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-slpe}
\item[name] \texttt{pst-slpe}
\item[caption] Sophisticated colour gradients
\item[author] Voß, Herbert
\index{Author!Voß, Herbert}
\item[author] Giese, Martin
\index{Author!Giese, Martin}
\item[copyright] Martin Giese, Herbert Voß (1998-2008)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.31
\item[description] (no language specified) This  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PStricks} package covers all the colour 
          gradient functionality of pst-grad (part of the base PSTricks distribution), and provides the following 
          facilities:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item it permits the user to specify an arbitrary number of colours, along with the points at which they are to be reached;
          \item it converts between RGB and HSV behind the scenes;
          \item it provides concentric and radial gradients;
          \item it provides a command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}psBall} that generates bullets with a three-dimensional appearance; and
          \item uses the xkeyval package for the extended key handling.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/contrib/pst-slpe/pst-slpe.pdf}

\item[name] \texttt{pst-solides3d}
\item[caption] Draw perspective views of 3D solids
\item[author] Schmittbuhl, Arnaud
\index{Author!Schmittbuhl, Arnaud}

\index{Author!Vignault, Jean-Paul}
\item[author] Luque, Manuel
\index{Author!Luque, Manuel}

\item[last changes] 2023-11-04
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package is designed to draw solids in 3d perspective. Features include:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item create primitive solids;
          \item create solids by including a list of its vertices and faces;
          \item faces of solids and surfaces can be colored by choosing from a very large palette of colors;
          \item draw parametric surfaces in algebraic and reverse polish notation;
          \item create explicit and parameterized algebraic functions drawn in 2 or 3 dimensions;
          \item project text onto a plane or onto the faces of a solid;
          \item support for including external database files.
          \end{itemize}

\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0 (2026-04-13)
\item[last changes] 2026-04-13
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) To represent the spectrum of light decomposition, we have several packages at our disposal with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} : \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-spectra}{pst-spectra} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xcolor}{xcolor} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-add}{pstricks-add} . All use the same source 
          code by Dan Bruton. This package provides an extended visible spectrum. However, it is possible to obtain 
          the representation of the spectrum directly from the data of the »International Commission on Illumination« 
          (CIE), and we have the choice between the data of (CIE 1931) and that of (CIE 1964{\textbraceright}). 
          Then we must choose a color space, sRGB, Adobe,etc.

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}postscript{\textbraceright}...{\textbackslash}end{\textbraceleft}postscript{\textbraceright}} \\ \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}pspicture{\textbraceright}...{\textbackslash}end{\textbraceleft}pspicture{\textbraceright}} and\\ \texttt{{\textbackslash}pspicture...{\textbackslash}endpspicture}

\index{Package!pstool}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstool}
\item[name] \texttt{pstool}
\item[caption] Support for psfrag within pdfLaTeX
\item[author] Robertson, Will
\index{Author!Robertson, Will}
\item[author] Prime, Zebb
\index{Author!Prime, Zebb}
\item[copyright] Zebb Prime (2008-2014)
\item[copyright] Will Robertson (2008-2018)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.5e (2018-01-20)
\item[last changes] 2018-01-20
\item[year] 2018
\index{Year!2018}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package works in the same sort of way as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-pdf}{pst-pdf} , 
          but it also processes the PostScript graphics with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/psfrag}{psfrag} to 
          add labels within the graphic, before conversion. Thus the bundle replaces two steps of an ordinary workflow. 
          (Naturally, the package requires that \texttt{{\textbackslash}write 18} is enabled.)

          Pstool ensures that each version of each graphic is compiled once only (the graphic is (re-)compiled 
          only if it has changed since the previous compilation of the document). This drastically speeds up the 
          running of the package in the typical case (though the first run of any document is inevitably just as 
          slow as with any similar package).
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/pstool/pstool.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pstricks-base} -- PostScript macros for TeX]{\texttt{pstricks-base} -- PostScript macros for TeX}\label{pkg:pstricks-base}
\index{Package!pstricks-base}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}

\index{Alias!pstricks (for pstricks-base)}
\item[name] \texttt{pstricks-base}
\item[caption] PostScript macros for TeX
\item[author] Girou, Denis
\index{Author!Girou, Denis}
\item[author] Voß, Herbert
\index{Author!Voß, Herbert}
\item[author] Van Zandt, Timothy
\index{Author!Van Zandt, Timothy}
\item[copyright] Herbert Voß (2006-2025)
\item[copyright] Timothy Van Zandt (1993, 1994, 2000)
\item[copyright] Denis Girou (2000-2003)

\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}

\item[version] 3.22a (2025-12-13)
\item[last changes] 2025-12-13
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) PSTricks offers an extensive collection of macros for generating PostScript that is usable with most 
          TeX macro formats, including Plain TeX, LaTeX, AMS-TeX, and AMS-LaTeX. Included are macros for colour, 
          graphics, pie charts, rotation, trees and overlays. It has many special features, including a wide variety 
          of graphics (picture drawing) macros, with a flexible interface and with colour support. There are macros 
          for colouring or shading the cells of tables.

          The package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-add}{pstricks-add} contains bug-fixes 
          and additions for PSTricks (among other things).

          PSTricks ordinarily uses PostScript  \texttt{{\textbackslash}special} commands, which 
          are not supported by pdf(La)TeX. This limitation may be overcome by using either the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pst-pdf}{pst-pdf} or 
          the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftricks}{pdftricks} package, to generate a PDF inclusion 
          from a PSTricks diagram.

          PSTricks macros can also generate PDF output when the document is processed  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xetex}{XeTeX} , 
          without the need for other supporting packages.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Latest news bulletin}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pstricks/base/doc/pst-news24.pdf}

\section[\texttt{ptolemaicastronomy} -- Diagrams of sphere models for variably strict conditionals (\ldots]{\texttt{ptolemaicastronomy} -- Diagrams of sphere models for variably strict conditionals (Lewis counterfactuals)}\label{pkg:ptolemaicastronomy}
\index{Package!ptolemaicastronomy}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ptolemaicastronomy}
\item[name] \texttt{ptolemaicastronomy}
\item[caption] Diagrams of sphere models for variably strict conditionals (Lewis counterfactuals)
\item[author] Zach, Richard
\index{Author!Zach, Richard}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) David K. Lewis (Counterfactuals, Blackwell 1973) introduced a sphere semantics for counterfactual conditionals. 
          He jokingly referred to the diagrams depicting such sphere models as Ptolemaic astronomy, hence the name 
          of this package.

          The macros provided in this package aid in the construction of sphere model diagrams in the style of 
          Lewis. The macros all make use of TikZ.

\item[description] (no language specified) This package contains LaTeX support for the font PT Sans developed by ParaType for the project ''public 
          Types of the Russian Federation'', and released under an open user license.

          The fonts are included in this distribution, in TrueType format and converted to Type 1 format (as kindly 
          allowed by ParaType). The fonts provide coverage of the T2* and X2 encodings, and partial coverage of 
          T1, OT1, TS1 and IL2 (sufficient for typesetting text in Czech and Slovak languages — the purpose of 
          encoding IL2).

\section[\texttt{punk} -- Donald Knuth's punk font]{\texttt{punk} -- Donald Knuth's punk font}\label{pkg:punk}
\index{Package!punk}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/punk}
\item[name] \texttt{punk}
\item[caption] Donald Knuth's punk font
\item[author] Knuth, Donald E.
\index{Author!Knuth, Donald E.}
\item[author] Grover, Rohit
\index{Author!Grover, Rohit}
\item[license] knuth = Knuth License (free)
\index{License!knuth}
\index{License!Knuth License}
\item[description] (no language specified) A response to the assertion in a lecture that ''typography tends to lag behind other stylistic changes 
          by about 10 years''. Knuth felt it was (in 1988) time to design a replacement for his designs of the 
          1970s, and came up with this font! The fonts are distributed as Metafont source.

          The package offers LaTeX support by Rohit Grover, from an original by Sebastian Rahtz, which is slightly 
          odd in claiming that the fonts are T1-encoded. A (possibly) more rational support package is to be found 
          in  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/punk-latex}{punk-latex}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{TUGboat paper}: \url{https://tug.org/TUGboat/Articles/tb09-2/tb21knut.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) The font was generated from a MetaPost version of the sources of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/punk}{‘original’ 
          punk font} .

          Knuth’s original fonts generated different shapes at random. This isn't actually possible in an OpenType 
          font; rather, the font contains several variants of each glyph, and uses the OpenType  \emph{randomize} function 
          to select a variant for each invocation.

\section[\texttt{purifyeps} -- Make EPS work with both LaTeX/dvips and pdfLaTeX]{\texttt{purifyeps} -- Make EPS work with both LaTeX/dvips and pdfLaTeX}\label{pkg:purifyeps}
\index{Package!purifyeps}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/purifyeps}
\item[name] \texttt{purifyeps}
\item[caption] Make EPS work with both LaTeX/dvips and pdfLaTeX
\item[author] Pakin, Scott
\index{Author!Pakin, Scott}
\item[copyright] Scott Pakin (2009)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.1
\item[description] (no language specified) While pdfLaTeX has a number of nice features, its primary shortcoming relative to standard LaTeX+dvips 
          is that it is unable to read ordinary Encapsulated PostScript (EPS) files, the most common graphics format 
          in the LaTeX world. Purifyeps converts EPS files into a ‘purified’ form that can be read by both LaTeX+dvips 
          and pdfLaTeX. The trick is that the standard LaTeX2e graphics packages can parse MetaPost-produced EPS 
          directly. Hence, purifyeps need only convert an arbitrary EPS file into the same stylized format that 
          MetaPost outputs.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/purifyeps/purifyeps.pdf}

\section[\texttt{pwebmac} -- Consolidated WEB macros for DVI and PDF output]{\texttt{pwebmac} -- Consolidated WEB macros for DVI and PDF output}\label{pkg:pwebmac}
\index{Package!pwebmac}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pwebmac}
\item[name] \texttt{pwebmac}
\item[caption] Consolidated WEB macros for DVI and PDF output
\item[author] Scherer, Andreas
\index{Author!Scherer, Andreas}
\item[license] pd = Public Domain Software (free)
\index{License!pd}
\index{License!Public Domain Software}
\item[version] 5.1 (2025-03-16)
\item[last changes] 2025-03-16
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The original  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/web}{WEB} system by Donald Knuth has the macros \texttt{webmac.tex} that 
          produce DVI output only; for historic reasons, it will never be modified (apart from catastrophic errors). 
          Hàn Thế Thành has modified these macros in his \texttt{pdfwebmac.tex} for PDF output (only) 
          with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftex}{pdfTeX} . Jonathan Kew’s \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xetex}{XeTeX} has 
          similar macros \texttt{xewebmac.tex} by Khaled Hosny that \emph{modify}  \texttt{webmac.tex} for 
          PDF output; these macros can only be used with a specific ''TeX engine'' each.

          The present  \texttt{pwebmac} package integrates these three WEB macro files similar to \texttt{cwebmac.tex} in 
          Silvio Levy’s and Don Knuth’s \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/cweb}{CWEB} system, so \texttt{pwebmac.tex} can 
          be used with ''plain TeX'', pdfTeX, and XeTeX alike.

          Its initial application is the production of PDF files for all major WEB programs for ''TeX and friends'' 
          as distributed in  \href{https://www.tug.org/texlive}{TeX Live} . For this purpose, the 
          shell script \texttt{makeall} was whipped together; it provides various commandline options 
          and works around several ''quirks'' in the WEB sources.

          WEB programmers who want to use  \texttt{pwebmac.tex} instead of the default \texttt{webmac.tex} in 
          their programs have to change the first line in the TeX file created by \texttt{weave} . 
          From there, all depends on the ''TeX engine'' you use.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/web/pwebmac/README.md}
\item[contact] \textit{support}: \url{https://lists.tug.org/tex-k}
\index{Contact!support}
\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{https://github.com/ascherer/web}
\index{Contact!repository}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/web/pwebmac}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package enables users to declare in their document which physical fonts should be used for the standard 
          Japanese (logical) fonts of pLaTeX and upLaTeX. Font setup is realized by changing the font mapping of 
          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dvipdfmx}{dvipdfmx} , and thus users can use any (monospaced) 
          physical fonts they like, once they properly install this package, without creating helper files for

\section[\texttt{pxjodel} -- Help change metrics of fonts from japanese-otf]{\texttt{pxjodel} -- Help change metrics of fonts from japanese-otf}\label{pkg:pxjodel}
\index{Package!pxjodel}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pxjodel}
\item[name] \texttt{pxjodel}
\item[caption] Help change metrics of fonts from japanese-otf
\item[author] Yato, Takayuki
\index{Author!Yato, Takayuki}
\item[copyright] Takayuki YATO (aka. “ZR”) (2019-2020)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 0.3 (2020-05-04)
\item[last changes] 2020-05-04
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package changes the setup of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/japanese-otf}{japanese-otf} package 
          so that the TFMs for direct input are all replaced by new ones with prefixed names; for example, \texttt{nmlminr-h} will 
          be replaced by \texttt{foo--nmlminr-h} , where \texttt{foo} is a prefix specified 
          by the user.

          This function will assist users who want to use the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/japanese-otf}{japanese-otf} package 
          together with tailored TFMs of Japanese fonts.

          The ''jodel'' part of the package name stands for '' \textbf{j} apanese- \textbf{o} tf \textbf{del} uxe''. 
          Here ''deluxe'' is the name of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/japanese-otf}{japanese-otf} ’s 
          option for employing multi-weight Japanese font families. This option is probably the most likely reason 
          for using \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/japanese-otf}{japanese-otf} . So \texttt{pxjodel} is 
          really about \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/japanese-otf}{japanese-otf} ’s ''deluxe'' option, 
          hence the name. It is not related to yodel singing, although some sense of word-play is intended.

\section[\texttt{pxufont} -- Emulate non-Unicode Japanese fonts using Unicode fonts]{\texttt{pxufont} -- Emulate non-Unicode Japanese fonts using Unicode fonts}\label{pkg:pxufont}
\index{Package!pxufont}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pxufont}
\item[name] \texttt{pxufont}
\item[caption] Emulate non-Unicode Japanese fonts using Unicode fonts
\item[author] Yato, Takayuki
\index{Author!Yato, Takayuki}
\item[copyright] Takayuki YATO (2017-2023)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 0.7 (2023-07-07)
\item[last changes] 2023-07-07
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) The set of the Japanese logical fonts (JFMs) that are used as standard fonts in  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ptex}{pTeX} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/uptex}{upTeX} contains 
          both Unicode JFMs and non-Unicode JFMs. This bundle provides an alternative set of non-Unicode JFMs that 
          are tied to the virtual fonts (VFs) that refer to the glyphs in the Unicode JFMs. Moreover it provides 
          a LaTeX package that redefines the NFSS settings of the Japanese fonts of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/uplatex}{(u)pLaTeX} so 
          that the new set of non-Unicode JFMs will be employed. As a whole, this bundle allows users to dispense 
          with the mapping setup on non-Unicode JFMs.

          Such a setup is useful in particular when users want to use OpenType fonts (such as Source Han Serif) 
          that have a glyph encoding different from Adobe-Japan1, because mapping setups from non-Unicode JFMs 
          to such physical fonts are difficult to prepare.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/jptex/latex/pxufont/README.md}
\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{https://github.com/zr-tex8r/PXufont}
\index{Contact!repository}

          ovid.com). Support for Refer is available. This bibliographical manager can be used for searching, editing, 
          reformatting, etc. It provides a simple framework that provides easy to use python classes and functions, 
          and therefore can be extended to any usage (generating HTML pages according to bibliographic searches, 
          etc). As an example, a simple tool called pybcheck is provided with the package to check for the validity 
          of BibTeX files. In addition to the scripting environment, a graphical GNOME interface is available, 
          providing editing capabilities in addition to a nice hierarchical search mechanism.

\item[description] (no language specified) The pyjupyter package provides a lightweight and elegant environment for typesetting Python code in LaTeX 
          documents with a visual style inspired by Jupyter notebooks.

          It leverages the listings package for syntax highlighting and tcolorbox for structured, breakable frames. 
          Key features include:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Full support for French accents and UTF-8 encoding.
          \item Intelligent syntax highlighting for Python operators and keywords.
          \item A dedicated numbered option for line numbering.
          \item Seamless integration with TeXstudio via an included .cwl file for auto-completion.
          \item Robust handling of Python comments (\#) using an optional argument syntax.
          \item Font selection.
          \item Code size modification.
          \end{itemize}

          in a  \emph{single compilation run} . LaTeX documents must be compiled with LuaLaTeX for 
          this to work.

          PyLuaTeX runs a Python  \emph{InteractiveInterpreter} (actually several if you use different 
          sessions) in the background for on-the-fly code execution. Python code from your LaTeX file is sent to 
          the background interpreter through a TCP socket. This approach allows your Python code to be executed 
          and the output to be integrated in your LaTeX file in a single compilation run. No additional processing 
          steps are needed. No intermediate files have to be written. No placeholders have to be inserted.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/luatex/latex/pyluatex/pyluatex.pdf}

\item[caption] Library to run Python code
\item[author] user202729
\index{Author!user202729}
\item[copyright] user202729 (2022-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}

\item[description] (no language specified) Just like  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/perltex}{PerlTeX} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pyluatex}{PyLuaTeX} (and 
          unlike \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pythontex}{PythonTeX} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lt3luabridge}{lt3luabridge} ), 
          this only requires a single run, and variables are persistent throughout the run.

          Unlike PerlTeX or PyLuaTeX, there is no restriction on compiler or script required to run the code.

          There are also debugging functionalities: TeX errors result in Python traceback, and Python errors result 
          in TeX traceback. Errors in code executed with the  \texttt{pycode} environment give the 
          correct traceback point to the Python line of code in the TeX file.

          For advanced users, this package allows the user to manipulate the TeX state directly from within Python, 
          so you don’t need to write a single line of TeX code.

          CAUTION: In addition to this LaTeX package you need the Python  \texttt{pythonimmediate-tex} package, 
          which can be obtained from \href{https://pypi.org/project/pythonimmediate-tex/}{https://pypi.org/project/pythonimmediate-tex/} .

\section[\texttt{pythontex} -- Run Python from within a document, typesetting the results]{\texttt{pythontex} -- Run Python from within a document, typesetting the results}\label{pkg:pythontex}
\index{Package!pythontex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/pythontex}
\item[name] \texttt{pythontex}
\item[caption] Run Python from within a document, typesetting the results
\item[author] Poore, Geoffrey
\index{Author!Poore, Geoffrey}
\item[copyright] Geoffrey M. Poore (2012-2026)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[license] bsd3 = 3-clause BSD License (free)
\index{License!bsd3}
\index{License!3-clause BSD License}
\item[version] 0.19 (2026-02-15)
\item[last changes] 2026-02-15
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package allows you to enter Python code within a LaTeX document, execute the code, and access its 
          output in the original document. There is also support for Bash, JavaScript, Julia, Octave, Perl, R, 
          Raku (Perl 6), Ruby, Rust, and SageMath.

          Code is only executed when it has been modified, or when it meets user-specified criteria. Code may be 
          divided into user-defined sessions, which automatically run in parallel.

          Errors and warnings are synchronized with the LaTeX document, so that they refer to the document's line 
          numbers. External dependencies can be tracked, so that code is re-executed when the data it depends on 
          is modified. PythonTeX also provides syntax highlighting for code in LaTeX documents via the Pygments 
          syntax highlighter.

          The package provides a  \texttt{depythontex} utility. This creates a copy of the document 
          in which all Python code has been replaced by its output. This is useful for journal submissions, sharing 
          documents, and conversion to other formats.

\item[caption] A LaTeX2e class for making multiple choice questionnaires
\item[author] Verna, Didier
\index{Author!Verna, Didier}
\item[copyright] Didier Verna (2004)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 2.1
\item[description] (no language specified) QCM is a package for making multiple choices questionnaires under LaTeX2e (''QCM'' is the French acronym 
          for this style of test). A special environment allows you to define questions and possible answers. You 
          can specify which answers are correct and which are not. QCM not only formats the questions for you, 
          but also generates a ‘form’ (a grid that your students will have to fill in), and a ‘mask’ (the same 
          grid, only with correct answers properly checked in). You can then print the mask on a slide and correct 
          the questionnaires more easily by superimposing the mask on top of students' forms. QCM can also typeset 
          exam corrections automatically, and comes with support for  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/auctex}{AUC-TeX} .

\item[description] (no language specified) IMPORTANT NOTICE: This package is now considered obsolete. Please use the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre}{TeX-Gyre} fonts 
          instead!

          A collection of Type 1 fonts based on the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/urw}{URW++ fonts} distributed 
          with Ghostscript. The fonts are encoded according to QX layout which facilitates multilingual and technical 
          typesetting using TeX, preserving usability in Windows applications.

          The fonts have been superseded by the by the following  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre}{TeX-Gyre} fonts:

          
          \begin{itemize}
          \item The Quasi-Bookman (qbk) fonts are now available as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-bonum}{TeX-Gyre Bonum} ;
          \item the Quasi-Chancery (qzc) fonts are now available as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-chorus}{TeX-Gyre Chorus} ;
          \item the Quasi-Courier (qcr) fonts are now available as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-cursor}{TeX-Gyre Cursor} ;
          \item the Quasi-Swiss and Quasi-Swiss-Condensed (qhv) fonts are now available as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-heros}{TeX-Gyre Heros} ;
          \item the Quasi-Palatino (qpl) fonts are now available as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-pagella}{TeX-Gyre Pagella} ; and
          \item the Quasi-Times (qtm) fonts are now available as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-termes}{TeX-Gyre Termes} .

\section[\texttt{qrcodetikz} -- Prettier QR codes]{\texttt{qrcodetikz} -- Prettier QR codes}\label{pkg:qrcodetikz}
\index{Package!qrcodetikz}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/qrcodetikz}
\item[name] \texttt{qrcodetikz}
\item[caption] Prettier QR codes
\item[author] Frasson, Miguel Vinícius Santini
\index{Author!Frasson, Miguel Vinícius Santini}
\item[copyright] Miguel V. S. Frasson (2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.0 (2025-05-28)
\item[last changes] 2025-05-28
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package improves the display of QR codes provided by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/qrcode}{qrcode} .

          The Quick Response (QR) codes provided by package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/qrcode}{qrcode} show 
          white borders on each square (from little to very prominent, depending on the pdf viewer). This is because 
          the QR code is printed square by square, not the connected regions of squares as such, and pdf screen 
          viewers show these undesired borders.

          This package overwrites the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/qrcode}{qrcode} printing functions 
          to fill connected regions of the QR code using \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} , 
          allowing prettier qrcodes on screen visualization, with possibility of customization.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/qrcodetikz/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/qrcodetikz/qrcodetikz.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides the preferred document class for papers to be submitted to ''Quantum — the open 
          journal of quantum science''. It is based on the widely used  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/article}{article} document 
          class and designed to allow a seamless transition from documents typeset with the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/article}{article} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/revtex4-1}{revtex4-1} , 
          and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/elsarticle}{elsarticle} document classes. As a service 
          to authors, the document class comes with a predefined bibilography style \texttt{quantum.bst} that 
          is optimized to be used with the \texttt{quantumarticle} document class. Additionally, the \texttt{quantumview} documentclass 
          is provided, which can be used as a proxy to typeset the HTML-only editorial pieces in Quantum Views 
          in a LaTeX editor.

          The quantumarticle document class also offers an option to remove the Quantum-related branding. In that 
          way, users appreciating the esthetics of this document class can use it for their notes as well.

\item[name] \texttt{quattrocento}
\item[caption] Quattrocento and Quattrocento Sans fonts with LaTeX support
\item[author] Tennent, Bob
\index{Author!Tennent, Bob}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[license] ofl = The SIL Open Font License (free)
\index{License!ofl}

\item[version]  (2022-09-13)
\item[last changes] 2022-09-13
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides LaTeX, pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX support for the Quattrocento and Quattrocento 
          Sans families of fonts, designed by Pablo Impallari; the fonts themselves are also provided, in both 
          TrueType and Type1 format.

          Quattrocento is a classic typeface with wide and open letterforms, and great x-height, which makes it 
          very legible for body text at small sizes. Tiny details that only show up at bigger sizes make it also

\item[last changes] 2024-09-07

\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package offers the user an easy way to typeset The Holy Quran. It has been inspired by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lipsum}{lipsum} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ptext}{ptext} packages 
          and provides several macros for typesetting the whole or any part of the Quran based on its popular division, 
          including surah, ayah, juz, hizb, quarter, and page.

          Besides the Arabic original, translations to English, German, French, and Persian are provided, as well 
          as an English transliteration.

\section[\texttt{qworld} -- Drawing string diagrams for monoidal categories and quantum \ldots]{\texttt{qworld} -- Drawing string diagrams for monoidal categories and quantum theory in TeX}\label{pkg:qworld}
\index{Package!qworld}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/qworld}
\item[name] \texttt{QWorld}
\item[caption] Drawing string diagrams for monoidal categories and quantum theory in TeX
\item[author] Ryota, Niina
\index{Author!Ryota, Niina}
\item[copyright] Niina Ryota (2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.1.2
\item[description] (no language specified) This LaTeX package has been designed for the typesetting of  \textbf{graphical languages} grounded 
          in \textbf{monoidal category theory} and its extensions. It provides a declarative, LaTeX-native 
          interface for rendering \textbf{string diagrams} , eliminating the need for any external 
          graphics software or manual image management.

          The package supports a wide spectrum of categorical structures frequently encountered in  \textbf{categorical 
          quantum mechanics} , algebraic structures, and diagrammatic reasoning, including but not limited 
          to:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Monoidal and symmetric monoidal categories
          \item Dual objects and pivotal / rigid categories
          \item Dagger categories
          \item Frobenius algebras and Hopf algebras
          \item Braided, balanced, and ribbon categories
          \end{itemize}
Internally, QWorld builds upon the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pgf}{TikZ} graphics framework, 
          but introduces a domain-specific layer of abstraction that aligns diagram syntax closely with categorical 
          semantics. This design facilitates accurate and transparent visual representations of morphisms, tensor 
          products, and composition, thereby supporting both formal exposition and pedagogical use.

          QWorld is intended for researchers and educators working in categorical logic, quantum foundations,  \textbf{topological 
          quantum field theory} ( \textbf{TQFT} ), and related domains where graphical calculi 
          constitute an essential mode of reasoning.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/qworld/README.md}
\item[documentation] \textit{Package documentation (Japanese)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/qworld/doc/qworld.pdf}

\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation (English)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/qworld/doc/qworld_en.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./8731711251-qworld_en.pdf|
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/pgf/contrib/qworld}

\item[description] (no language specified) \texttt{qyxf-book} is a LaTeX document class (template) developed by Qian Yuan Xue Fu (QYXF), 
          a student club of Xi’an Jiaotong University (XJTU). Up to now, this template has been applied to academic 
          counselling material (''course helpers'') written by members of QYXF, including

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Solutions to University Physics:  \href{https://qyxf.site/latest/大物题解（上）.pdf}{https://qyxf.site/latest/大物题解（上）.pdf}

          \end{itemize}

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Minimalistic document style, as preferred for ''course helpers''.
          \item Several color schemes are offered, and it is easy to customize your own scheme.
          \item Simple interfaces for users to customize the style of preface, main part and so on.
          \end{itemize}
Currently the template is only designed for  \emph{Chinese} typesetting.

\item[description] (no language specified) R2bib and EndNote2bib read files (respectively in refer and EndNote format) and produces a BibTeX reference 
          list on the standard output.

          to invent a key for an entry, and it has to guess what BibTeX entry type to generate).

          is provided

          typesets the characters of \texttt{TEXT} in random order, such that the resulting output 
          appears correct, but most automated attempts to read the file will misunderstand it.

          fear of email address harvesters or spammers easily picking up the address.

\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.01
\item[description] (no language specified) A package to define the low-level font commands that existed in LaTeX 2.09, for the benefit of old documents 
          (or packages) that used them.

          Since this is potentially an expensive operation (loading lots of fonts), the package allows you to chop 
          and choose:

          \begin{verbatim}
\usepackage[only,tenrm,sevsf]{rawfonts}
          \end{verbatim}
will load just  \texttt{{\textbackslash}tenrm} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}sevsf} . 
          (This facility uses the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/somedefs}{somedefs} package).

          The package is part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latex-tools}{latex-tools} bundle 
          in the LaTeX \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/required}{required} distribution.

\section[\texttt{rcs} -- Use RCS (revision control system) tags in LaTeX documents]{\texttt{rcs} -- Use RCS (revision control system) tags in LaTeX documents}\label{pkg:rcs}
\index{Package!rcs}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/rcs}
\item[name] \texttt{rcs}
\item[caption] Use RCS (revision control system) tags in LaTeX documents
\item[author] Gilbey, Julian

\item[author] Schrod, Joachim
\index{Author!Schrod, Joachim}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)

\item[version]  (2007-06-06)
\item[last changes] 2007-06-06
\item[year] 2007
\index{Year!2007}
\item[description] (no language specified) The rcs package utilizes the inclusion of RCS supplied data in LaTeX documents. It's upward compatible 
          to *all* rcs styles I know of.

          In particular, you can easily

          \begin{itemize}
          \item access values of every RCS field in your document
          \item put the checkin date on the titlepage
          \item put RCS fields in a footline
          \end{itemize}
You can typeset revision logs. Not in verbatim -- real LaTeX text! But you need a configurable RCS for 
          that. Refer to the user manual for more detailed information.

          You can also configure the rcs package easily to do special things for any keyword.

          This bundle comes with a user manual, an internal interface description, full documentation of the implementation, 
          style information for AUC-TeX, and test cases.

          that data at will by individual cell number. The data can be but need not be numerical in nature. It 
          can be, for example, formatted text.

          particularly useful when elements of multiple arrays must be recallable and dynamically combined at time 
          of compilation, rather than in advance.

\index{Package!readprov}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/readprov}
\item[name] \texttt{readprov}
\item[caption] Provides GetFileInfo without the need to load the file
\item[author] Lück, Uwe
\index{Author!Lück, Uwe}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.5
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a  \texttt{{\textbackslash}GetFileInfo} command (as in the LaTeX 
          standard \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/doc}{doc} package, but without the need to load the 
          doc package). The package also provides new robust (expandable) variants of \texttt{{\textbackslash}GetFileInfo} , 
          even without loading the file itself (reading the file is stopped when the requisite information is found). 
          So, for exaple, you can describe packages that are incompatible with each other or with packages that 
          your document uses, or even report about class files (that are plainly not loadable).

          Files examined in this way also enter the output of  \texttt{{\textbackslash}listfiles} .

          The package is part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fileinfo}{fileinfo} bundle.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Bundle readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/fileinfo/README.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) The package uses the author’s package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/collectbox}{collectbox} to 
          define variants of common box related macros which read the content as real box and not as macro argument. 
          This enables the use of verbatim or other special material as part of this content.

          The provided macros have the same names as the original versions but start with an upper-case letter 
          instead. The ''long-form'' macros, like  \texttt{{\textbackslash}Makebox} , can also 
          be used as environments, but not the ''short-form'' macros, like \texttt{{\textbackslash}Mbox} . 
          However, normally the long form uses the short form anyway when no optional arguments are used.

\item[description] (no language specified) This small package replaces  \texttt{{\textbackslash}textsuperscript} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}textsubscript} commands 
          by equivalent commands that use OpenType font features to access appropriate glyphs if possible.

          The package also patches LaTeX’s default footnote command to use this new  \texttt{{\textbackslash}textsuperscript} for 
          footnote symbols.

          The package requires  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontspec}{fontspec} running on either 
          XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX.

          The package holds functions that were once parts of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xltxtra}{xltxtra} package, 
          which now loads realscripts by default.

\item[description] (no language specified) Provides commands  \texttt{{\textbackslash}setcounterref} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}addtocounterref} which use the section (or whatever) number from the reference as the value to put into the counter, as in:
          \begin{verbatim}
...\label{sec:foo}
...
\setcounterref{foonum}{sec:foo}
          \end{verbatim}
Commands \texttt{{\textbackslash}setcounterpageref} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}addtocounterpageref} do the corresponding thing with the page reference of the label.

          No  \texttt{.ins} file is distributed; process the \texttt{.dtx} with plain TeX 
          to create one.

\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a consistent way of producing references throughout a project. Enough flexibility 
          is provided to make local changes to a single reference. The user can configure their own setup. The 
          package offers a direct interface to  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/varioref}{varioref} (for 
          use, for example, in large projects such as a series of books, or a multivolume thesis written as a series 
          of documents), and name references from the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/nameref}{nameref} package 
          may be incorporated with ease. For large projects such as a series of books or a multi volume thesis, 
          written as freestanding documents, a facility is provided to interface to the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xr}{xr} package 
          for external document references.

\section[\texttt{register} -- Typeset programmable elements in digital hardware (registers\ldots]{\texttt{register} -- Typeset programmable elements in digital hardware (registers)}\label{pkg:register}
\index{Package!register}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/register}
\item[name] \texttt{register}
\item[caption] Typeset programmable elements in digital hardware (registers)
\item[author] Lovell, Matthew
\index{Author!Lovell, Matthew}
\item[copyright] Matthew B. Lovell (2001-2020)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 2.0 (2020-03-22)
\item[last changes] 2020-03-22
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package is designed for typesetting the programmable elements in digital hardware, i.e., registers. 
          Such registers typically have many fields and can be quite wide; they are thus a challenge to typeset 
          in a consistent manner. Register is similar in some aspects to the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bytefield}{bytefield} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bitpattern}{bitpattern} packages. 
          Anyone doing hardware documentation using LaTeX should examine those packages.

          Register requires version 2001/07/25 or newer of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/float}{float} package.

          An example Perl module and script are provided, to convert the register specifications into structures 
          suitable for, say, a pre-silicon test environment.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/register/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/register/register.pdf}

\index{Package!reptheorem}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/reptheorem}
\item[name] \texttt{reptheorem}
\item[caption] Repetition of theorem environments
\item[author] Straat, Jesse
\index{Author!Straat, Jesse}
\item[copyright] Jesse Straat (2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.3 (2024-10-07)
\item[last changes] 2024-10-07
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) When writing a large manuscript, it is sometimes beneficial to repeat a theorem (or lemma or...) at an 
          earlier or later point for didactical purposes. However,  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/thmtools}{thmtools} ’s 
          built-in \texttt{restatable} only allows replicating theorems \emph{after} they 
          have been stated, and only in the same document.

          This package solves the issue by making use of the  \texttt{.aux} file, and also introduces 
          its own file extension, \texttt{.thm} , to replicate theorems in other files.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/reptheorem/reptheorem-doc.pdf}

\index{License!lppl}

\item[description] (no language specified) A macro package for use with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/epsf}{epsf.tex} which allows 
          PostScript labels in an Encapsulated PostScript file to be replaced by TeX labels. The package provides 
          commands \texttt{{\textbackslash}relabel} (simply replace a PostScript string), \texttt{{\textbackslash}adjustrelabel} (replace 
          a PostScript string, with position adjustment), and \texttt{{\textbackslash}extralabel} (add 
          a label at given coordinates).

          You can, if you so choose, use the facilities of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/labelfig}{labelfig} package 
          in place of using \texttt{{\textbackslash}extralabel} .

\index{Package!rmligs}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/rmligs}
\item[name] \texttt{rmligs}
\item[caption] Remove incorrect ligatures in German documents
\item[author] Jacke, Björn
\index{Author!Jacke, Björn}
\item[copyright] Björn Jacke (1999-2002)
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 0.84
\item[description] (no language specified) Ligatures, which are a pleasing feature of TeX's use of fonts, should not be placed in German words between 
          the word stem and the rest of the word.

          The rmligs package is a perl script that takes input in ISO 8859-1 or -15, UTF-8 or LaTeX-style umlaut 
          encodings ( \texttt{"a} , \texttt{"u} , etc.), and inserts a break where an inappropriate 
          ligature would appear. So, for example, ‘Auflage’ will be changed to ‘Auf"|lage’, which typesets in a 
          typographically correct fashion.
\item[documentation]  (German) \textit{Package README}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/rmligs/README}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}

\item[name] \texttt{romandeadf}
\item[caption] Romande ADF fonts and LaTeX support
\item[author] Rees, Clea F.
\index{Author!Rees, Clea F.}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[license] gpl2 = GNU General Public License, version 2 (free)
\index{License!gpl2}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 2}
\item[version] 2.1
\item[description] (no language specified) Romande ADF is a serif font family with oldstyle figures, designed as a substitute for Times, Tiffany 
          or Caslon. The family currently includes upright, italic and small-caps shapes in each of regular and 
          demi-bold weights and an italic script in regular. The support package renames the fonts according to 
          the Karl Berry fontname scheme and defines four families. Two of these primarily provide access to the 
          ''standard'' or default characters while the ''alternate'' families support alternate characters, additional 
          ligatures and the long s. The included package files provide access to these features in LaTeX as explained 
          in the documentation.

          The LaTeX support requires the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/nfssext-cfr}{nfssext-cfr} and 
          the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xkeyval}{xkeyval} packages.

\item[author] The LaTeX Project Team
\index{Author!The LaTeX Project Team}
\item[author] Fairbairns, Robin
\index{Author!Fairbairns, Robin}
\item[author] Rahtz, Sebastian
\index{Author!Rahtz, Sebastian}

\item[last changes] 2016-08-11
\item[year] 2016
\index{Year!2016}
\item[description] (no language specified) A package built on the standard LaTeX  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphics}{graphics} package 
          to perform all the different sorts of rotation one might like, including complete figures and tables 
          with their captions.

          If you want continuous text (i.e., more than one page) set in landscape mode, use the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/lscape}{lscape} package 
          instead. The rotating packages only deals in rotated boxes (or floats, which are themselves boxes), and 
          boxes always stay on one page.

          If you need to use the facilities of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/float}{float} in 
          the same document, load rotating.sty via \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/rotfloat}{rotfloat} , 
          which smooths the path between the rotating and float packages.

          The package is now part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/latex-graphics}{latex-graphics} bundle, 
          which is one of the collections in the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/required}{LaTeX ‘required’} set 
          of packages.

\item[version] 1.2
\item[description] (no language specified) The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/float}{float} package provides commands to define new 
          floats of various styles (plain, boxed, ruled, and userdefined ones); the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/rotating}{rotating} package 
          provides new environments (sidewaysfigure and sidewaystable) which are rotated by 90 or 270 degrees. 
          But what about new rotated floats, e.g. a rotated ruled one? This package makes this possible; it builds 
          a bridge between the two packages and extends the commands from the float package to define rotated versions 
          of the new floats, too.

\index{License!License that prevents distribution}
\item[version] 1.3
\item[description] (no language specified) This package is of interest for people working in linguistics and language technology.

          Drawing rhetorical analyses is no fun when you need to change and update diagrams as you refine your 
          work, or, more importantly, if a lot of analyses are to be drawn. Voila, there we go: This package enables 
          us to typeset beautiful diagrams with no hassle. It is oriented towards the style of the diagrams shown 
          in Mann\&Thompson's Rhetorical Structure Theory and subsequent works. This package works perfectly 
          with (LaTeX) and pdfLaTeX and does not require any special PostScript capabilities in the output side.

\section[\texttt{rtkinenc} -- Input encoding with fallback procedures]{\texttt{rtkinenc} -- Input encoding with fallback procedures}\label{pkg:rtkinenc}
\index{Package!rtkinenc}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/rtkinenc}
\item[name] \texttt{rtkinenc}
\item[caption] Input encoding with fallback procedures
\item[author] Hellström, Lars
\index{Author!Hellström, Lars}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The rtkinenc package is functionally similar to the standard LaTeX package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/inputenc}{inputenc} : 
          both set up active characters so that an input character outside the range of 7-bit visible ASCII is 
          coverted into one or more corresponding LaTeX commands. The main difference lies in that rtkinenc allows 
          the user to specify a fallback procedure to use when the text command corresponding to some input character 
          isn't available.

          Names of commands in rtkinenc have been selected so that it can read inputenc encoding definition files, 
          and the aim is that rtkinenc should be backwards compatible with inputenc. rtkinenc is not a new version 
          of inputenc though, nor is it part of standard LaTeX.

          For an example of how rtkinenc is used, the user may look at the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tclldoc}{tclldoc} class.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/rtkinenc/rtkinenc-doc.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./4159954949-rtkinenc-doc.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/rtkinenc/README}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/rtkinenc}

\section[\texttt{runtexshebang} -- A Lua script running LaTeX document files with TeX-style she\ldots]{\texttt{runtexshebang} -- A Lua script running LaTeX document files with TeX-style shebang}\label{pkg:runtexshebang}
\index{Package!runtexshebang}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/runtexshebang}
\item[name] \texttt{runtexshebang}
\item[caption] A Lua script running LaTeX document files with TeX-style shebang
\item[author] Yamamoto, Munehiro
\index{Author!Yamamoto, Munehiro}
\item[copyright] Munehiro Yamamoto (2021-2023)
\item[license] mit = MIT License (free)
\index{License!mit}
\index{License!MIT License}
\item[version] 0.5 (2023-11-17)
\item[last changes] 2023-11-17
\item[year] 2023
\index{Year!2023}
\item[description] (no language specified) In short, a TeX-style shebang ( \texttt{\%\#!} ) is a special kind of TeX comment 
          that you include in your TeX/LaTeX document file to tell the operating system’s shell how to run the 
          file for the rest of the file:

          \begin{verbatim}
%#!lualatex foo.tex
\documentclass{article}
\begin{document}
Hello, {\LaTeX} World!

Happy {\TeX}ing.
\end{document}
          \end{verbatim}
If you are using a TeX-style shebang, it must appear on the line that matched 20 lines or less in your 
          LaTeX document, and it has to start with a TeX comment symbol ( \texttt{\%} ) followed 
          by a hash sign ( \texttt{\#} ) and an exclamation mark ( \texttt{!} ), colloquially 
          known as the bang, hence the name shebang for TeX/LaTeX.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/runtexshebang/README.md}

\section[\texttt{rviewport} -- Relative Viewport for Graphics Inclusion]{\texttt{rviewport} -- Relative Viewport for Graphics Inclusion}\label{pkg:rviewport}
\index{Package!rviewport}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/rviewport}
\item[name] \texttt{rviewport}
\item[caption] Relative Viewport for Graphics Inclusion
\item[author] Veytsman, Boris
\index{Author!Veytsman, Boris}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) Package  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphicx}{graphicx} provides a useful keyword viewport 
          which allows to show just a part of an image. However, one needs to put there the actual coordinates 
          of the viewport window. Sometimes it is useful to have relative coordinates as fractions of natural size. 
          For example, one may want to print a large image on a spread, putting a half on a verso page, and another 
          half on the next recto page. For this one would need a viewport occupying exactly one half of the file's 
          bounding box, whatever the actual width of the image may be.

          This package adds a new keyword rviewport to the graphicx package specifiying Relative Viewport for graphics 
          inclusion: a window defined by the given fractions of the natural width and height of the image.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/rviewport/README}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/rviewport/rviewport.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./8622483210-rviewport.pdf|
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/rviewport}
\item[on Mik\TeX] \texttt{rviewport}
