\section[\texttt{sty2dtx} -- Create a .dtx file from a .sty file]{\texttt{sty2dtx} -- Create a .dtx file from a .sty file}\label{pkg:sty2dtx}
\index{Package!sty2dtx}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/sty2dtx}
\item[name] \texttt{sty2dtx}
\item[caption] Create a .dtx file from a .sty file
\item[author] Scharrer, Martin
\index{Author!Scharrer, Martin}
\item[copyright] Martin Scharrer (2010-2022)
\item[license] gpl3 = GNU General Public License, version 3 (free)
\index{License!gpl3}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 3}
\item[version] 2.4 (2022-10-18)
\item[last changes] 2022-10-18
\item[year] 2022
\index{Year!2022}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a Perl script that converts a  \texttt{.sty} file (LaTeX package) to \texttt{.dtx} format 
          (documented LaTeX source), by surrounding macro definitions with \texttt{macro} and \texttt{macrocode} environments. 
          The macro name is automatically inserted as an argument to the \texttt{macro} environemnt.

          Code lines outside macro definitions are wrapped only in  \texttt{macrocode} environments. 
          Empty lines are removed.

          The script should not be thought to be fool proof and 100\% accurate but rather as a good start to 
          the business of making a  \texttt{.dtx} file from an undocumented style file.

          Full  \texttt{.dtx} files are generated. A template based on the skeleton file from \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/dtxtut}{dtxtut} is 
          used. User level macros are added automatically to the ''Usage'' section of the \texttt{.dtx} file. 
          A corresponding \texttt{.ins} file can be generated as well.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/sty2dtx/README.txt}

\section[\texttt{styleitems} -- Independent auto-numbered list labels drawn with TikZ]{\texttt{styleitems} -- Independent auto-numbered list labels drawn with TikZ}\label{pkg:styleitems}
\index{Package!styleitems}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/styleitems}
\item[name] \texttt{styleitems}
\item[caption] Independent auto-numbered list labels drawn with TikZ
\item[author] Hameed, Faris
\index{Author!Hameed, Faris}
\item[copyright] Faris Hameed (null)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides a fully self-contained auto-numbering system for decorative list labels based on 
          TikZ. Unlike packages such as enumitem, each label is rendered as a live TikZ node, allowing full control 
          over shape, colour, stroke, and numbering style. Each list instance maintains its own counter using an 
          internal stack mechanism, ensuring that nested lists at any depth remain independent and never interfere 
          with their parent counters.

          Available label shapes (16 total): Circle, Square, Rectangle, Diamond, Triangle, Pentagon, Hexagon, Octagon, 
          Star (5-point), Star (12-point), Ellipse Callout (left/right), Cloud Callout (left/right), and four arrow 
          directions (right, left, up, down). Every shape is available in two modes: vertical and inline.

          Numbering styles (8): arabic, indic (Arabic-Indic digits), alph, Alph, roman, Roman, aralph (Hijai order), 
          aralphabjad (Abjad order).

          All environments accept optional arguments for colour, numbering style, text rotation, and text scale. 
          The package fully supports bidirectional (Arabic/RTL) documents alongside standard LTR typesetting.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/styleitems/styleitems-doc.pdf}

\section[\texttt{suanpan-l3} -- Traditional Chinese 7-bids suanpan (abacus) package based on\ldots]{\texttt{suanpan-l3} -- Traditional Chinese 7-bids suanpan (abacus) package based on l3draw}\label{pkg:suanpan-l3}
\index{Package!suanpan-l3}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/suanpan-l3}
\item[name] \texttt{suanpan-l3}
\item[caption] Traditional Chinese 7-bids suanpan (abacus) package based on l3draw
\item[author] Geng, Nan
\index{Author!Geng, Nan}
\item[copyright] Nan Geng (2020-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 1.2.4 (2024-10-13)
\item[last changes] 2024-10-13
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) This traditional Chinese 7-bids abacus drawing package utilizes  \texttt{l3draw} and is developed 
          with \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/expl3}{expl3} . It can effectively manage both upper 
          and lower bids, while also considering bottom bid, top bid, and hanging bid.

          The package offers a unique environment for drawing abacuses, denoted as  \texttt{suanpan} . 
          Within this environment, 7 specialized macros are available for the creation of abacuses. The \texttt{{\textbackslash}rod} macro 
          is used to lay out a single rod, while the \texttt{{\textbackslash}rod*} macro draws 
          a counting point on this rod’s beam. The \texttt{{\textbackslash}rods} macro is capable 
          of laying out a set of rods. The \texttt{{\textbackslash}bid} macro colors the specified 
          bid. The \texttt{{\textbackslash}bids} macro colors all inner bids that are near the 
          beam, while the \texttt{{\textbackslash}bids*} macro colors all outer bids that are 
          far from the beam. Lastly, the \texttt{{\textbackslash}lrframe} macro is used to lay 
          out the left and right frames of an abacus.

          At the same time, the package offers customization options for abacus, including line width, draw color, 
          fill color, bid space, rod space, etc. These can be configured through package options,  \texttt{suanpan} environment 
          options, or the \texttt{{\textbackslash}suanpanset} macro.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/suanpan-l3/README.md}

\section[\texttt{subfig} -- Figures broken into subfigures]{\texttt{subfig} -- Figures broken into subfigures}\label{pkg:subfig}
\index{Package!subfig}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/subfig}
\item[name] \texttt{subfig}
\item[caption] Figures broken into subfigures
\item[author] Cochran, Steven Douglas
\index{Author!Cochran, Steven Douglas}
\item[author] bidi-tex GitHub Organisation
\index{Author!bidi-tex GitHub Organisation}
\item[author] Khalighi, Vafa
\index{Author!Khalighi, Vafa}

\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.3
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides support for the manipulation and reference of small or ‘sub’ figures and tables 
          within a single figure or table environment. It is convenient to use this package when your subfigures 
          are to be separately captioned, referenced, or are to be included in the List-of-Figures. A new  \texttt{{\textbackslash}subfigure} command 
          is introduced which can be used inside a figure environment for each subfigure. An optional first argument 
          is used as the caption for that subfigure.

          This package supersedes the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/subfigure}{subfigure} package 
          (which is no longer maintained). The name was changed since the package is not completely backward compatible 
          with the older package The major advantage of the new package is that the user interface is keyword/value 
          driven and easier to use. To ease the transition from the subfigure package, the distribution includes 
          a configuration file ( \texttt{subfig.cfg} ) which nearly emulates the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/subfigure}{subfigure} package.

          The functionality of the package is provided by the (more recent still)  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/subcaption}{subcaption} package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/subfig/README}

          It has been  \emph{obsoleted} by the NFSS command \texttt{{\textbackslash}DeclareFontFamilySubstitution} added

          Existing documents can be updated by removing  \texttt{{\textbackslash}usepackage{\textbraceleft}substitutefont{\textbraceright}} and 
          replacing all instances of \texttt{{\textbackslash}substitutefont} with \texttt{{\textbackslash}DeclareFontFamilySubstitution} .

\index{Package!sudoku}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}

\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The sudoku package provides an environment for typesetting sudoku grids.

          A sudoku puzzle is a 9x9 grid where some of the squares in the grid contain numbers. The rules are simple: 
          every column can only contain the digits 1 to 9, every row can only contain the digits 1 to 9 and every 
          3x3 box can only contain the digits 1 to 9.

          More information, including help and example puzzles, can be found at  \href{http://www.sudoku.org.uk}{sudoku.org.uk} . 
          This site also has blank sudoku grids (or worksheets), but you will not need to print them from there 
          if you have this package installed.

\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.0a
\item[description] (no language specified) The bundle provides three packages:\\

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{printsudoku} , which provides a command \texttt{{\textbackslash}sudoku} whose argument is the name of a file containing a puzzle specification;\\
          \item  \texttt{solvesudoku} , which attempts to find a solution to the puzzle in the file named in the argument; and\\
          \item  \texttt{createsudoku} , which uses the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/random}{random} package to generate a puzzle according to a bunch of parameters that the user sets via macros.
          \end{itemize}
The bundle comes with a set of ready-prepared puzzle files.

\item[description] (no language specified) This bundle contains the two packages  \texttt{svg} and \texttt{svg-extract} .

          The  \texttt{svg} package is intended for the automated integration of SVG graphics into 
          LaTeX documents. Therefore the capabilities provided by \texttt{Inkscape} — or more precisely 
          its command line tool — are used to export the text within an SVG graphic to a separate file, which is 
          then rendered by LaTeX. For this purpose the two commands \texttt{{\textbackslash}includesvg} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}includeinkscape} are 
          provided which are very similar to the \texttt{{\textbackslash}includegraphics} command 
          of the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/graphicx}{graphicx} package.

          In addition, the package  \texttt{svg-extract} allows the extraction of these graphics into 
          independent files in different graphic formats, exactly as it is rendered within the LaTeX document, 
          using either \texttt{ImageMagick} or \texttt{Ghostscript} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/svg/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/svg/doc/svg.pdf}

\section[\texttt{svg-animate} -- Generate animated SVG diagrams with TikZ]{\texttt{svg-animate} -- Generate animated SVG diagrams with TikZ}\label{pkg:svg-animate}
\index{Package!svg-animate}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/svg-animate}
\item[name] \texttt{svg-animate}
\item[caption] Generate animated SVG diagrams with TikZ
\item[author] Gross, Sébastien
\index{Author!Gross, Sébastien}
\item[copyright] Sébastien Gross (2026)
\item[license] agpl3 = GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 (free)
\index{License!agpl3}
\index{License!GNU Affero General Public License, version 3}
\item[version] 1.0 (2026-03-16)
\item[last changes] 2026-03-16
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides step-by-step animations for TikZ diagrams in SVG format. The resulting animations 
          run natively in web browsers and do not require JavaScript or plugins.

          From a single source file, both an animated SVG and a static PDF can be generated. In the PDF output, 
          steps may be stacked or collapsed into a single frame.

          The animation model is based on discrete  \emph{steps} . A TikZ picture is enclosed in \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}animate{\textbraceright}} , 
          material to be shown at a given step is marked with \texttt{{\textbackslash}reveal{\textbraceleft}...{\textbraceright}} , 
          and \texttt{{\textbackslash}animstep} is used to advance to the next step.

          Additional features include per-step durations, visibility over multiple steps or step ranges, blinking 
          elements, one-shot or looping playback, and a  \texttt{{\textbackslash}noanimate} fallback 
          for PDF output.

          In SVG output, visibility changes are implemented by means of SMIL animations with instantaneous opacity 
          transitions.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/svg-animate/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/svg-animate/svg-animate.pdf}

\section[\texttt{swimgraf} -- Graphical/textual representations of swimming performances]{\texttt{swimgraf} -- Graphical/textual representations of swimming performances}\label{pkg:swimgraf}
\index{Package!swimgraf}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/swimgraf}
\item[name] \texttt{Swimgraf}
\item[caption] Graphical/textual representations of swimming performances
\item[author] Osborne, Martin J.
\index{Author!Osborne, Martin J.}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version]  (2002-05-30)
\item[last changes] 2002-05-30
\item[year] 2002
\index{Year!2002}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides two macros that produce representations of a swimmer's performances. The user records 
          data in a text file and specifies as arguments of the macros the date range of interest. The macros extract 
          the relevant information from the file and process it:  \texttt{{\textbackslash}swimgraph} produces 
          a graph of the times in a single swimming event (specified as an argument), plotting long course and 
          short course times in separate lines. Records and qualifying times, stored in text files, may optionally 
          be included on the graph. \texttt{{\textbackslash}swimtext} produces a written record 
          of the times in all events.

          Files of current world and Canadian records are included.

          The package requires the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pstricks-base}{PSTricks} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/keyval}{keyval} packages. 
          For attractive output it also requires a colour output device.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/swimgraf/swimgraf.pdf}

\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/synapsen}
\item[name] \texttt{Synapsen}
\item[caption] Reference management tool for BibTeX
\item[author] Krajewski, Markus
\index{Author!Krajewski, Markus}
\item[copyright] Markus Krajewski (2007)
\item[license] shareware = Shareware: A fee is required (not free)
\index{License!shareware}
\index{License!Shareware: A fee is required}
\item[version] 3.0
\item[description] (no language specified) Synapsen is a hypertextual card index or reference organizer, especially designed for BibTeX, and offering 
          support for the requirements of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/biblatex}{BibLaTeX} .

          The Software is written in JAVA, and runs on all major operating systems (Windows, Mac OS X, Linux, Unix).

          The software features automatic or individual connections between cards; direct search and download from 
          public bibliographic sources; fully compliant BibTeX output for LaTeX; support for word processors via

\section[\texttt{t1infos} -- Utilities for PostScript fonts]{\texttt{t1infos} -- Utilities for PostScript fonts}\label{pkg:t1infos}
\index{Package!t1infos}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/t1infos}
\item[name] \texttt{t1infos}
\item[caption] Utilities for PostScript fonts
\item[author] Baruchel, Thomas
\index{Author!Baruchel, Thomas}
\item[license] bsd = BSD Style License (free)
\index{License!bsd}
\index{License!BSD Style License}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) There are here two little programs written in C (using t1lib) for scanning Type 1 fonts, and doing:\\– 
          compute the ‘black area’ of each glyph, with how much percent of the square containing the glyph is black, 
          and\\– checking if the ‘extremas’ (see Adobe Type 1 specifications) of the outline are correct, and 
          tell which one are missing.

          There is also here a PostScript dictionary containing three algorithms for automatic kerning (the kerning 
          is computed ‘on the fly’ instead of being pre-computed by external software like TeX, groff or lout; 
          very useful for some PostScript hacking). Two of these algorithms are quite classical; the third is original 
          and is PostScript-optimized. The PostScript file in the distribution contains both demonstration code 
          and the dictionary itself.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{README file}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/utilities/t1infos/README}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/utilities/t1infos}
\item[keyword] \texttt{ps-manip} (manipulate PostScript files)
\index{Topic!ps-manip}
\item[language(s)] no language specified
\index{Language in description/documentation!no language specified}
\item[year] without year
\index{Year!without year}
\item[last access] 2026-04-10
\end{labeling}

\item[description] (no language specified) T1Subset creates a subset of a PostScript Type 1 font. It is a header-only library as the complete functionalities 
          are done in the header.

          Note that only the unused glyphs are removed; subsetting of subroutines is not currently supported, although 
          this may change in a future version.

          In addition, only the following built-in encodings are currently supported: StandardEncoding, WinAnsiEncoding, 
          and MacRomanEncoding. Other encodings may be supported in a future version.

          convert PFB (binary) to PFA (ascii) fonts;\\– \texttt{t1binary} : convert PFA to PFB 
          fonts;\\– \texttt{t1disasm} : convert PFA or PFB fonts to human-readable and -editable 
          format;\\– \texttt{t1asm} : reassemble such editable formats to a font;\\– \texttt{t1unmac} :

          Macintosh font from a Type 1 font.

\item[caption] Tagging tables of contents

\index{Author!Burnol, Jean-François}
\item[copyright] Jean-François Burnol (2012, 2013, 2015, 2018, 2021, 2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.4d (2024-09-17)
\item[last changes] 2024-09-17
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides the commands to flag chapters or sections (or anything else destined to become a 
          TOC line). The command  \texttt{{\textbackslash}nexttocwithtags{\textbraceleft}req1,req2,...{\textbraceright}{\textbraceleft}excl1,excl2,...{\textbraceright}} specifies 
          which tags are to be required and which ones are to be excluded by the next \texttt{{\textbackslash}tableofcontents} (or 
          equivalent) command. In a document that uses a class where \texttt{{\textbackslash}tableofcontents} may 
          only be used once, the command \texttt{{\textbackslash}tableoftaggedcontents{\textbraceleft}req1,req2,...{\textbraceright}{\textbraceleft}excl1,excl2,...{\textbraceright}} may 
          be used to provide several tables.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/tableof/tableof.pdf}

\section[\texttt{tabu} -- Flexible LaTeX tabulars]{\texttt{tabu} -- Flexible LaTeX tabulars}\label{pkg:tabu}
\index{Package!tabu}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/tabu}
\item[name] \texttt{tabu}
\item[caption] Flexible LaTeX tabulars
\item[author] Chervet, Florent
\index{Author!Chervet, Florent}
\item[copyright] Florent Chervet (2010)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 2.9 (2019-01-11)
\item[last changes] 2019-01-11
\item[year] 2019
\index{Year!2019}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package provides an environment,  \texttt{tabu} , which will make any sort of tabular 
          (that doesn’t need to split across pages), and an environment \texttt{longtabu} which provides 
          the facilities of \texttt{tabu} in a modified \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/longtable}{longtable} environment. 
          (Note that this latter offers an enhancement of \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/ltxtable}{ltxtable} .)

          The package requires the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/array}{array} package, and needs \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/etex}{e-TeX} to 
          run (since \texttt{array.sty} is present in every conforming distribution of LaTeX, and since 
          every publicly available LaTeX format is built using \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/etex}{e-TeX} , 
          the requirements are provided by default on any reasonable system). The package also requires \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xcolor}{xcolor} for 
          coloured rules in tables, and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/colortbl}{colortbl} for coloured 
          cells. The \texttt{longtabu} environment further requires that \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/longtable}{longtable} be 
          loaded. The package itself does not load any of these packages for the user.

          The  \texttt{tabu} environment may be used in place of \texttt{tabular} , \texttt{tabular*} and \texttt{tabularx} environments, 
          as well as the \texttt{array} environment in maths mode. It overloads \texttt{tabularx} ’s \texttt{X} -column 
          specification, allowing a width specification, alignment ( \texttt{l} , \texttt{r} , \texttt{c} and \texttt{j} ) 
          and column type indication ( \texttt{p} , \texttt{m} and \texttt{b} ).

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}tabu{\textbraceright} to <dimen>} specifies 
          a target width, and \texttt{{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}tabu{\textbraceright} 
          spread <dimen>} enlarges the environment’s ''natural'' width.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/tabu/tabu.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./3475260523-tabu.pdf|

\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{https://github.com/tabu-issues-for-future-maintainer/tabu}
\index{Contact!repository}

          defined environments are:  \texttt{tabularht} , \texttt{tabularht*} and \texttt{arrayht} . 
          If package \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tabularx}{tabularx} is also loaded, the package 
          also defines environments \texttt{tabularxht} and \texttt{tabularxht*} .

          The places where stretching is to happen are signalled by\\ \texttt{{\textbackslash}noalign{\textbraceleft}{\textbackslash}vfill{\textbraceright}} \\immediately 
          after the \texttt{{\textbackslash}{\textbackslash}} that ends a row of the table 
          or array.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/oberdiek/tabularht.pdf}

\section[\texttt{tabularray} -- Typeset tabulars and arrays with LaTeX3]{\texttt{tabularray} -- Typeset tabulars and arrays with LaTeX3}\label{pkg:tabularray}
\index{Package!tabularray}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/tabularray}
\item[name] \texttt{tabularray}
\item[caption] Typeset tabulars and arrays with LaTeX3
\item[author] Lyu, Jianrui
\index{Author!Lyu, Jianrui}
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 2025C (2025-11-27)
\item[last changes] 2025-11-27
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) LaTeX tables are implemented using TeX commands such as  \texttt{{\textbackslash}halign} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}noalign} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}span} , 
          and \texttt{{\textbackslash}omit} . In order to implement new features, many macro 
          packages have modified the inner table commands inside LaTeX. This makes package code complicated, difficult 
          to maintain, and often conflicts with each other.

          At present, the LaTeX3 programming layer is basically mature. This  \texttt{tabularray} package 
          will discard the old \texttt{{\textbackslash}halign} commands and directly use LaTeX3 
          functions to parse the table, and then typeset the entire table. Under the premise of being compatible 
          with the basic syntax of LaTeX2 tables, this macro package will completely separate the content and style 
          of the table, and the style of the table can be completely set in keyval way.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/tabularray/tabularray.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./9371288773-tabularray.pdf|
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/tabularray/README.md}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/tabularray}

\section[\texttt{talk} -- A LaTeX class for presentations]{\texttt{talk} -- A LaTeX class for presentations}\label{pkg:talk}
\index{Package!talk}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/talk}
\item[name] \texttt{talk}
\item[caption] A LaTeX class for presentations
\item[author] Wiebusch, Martin
\index{Author!Wiebusch, Martin}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 2.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The talk document class allows you to create slides for screen presentations or printing on transparencies. 
          It also allows you to print personal notes for your talk. You can create overlays and display structure 
          information (current section / subsection, table of contents) on your slides. The main feature that distinguishes 
          talk from other presentation classes like  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/beamer}{beamer} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/prosper}{prosper} is 
          that it allows the user to define an arbitrary number of slide styles and switch between these styles 
          from slide to slide. This way the slide layout can be adapted to the slide content. For example, the 
          title or contents page of a talk can be given a slightly different layout than the other slides.

          The talk class makes no restrictions on the slide design whatsoever. The entire look and feel of the 
          presentation can be defined by the user. The style definitions should be put in a separate sty file. 
          Currently the package comes with two sets of pre-defined slide styles ( \texttt{talk-simple.sty} and \texttt{talk-sidebars.sty} ). 
          Contributions from people who are artistically more gifted than the author are more than welcome!
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Example of use (2)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/talk/sidebars-example.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./6171908168-sidebars-example.pdf|

\item[version] 0.42
\item[description] (no language specified) LaTeX’s figures, tables, and  \texttt{{\textbackslash}marginpar} s are dangerous for 
          footnotes (and probably also \texttt{{\textbackslash}enlargethispage} ). Here is a 
          proposal (a ‘patch’ package) to help, by using \texttt{{\textbackslash}holdinginserts} in 
          a simple way. It replaces the original problem with a new one — it is an experiment to find out whether 
          the new problem is less bad (or it is just a contribution to the discussion, maybe just a summary of 
          previous work). The files provide further information.

\item[description] (no language specified) The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tabularray}{tabularray} package offers a modern and nice 
          way to typeset tables, keeping contents and style separated.

          The  \texttt{tblr-extras} package implements extra libraries to use the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/caption}{caption} package 
          alongside \texttt{tabularray} , and translated strings for continuation text in tabularray 
          headers:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{caption} library: Use the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/caption}{caption} package captions with \texttt{tabularray} environments ( \texttt{talltblr} and \texttt{longtblr} ),

          \end{itemize}

          such a box may be split in an upper and a lower part; thus the package may be used for the setting of 
          LaTeX examples where one part of the box displays the source code and the other part shows the output.

          and text parts.

\section[\texttt{ted} -- A (primitive) token list editor]{\texttt{ted} -- A (primitive) token list editor}\label{pkg:ted}
\index{Package!ted}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/ted}
\item[name] \texttt{ted}
\item[caption] A (primitive) token list editor
\item[author] Pégourié-Gonnard, Manuel
\index{Author!Pégourié-Gonnard, Manuel}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.06
\item[description] (no language specified) Just like sed is a stream editor, ted is a token list editor. Actually, it is not as powerfull as sed, 
          but its main feature is that it really works with tokens, not only characters.

          The ted package provides two user macros:  \texttt{{\textbackslash}Substitute} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}ShowTokens} . 
          The first is maybe the most useful: it performs substitutions in token lists (even inside braces). The 
          second displays each token of the list (one per line) with its catcode (in the list, not just the current 
          one), and can be useful for debugging or for TeX learners.

          Ted is designed to work well even if strange tokens (that is, unusual {\textbraceleft}charcode, 
          catcode{\textbraceright} pairs or tokens with a confusing meaning) occur in the list.
\item[documentation] \textit{Package documentation (French)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ted/ted-fr.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./2789129398-ted-fr.pdf|

\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation (English)}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ted/ted.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./8317254744-ted.pdf|
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/ted}

          for specifying which days of the week are to be included and for inserting text either regularly on the 
          same day each week, or on selected days, or for a series of consecutive days. It also has a flexible 
          mechanism for specifing class and nonclass days. Text may be inserted into consecutive days so that it 
          automatically flows around nonclass days.

\section[\texttt{testeq} -- An equality test for use in MetaPost]{\texttt{testeq} -- An equality test for use in MetaPost}\label{pkg:testeq}
\index{Package!testeq}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/testeq}
\item[name] \texttt{testeq}
\item[caption] An equality test for use in MetaPost
\item[author] Vieth, Ulrik
\index{Author!Vieth, Ulrik}
\item[license] noinfo = noinfo 
\index{License!noinfo}
\index{License!noinfo}
\item[version] 1.05
\item[description] (no language specified) This file provides a general equality test macro for objects of any type based on code from Appendix 
          D of The Metafont book, but adapted for MetaPost. Unfortunately it is no longer fully general, because 
          MetaPost lacks the bitmap-oriented operations like cull and totalweight, which are needed when testing 
          for the equality of two pictures.

          A particular useful feature of this package is the patheq macro to test for equality of two paths. This 
          might prove handy when processing data files with the MetaPost graph package, that contain data for an 
          unknown number of paths separated by blank lines. In that case one might use patheq to check whether 
          the last path read is actually the same as the first one, having started over from the beginning.
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/graphics/metapost/contrib/macros/misc/testeq.mp}
\item[keyword] \texttt{mp-supp} (support tools and macros for MetaPost programming)

\item[year] without year

\item[last access] 2025-02-07
\end{labeling}

\index{Package!tex}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}

\item[author] Knuth, Donald E.
\index{Author!Knuth, Donald E.}
\item[copyright] D. E. Knuth (null)

\item[version] 3.141592653 (2021-02-05)
\item[last changes] 2021-02-05
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) TeX is a typesetting system that incorporates a macro processor. A TeX source document specifies or incorporates 
          a number of macro definitions that instruct the TeX engine how to typeset the document. The TeX engine 
          also uses font metrics generated by  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/metafont}{Metafont} , 
          or by any of several other mechanisms that incorporate fonts from other sources into an environment suitable 
          for TeX.

          TeX has been, and continues, a basis and an inspiration for several other programs, including  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/etex}{e-TeX} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/pdftex}{PDFTeX} .

          The distribution includes the source of Knuth’s  \emph{TeX book} ; this source is there to 
          read, as an example of writing TeX — it should not be processed without Knuth’s direct permission.

\section[\texttt{tex-extensions} -- Proposals for extensions to TeX]{\texttt{tex-extensions} -- Proposals for extensions to TeX}\label{pkg:tex-extensions}
\index{Package!tex-extensions}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-extensions}
\item[name] \texttt{tex-extensions}
\item[caption] Proposals for extensions to TeX
\item[author] Clasen, Matthias
\index{Author!Clasen, Matthias}
\item[license] noinfo = noinfo 
\index{License!noinfo}
\index{License!noinfo}
\item[version]  (2003-02-07)
\item[last changes] 2003-02-07
\item[year] 2003
\index{Year!2003}
\item[description] (no language specified) A bundle of proposals for extensions to TeX, implemented as change files to  \texttt{web2c} v7.2. 
          The extesions cover:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item replacing floating point by integer arithmetic, in glue calculations;
          \item introducing hyphenation classes (with a corresponding change to  \texttt{patgen} );
          \item implenting demerits for more than 2 consecutive hyphens;
          \item providing ‘nestable’ and ‘under’ math accents; a primitive to switch to ‘cramped’ styles; provides generalised radicals with a left- and right-delimiter; implementation work for using the hz algorithm;
          \item marginal tokens for hanging punctuation and hyphens.
          \end{itemize}
Several files offering examples of use are also provided.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/systems/tex-extensions/clasen/README}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/systems/tex-extensions/clasen}

\section[\texttt{tex-gyre} -- TeX Fonts extending freely available URW fonts]{\texttt{tex-gyre} -- TeX Fonts extending freely available URW fonts}\label{pkg:tex-gyre}
\index{Package!tex-gyre}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre}
\item[name] \texttt{tex-gyre}
\item[caption] TeX Fonts extending freely available URW fonts
\item[author] Jackowski, Bogusław
\index{Author!Jackowski, Bogusław}
\item[author] Nowacki, Janusz Marian
\index{Author!Nowacki, Janusz Marian}
\item[license] gfl = The GUST Font License (GFL) (free)
\index{License!gfl}
\index{License!The GUST Font License (GFL)}
\item[version] 2.501
\item[description] (no language specified) The TeX-GYRE bundle consists of six font families:

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-adventor}{TeX Gyre Adventor} is based on the URW 
          Gothic L family of fonts (which is derived from ITC Avant Garde Gothic, designed by Herb Lubalin and 
          Tom Carnase).

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-bonum}{TeX Gyre Bonum} is based on the URW Bookman 
          L family (from Bookman Old Style, designed by Alexander Phemister).

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-chorus}{TeX Gyre Chorus} is based on URW Chancery 
          L Medium Italic (from ITC Zapf Chancery, designed by Hermann Zapf in 1979).

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-cursor}{TeX-Gyre Cursor} is based on URW Nimbus 
          Mono L (based on Courier, designed by Howard G. Kettler in 1955, for IBM).

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-heros}{TeX Gyre Heros} is based on URW Nimbus Sans 
          L (from Helvetica, prepared by Max Miedinger, with Eduard Hoffmann in 1957).

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-pagella}{TeX Gyre Pagella} is based on URW Palladio 
          L (from Palatino, designed by Hermann Zapf in the 1940s).

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-schola}{TeX Gyre Schola} is based on the URW Century 
          Schoolbook L family (from Century Schoolbook, designed by Morris Fuller Benton for the American Type 
          Founders).

          \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-termes}{TeX Gyre Termes} is based on the URW Nimbus 
          Roman No9 L family of fonts (from Times New Roman, designed by Stanley Morison together with Starling 
          Burgess and Victor Lardent and first offered by Monotype).

          The constituent standard faces of each family have been greatly extended (though Chorus omits Greek support 
          and has no small-caps family). Each family is available in Adobe Type 1 and Open Type formats, and LaTeX 
          support (for use with a variety of encodings) is provided. Vietnamese characters were added by Han The 
          Thanh.

          There are companion maths fonts for several of these designs, listed in the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-math}{TeX 
          Gyre Math} package.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/tex-gyre/README.txt}

\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/fonts/tex-gyre}

\section[\texttt{tex-gyre-adventor} -- A font family that extends URW Gothic L]{\texttt{tex-gyre-adventor} -- A font family that extends URW Gothic L}\label{pkg:tex-gyre-adventor}
\index{Package!tex-gyre-adventor}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre-adventor}
\item[name] \texttt{tex-gyre-adventor}
\item[caption] A font family that extends URW Gothic L
\item[author] Jackowski, Bogusław
\index{Author!Jackowski, Bogusław}
\item[author] Nowacki, Janusz Marian

\item[license] gfl = The GUST Font License (GFL) (free)

\item[version] 2.501
\item[description] (no language specified) The TeX Gyre Adventor family of sans serif fonts is based on the URW Gothic L family. The original font, 
          ITC Avant Garde Gothic, was designed by Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnase in 1970; the URW font is commonly 
          used as a substitute for the ITC original.

          The standard faces of Adventor have been greatly extended. The family is available both in Adobe Type 
          1 and in OpenType formats, and LaTeX support (for use with a variety of encodings) is provided. Vietnamese 
          characters were added by Han The Thanh.

          TeX Gyre Adventor is distributed as part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre}{TeX 
          Gyre collection}

\index{License!gfl}

\item[version] 2.003
\item[description] (no language specified) The TeX Gyre Chorus font is based on the URW Chancery L Medium Italic. The original font, ITC Zapf Chancery, 
          was designed in 1979 by Hermann Zapf who was inspired by handwritten letterforms of the Italian Renaissance.

          Chorus has been greatly extended. Unlike the rest of the TeX Gyre bundle, there are no Greek glyphs, 
          and there are no small caps. The font is available both in Adobe Type 1 and in OpenType formats, and 
          LaTeX support (for use with a variety of encodings) is provided. Vietnamese characters were added by 
          Han The Thanh.

          TeX Gyre Chorus is distributed as part of the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex-gyre}{TeX Gyre 
          collection} .

          was prepared by Max Miedinger (with Eduard Hoffmann) in 1957 at the Haas type foundry. TeX Gyre Heros 
          may be used as a substitute for Adobe Helvetica in documents.

          and in OpenType formats, and LaTeX support (for use with a variety of encodings) is provided. Vietnamese 
          characters were added by Han The Thanh.

\item[description] (no language specified) This package uses both  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tracklang}{tracklang} and \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texosquery}{texosquery} to 
          look up the locale information from the operating system and provide commands that can access locale-dependent 
          information, such as the currency symbol and decimal separator.

          The file  \texttt{tex-locale.tex} provides generic TeX code. The LaTeX package \texttt{tex-locale.sty} can 
          additionally load \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/babel}{babel} or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/polyglossia}{polyglossia} with 
          the locale’s language setting, as well as various other packages such as \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontspec}{fontspec} (XeLaTeX/LuaLaTeX) 
          or \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/fontenc}{fontenc} + \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/inputenc}{inputenc} (pdfLaTeX).

\index{Package!tex2page}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex2page}
\item[name] \texttt{tex2page}
\item[caption] Produce HTML from TeX/LaTeX
\item[author] Sitaram, Dorai
\index{Author!Sitaram, Dorai}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version]  (2020-01-31)
\item[last changes] 2020-01-31
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) TeX2page makes Web pages from TeX manuscripts. It reads an input document that is marked up in a TeX 
          format (viz, plain TeX, LaTeX, Texinfo), and produces an output document with the functionally equivalent 
          HTML markup. TeX2page uses the same input file syntax, calling conventions, and error-recovery mechanisms 
          as TeX, and thus demands no additional expertise of a user already familiar with TeX. TeX2page runs on 
          modern instances of Scheme (e.g., mzscheme, where it is included as part of the install package on Debian 
          GNU/Linux) and Common Lisp.

          The package does not appear on CTAN.

\section[\texttt{tex4ht} -- Convert (La)TeX to HTML/XML]{\texttt{tex4ht} -- Convert (La)TeX to HTML/XML}\label{pkg:tex4ht}
\index{Package!tex4ht}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/tex4ht}
\item[name] \texttt{TeX4ht}
\item[caption] Convert (La)TeX to HTML/XML
\item[author] The TeX4ht Team
\index{Author!The TeX4ht Team}
\item[author] Gurari, Eitan M.
\index{Author!Gurari, Eitan M.}
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[description] (no language specified) A converter from TeX and LaTeX to SGML-based formats such as (X)HTML, MathML, OpenDocument, and Docbook, 
          providing a configurable (La)TeX-based authoring system for hypertext.

          TeX4ht does not independently parse (La)TeX source (so it avoids the difficulties encountered by many 
          other converters, arising from the irregularity of (La)TeX syntax). Instead, TeX4ht uses (La)TeX itself 
          (with myriad macro modifications) to produce a helper DVI file that it can then process. This technique 
          allows TeX4ht to approach the robustness characteristic of restricted-syntax systems such as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/gellmu}{gellmu} .

          Full releases of TeX4ht are no longer made, both because it is technically difficult to do so and because 
          their utility is questionable. Nevertheless, TeX4ht is actively maintained. So, current source files 
          are held on CTAN, and updated from the development repository frequently. Creating the myriad derived 
          files from them is nontrivial, and generally done with the Makefile in development, from which the TeX4ht 
          package in TeX Live is updated.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{More recent paper including customization}: \url{https://tug.org/TUGboat/tb40-1/tb124hoftich-make4ht.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./4260441963-tb124hoftich-make4ht.pdf|

\item[description] (no language specified) TeX and LaTeX provide few facilities for dates by default, though many packages have filled this gap. 
          This package fills it, as well, with a pure TeX-primitive implementation. It can print dates, advance 
          them by numbers of days, weeks, or months, determine the weekday automatically (with an algorithm cribbed 
          from the  \texttt{dayofweek.tex} file written by Martin Minow), and print them in (mostly) 
          arbitrary format. It can also print calendars (monthly and yearly) automatically, and can be easily localized 
          for non-English languages.

\section[\texttt{texdef} -- Display the definitions of TeX commands]{\texttt{texdef} -- Display the definitions of TeX commands}\label{pkg:texdef}
\index{Package!texdef}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/texdef}
\item[name] \texttt{texdef}
\item[caption] Display the definitions of TeX commands
\item[author] Scharrer, Martin
\index{Author!Scharrer, Martin}
\item[copyright] Martin Scharrer (2011-2025)
\item[license] gpl3 = GNU General Public License, version 3 (free)
\index{License!gpl3}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 3}
\item[version] 1.10 (2025-02-17)
\item[last changes] 2025-02-17
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This (Perl) script displays the definitions of (La)TeX command sequences/macros. Various options allow 
          the selection of the used class as well as package files and other factors that may influence the definition 
          (before/after the preamble, inside an environment, …).

          The script creates a temporary TeX file which is then compiled using (La)TeX to find the ‘ \texttt{{\textbackslash}meaning} ’ 
          of the command sequence. The result is formatted and presented to the user. Length or number command 
          sequences (dimensions, \texttt{{\textbackslash}char…} , count registers, …) are recognized 
          and the contained value is also shown (using \texttt{{\textbackslash}the} ). Special 
          definitions like protected macros are also recognized and the underlying macros are shown as well.

          The script will show plain TeX definitions by default. LaTeX and ConTeXt are supported, including flavours 
          (pdf(La)TeX, Lua(La)TeX, Xe(La)TeX, …). The flavour can be selected using a command line option, or via 
          the script name:  \texttt{latexdef} will use LaTeX as default, etc.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/texdef/texdef.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./4322014290-texdef.pdf|

          it uses are based on the texmf/doc subtrees of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/tetex}{teTeX} , 
          but database files for local configurations with modified/extended directories can be derived from them. 
          Note that texdoctk is not a viewer itself, but an interface for finding documentation files and opening 
          them with the appropriate viewer; so it relies on appropriate programs to be installed on the system. 
          However, the choice of these programs can be configured by the sysadmin or user.

          Now only distributed as part of  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texlive}{TeX Live} , which 
          includes a Windows executable.

          self-contained units. Using a combination of TeX’s grouping mechanism and the gsave/grestore mechanism

\section[\texttt{texgit} -- Download, access, and potentially execute files from git]{\texttt{texgit} -- Download, access, and potentially execute files from git}\label{pkg:texgit}
\index{Package!texgit}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/texgit}
\item[name] \texttt{texgit}
\item[caption] Download, access, and potentially execute files from git
\item[author] Weise, Thomas
\index{Author!Weise, Thomas}
\item[copyright] Thomas Weise (2023-2025)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 0.9.6 (2025-06-20)
\item[last changes] 2025-06-20
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package allows you to do the following things:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item download files from a  \texttt{git} repository and access them from LaTeX,
          \item apply some post-processor to the downloaded files (e.g., strip comments and type hints from Python code) and access the post-processed files instead,
          \item execute scripts or programs — either locally or downloaded from  \texttt{git} repositories — and fetch their output into local files accessible from LaTeX,
          \item create local paths accessible from LaTeX which can be passed as arguments to the scripts or programs that are executed, e.g., as argument to a Python script that creates and stores a ''matplotlib'' plot under the path that it received as argument, allowing you to programmatically create figures and include them in LaTeX documents.
          \end{itemize}
The package works a bit like  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/bibtex}{BibTeX} : Let’s say your document is named \texttt{document.tex} . During the first \texttt{pdflatex} run, executed as \verb|pdflatex document| , all the requests mentioned above, say, to download files from \texttt{git} repositories, are stored in the \texttt{aux} file. The paths corresponding to the requests point to an empty file at this stage. Then you would apply the \texttt{texgit} post-processor by calling \verb|python3 -m texgit.run document| . \href{https://pypi.org/project/texgit}{This Python program} executes all the requests and caches their results locally. During the second run of \verb|pdflatex document| , the paths corresponding to the requests then point to the actual downloaded or generated files. All downloaded or generated files will be locally cached in a folder named \texttt{\_\_git\_\_} in your document’s directory. You can delete this folder to refresh the files.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/texgit/README.md}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/texgit/texgit-doc.pdf}
\item[-- local file] \verb|./7026600620-texgit-doc.pdf|
\item[contact] \textit{bugs}: \url{https://github.com/thomasWeise/texgit_tex/issues}
\index{Contact!bugs}
\item[contact] \textit{repository}: \url{https://github.com/thomasWeise/texgit_tex}
\index{Contact!repository}
\item[on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/texgit}

\index{Topic!data-import}

          system architectures, including GNU/Linux and MacOS, and for Windows. The  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/mactex}{MacTeX} distribution 
          is an unchanged TeX Live plus some Mac-specific software, but is distributed in a separate archive.

          The TeX, PDF(e)TeX, XeTeX, LuaTeX, and other engines are provided in the distribution, with several different

\section[\texttt{texlive-dummy-opensuse} -- Dummy TeX Live RPM for use with Open SUSE]{\texttt{texlive-dummy-opensuse} -- Dummy TeX Live RPM for use with Open SUSE}\label{pkg:texlive-dummy-opensuse}
\index{Package!texlive-dummy-opensuse}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/texlive-dummy-opensuse}
\item[name] \texttt{texlive-dummy-opensuse}
\item[caption] Dummy TeX Live RPM for use with Open SUSE
\item[author] Niepraschk, Rolf
\index{Author!Niepraschk, Rolf}
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 2024.9999-2 (2024-11-14)
\item[last changes] 2024-11-14
\item[year] 2024
\index{Year!2024}
\item[description] (no language specified) The package solves a problem relating to use of TeX Live under a Linux distribution: Linux distributions 
          typically require LaTeX by default, but only distribute a rather out-of-date version. So, by default, 
          the user who wants to use current TeX Live has to undertake ''dirty tricks'' to override the default 
          Linux TeX.

          The solution is to declare that LaTeX is already installed; a later installation of TeX Live will therefore 
          have no problem running on the system. The present package solves the problem for openSUSE Linux distributions.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Readme}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/texlive/texlive-dummy/openSUSE/README.md}

\section[\texttt{texlogsieve} -- Filter and summarize LaTeX log files]{\texttt{texlogsieve} -- Filter and summarize LaTeX log files}\label{pkg:texlogsieve}
\index{Package!texlogsieve}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/texlogsieve}
\item[name] \texttt{texlogsieve}
\item[caption] Filter and summarize LaTeX log files
\item[author] Lago, Nelson
\index{Author!Lago, Nelson}
\item[copyright] Nelson Lago (2021-2025)
\item[license] gpl3+ = GNU General Public License, version 3 or newer (free)
\index{License!gpl3+}
\index{License!GNU General Public License, version 3 or newer}
\item[version] 1.6.0 (2025-03-11)
\item[last changes] 2025-03-11
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) texlogsieve reads a LaTeX log file (or the standard input if no file is specified), filters out less 
          relevant messages, and displays a summary report. It is a texlua script, similar in spirit to tools such 
          as  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texfot}{texfot} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texloganalyser}{texloganalyser} , \href{https://gitlab.com/latex-rubber/rubber}{rubber-info} , \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/texlog-extract}{textlog-extract} , \href{https://github.com/reitzig/texlogparser}{texlogparser} , \href{https://gricad-gitlab.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/labbeju/latex-packages}{texlogfilter} , \href{http://github.com/dmwit/pulp}{pulp} , 
          and others. Highlights:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Two reports: the most important messages from the log file followed by a summary of repeated messages, undefined references etc.;
          \item The program goes to great lengths to correctly handle TeX line wrapping and does a much better job at that than existing tools;
          \item Multiline messages are treated as a single entity;
          \item Several options to control which messages should be filtered out;
          \item No messages are accidentally removed;
          \item The summary report is currently simple, but useful.
          \end{itemize}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/texlogsieve/texlogsieve.pdf}

\section[\texttt{texmacs} -- Structured text editor for TeX]{\texttt{texmacs} -- Structured text editor for TeX}\label{pkg:texmacs}
\index{Package!texmacs}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/texmacs}
\item[name] \texttt{TeXmacs}
\item[caption] Structured text editor for TeX
\item[author] van der Hoeven, Joris
\index{Author!van der Hoeven, Joris}
\item[license] gpl = GNU General Public License (free)
\index{License!gpl}
\index{License!GNU General Public License}
\item[version] 1.0.7.20
\item[description] (no language specified) TeXmacs is a ''structured text editor'' with special support for mathematical expressions. The typesetting 
          quality of the produced documents is intended to be as high as possible, i.e., comparable to the quality 
          of documents produced with TeX; The user interface aims to be as natural and powerful as possible. In 
          particular, the text you see on the screen corresponds exactly to what you get after printing. TeXmacs 
          comes with a typed lisp extension language. Like emacs, this allows you for instance to redefine keyboard 
          and menu actions. TeXmacs can also be used as an interface for computer algebra systems. In particular, 
          automatically generated mathematical formulas are typeset in a satisfactory way. It is possible to generate 
          LaTeX and PostScript output from TeXmacs. After compilation, the LaTeX output will resemble the PostScript 
          output, although we guarantee no complete compatibility between TeXmacs and TeX. It is also possible 
          to import ''well written'' LaTeX documents. The present release includes an interface with Ghostscript, 
          which enables you to include PostScript (and some other formats) of images.

\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 2
\item[description] (no language specified) TeXmate formats chess games from very simple ascii input. The clean '' \texttt{1. e4 e5; 2. Nf3 
          Nc6; 3. Bb5 a6} '' will produce the same results as the sloppier '' \texttt{1 e4 e5; Nf3 
          Nc6 3.. Bb5 a6} ''. The resulting format is fully customizable.

          There are 4 levels of commentary: 1 is the main game, 2-3 are commentaries. Each has its fonts, punctuation 
          marks, etc., and these are also customizable. The package includes a tool for the creation of diagrams.

          The package works in conjunction with  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/skak}{skak} to produce 
          diagrams of the current position automatically. For chess fonts, the package uses the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/chessfss}{chessfss} system.

\section[\texttt{texnegar} -- Kashida justification in XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX]{\texttt{texnegar} -- Kashida justification in XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX}\label{pkg:texnegar}
\index{Package!texnegar}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/texnegar}
\item[name] \texttt{texnegar}
\item[caption] Kashida justification in XeLaTeX and LuaLaTeX
\item[author] Movahhedian, Hossein
\index{Author!Movahhedian, Hossein}
\item[copyright] Hossein Movahhedian (2020-2021)
\item[license] lppl1.3c = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3c}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3c}
\item[version] 0.1e (2021-02-09)
\item[last changes] 2021-02-09
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) In some cursive scripts such as Persian or Arabic, kashida is used to create justification. In this type 
          of justification characters are elongated rather than expanding spaces between words.

          The kashida justification in  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xepersian}{xepersian} has many 
          bugs. Also it has problems with some fonts. The \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xepersian-hm}{xepersian-hm} package 
          was the first attempt to fix these bugs in \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xepersian}{xepersian} , 
          which uses the \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/xetex}{XeTeX} engine.

          This package extends the kashida justification to be used with the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/luatex}{LuaTeX} engine, 
          too.

          Explanation of the package name: \\ \emph{Negar} , in Persian, is the present stem of \emph{negaashtan} meaning 
          to design, to paint, to write; and as a noun it means ''sweetheart, idol, beloved, figuratively referring 
          to a beautiful woman, pattern, painting, and artistic design''.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{User documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/unicodetex/latex/texnegar/texnegar-doc.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) TeXnicCenter is an integrated development environment (IDE) for developing LaTeX documents on MS Windows 
          (Windows 9x/ME, NT/2000/XP/Vista/7). Features include:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item Project orientated integrated development environment for LaTeX documents;
          \item Definition of unlimited ‘output types’ (i.e. DVI, PostScript, PDF);
          \item Fully customizable editor;
          \item Structure View that shows the structure of the whole LaTeX document, even if it is split into several files using  \texttt{{\textbackslash}input} or \texttt{{\textbackslash}include} ;
          \item Simple insertion of LaTeX constructs by menu or toolbar;
          \item Compilation of the project in the IDE: simple jumping to errors, warnings and bad boxes;
          \item Support for document templates;
          \item Fully customizable menu and toolbars in modern look and feel;
          \item Support for English and German languages.
          \end{itemize}

\section[\texttt{texosquery} -- Cross-platform Java application to query OS information]{\texttt{texosquery} -- Cross-platform Java application to query OS information}\label{pkg:texosquery}
\index{Package!texosquery}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/texosquery}
\item[name] \texttt{texosquery}
\item[caption] Cross-platform Java application to query OS information
\item[author] Talbot, Nicola
\index{Author!Talbot, Nicola}
\item[copyright] Nicola Talbot (2016-2020)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.7 (2020-02-04)
\item[last changes] 2020-02-04
\item[year] 2020
\index{Year!2020}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides a cross-platform Java application to query OS information designed for use in TeX’s 
          shell escape mechanism.

          The application can query the following:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item locale and codeset
          \item current working directory
          \item user home directory
          \item temporary directory
          \item OS name, arch and version
          \item Current date and time in PDF format (for TeX formats that don’t provide  \texttt{{\textbackslash}pdfcreationdate} )
          \item Date-time stamp of a file in PDF format (for TeX formats that don't provide  \texttt{{\textbackslash}pdffilemoddate} )
          \item Size of a file in bytes (for TeX formats that don’t provide  \texttt{{\textbackslash}pdffilesize} )
          \item Contents of a directory (captured as a list)
          \item Directory contents filtered by regular expression (captured as a list)
          \item URI of a file
          \item Canonical path of a file
          \end{itemize}
All paths use a forward slash as directory divider so results can be used, for example, in commands like 
          \texttt{{\textbackslash}includegraphics} .

          There are files provided for easy access in TeX documents:

          \begin{itemize}
          \item  \texttt{texosquery.tex} : generic TeX code
          \item  \texttt{texosquery.sty} : LaTeX package
          \end{itemize}
This provides commands to run  \texttt{texosquery} using TeX’s shell escape mechanism and 
          capture the result in a control sequence. The category code of most of TeX’s default special characters 
          (and some other potentially problematic characters) is temporarily changed to 12 while reading the result.
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/support/texosquery/texosquery.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) Texpack is a little bundle of scripts to create documented LaTeX style, class files and docs. Texpack 
          provides useful scripts for the automated creation of the skeleton required by  \texttt{*.dtx} documented 
          TeX files. It is useful both for creating packages ( \texttt{*.sty} ) and new classes ( \texttt{*.cls} ). 
          Texpack also provides a command to automate the creation of commonly needed LaTeX skeleton files. This 
          feature is mostly useful for the Italian author, but also provides the fast creation of a conditional 
          preamble for handling \texttt{dvi} / \texttt{pdf} compilation.

          Offering TeX Courses and Relevant Resources in Chongqing University''.

          This proposal could be helpful if one is considering to suggest his/her university or company to use 
          TeX (or LaTeX, or XeLaTeX) as a typesetting system, especially for Chinese universities and companies.

          The present proposal mainly explains the importance and necessity of introducing TeX, a typesetting system 
          often used in academic writing, to students and teachers.

          This proposal starts from a brief introduction of TeX, then steps further into its fascinating application 
          to academic writing and dissertation formatting. Finally, a set of possible implementation strategies 
          with regard to the proper introduction of TeX and relevant resources to our university, is proposed.

          \begin{itemize}
          \item virtual environment: all TeX packages are installed to  \texttt{.lux/5.3/XXXXX-package\_name@version/} , like nodejs's \texttt{node\_modules/} and python's \texttt{.venv/} . After development of PDF, you can delete it safely, and it will not affect your next development of PDF.
          \item minimal: we only install required packages
          \item package version control: when you declare  \texttt{latex-base == "2025.06.01-1"} , it will install exactly \href{https://luarocks.org/modules/freed-wu/latex-base/2025.06.01-1}{latex-base} and no other versions! Pin the version like nodejs's \texttt{package.json} and python's \texttt{requirements.txt} 
          \item package installation in parallel: install many packages at the same time
          \item a server to host compiled TeX packages:  \href{https://ustctug.github.io/texrocks}{TeXRocks} 
          \item use lua to develop TeX packages:  \href{https://luarocks.org/m/texmf}{texmf} 
          \end{itemize}
We also provide some related TeX tools, like  \href{https://texrocks.readthedocs.io/en/latest/topics/kpathsea.md.html}{kpsewhich} and \href{https://texrocks.readthedocs.io/en/latest/modules/texdef.html}{texdef} written 
          in lua. See official website \href{https://texrocks.readthedocs.io/}{TeXRocks}
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{TeXRocks, a minimal (La)TeX distribution}: \url{https://texrocks.readthedocs.io/en/latest/}

\item[description] (no language specified) TeXsis is a TeX macro package which provides useful features for typesetting research papers and related 
          documents. For example, it includes support specifically for: Automatic numbering of equations, figures, 
          tables and references; Simplified control of type sizes, line spacing, footnotes, running headlines and 
          footlines, and tables of contents, figures and tables; Specialized document formats for research papers, 
          preprints and ''e-prints'', conference proceedings, theses, books, referee reports, letters, and memoranda; 
          Simplified means of constructing an index for a book or thesis; Easy to use double column formatting; 
          Specialized environments for lists, theorems and proofs, centered or non-justified text, and listing 
          computer code; Specialized macros for easily constructing ruled tables. TeXsis was originally developed 
          for physicists, but others may also find it useful. It is completely compatible with Plain TeX.

\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/textcase}
\item[name] \texttt{textcase}
\item[caption] Case conversion ignoring mathematics, etc
\item[author] Carlisle, David
\index{Author!Carlisle, David}
\item[copyright] David Carlisle (1997, 1998, 2019, 2022, 2023, 2025)
\item[license] lppl = The LaTeX Project Public License (free)
\index{License!lppl}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License}
\item[version] 1.05 (2025-02-16)
\item[last changes] 2025-02-16
\item[year] 2025
\index{Year!2025}
\item[description] (no language specified) The textcase package offers commands  \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeTextUppercase} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeTextLowercase} which 
          are similar to the standard \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeUppercase} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeLowercase} , 
          but they do not change the case of any sections of mathematics, or the arguments of \texttt{{\textbackslash}cite} , \texttt{{\textbackslash}label} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}ref} commands 
          within the argument. A further command \texttt{{\textbackslash}NoCaseChange} does nothing 
          but suppress case change within its argument, so to force uppercase of a section including an environment, 
          one might say:

          \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeTextUppercase{\textbraceleft}...{\textbackslash}NoCaseChange{\textbraceleft}{\textbackslash}begin{\textbraceleft}foo{\textbraceright}{\textbraceright} 
          ...{\textbackslash}NoCaseChange{\textbraceleft}{\textbackslash}end{\textbraceleft}foo{\textbraceright}{\textbraceright}...{\textbraceright}} 

          In current LaTeX this package is obsolete. You can use the standard  \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeUppercase} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeLowercase} , 
          but it defines legacy names \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeTextUppercase} and \texttt{{\textbackslash}MakeTextLowercase} .
\item[documentation]  (no language specified) \textit{Package documentation}: \url{https://ctan.org/tex-archive/macros/latex/contrib/textcase/textcase.pdf}

\item[description] (no language specified) This package provides the TheanoDidot font designed by Alexey Kryukov, in both TrueType and Type1 formats, 
          with support for both traditional and modern LaTeX processors. An artificially-emboldened variant has 
          been provided but there are no italic variants. The package is named after Theano, a famous Ancient Greek 
          woman philosopher, who was first a student of Pythagoras, and supposedly became his wife.

          The Didot family were active as designers for about 100 years in the 18th and 19th centuries. They were 
          printers, publishers, typeface designers, inventors and intellectuals. Around 1800 the Didot family owned 
          the most important print shop and font foundry in France. Pierre Didot, the printer, published a document 
          with the typefaces of his brother, Firmin Didot, the typeface designer. The strong clear forms of this 
          alphabet display objective, rational characteristics and are representative of the time and philosophy 
          of the Enlightenment.

\section[\texttt{thermodynamics} -- Macros for multicomponent thermodynamics documents]{\texttt{thermodynamics} -- Macros for multicomponent thermodynamics documents}\label{pkg:thermodynamics}
\index{Package!thermodynamics}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/thermodynamics}
\item[name] \texttt{thermodynamics}
\item[caption] Macros for multicomponent thermodynamics documents
\item[author] Hammond, Karl D.
\index{Author!Hammond, Karl D.}
\item[copyright] Karl D. Hammond (2022-2024)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 2.04 (2026-03-22)
\item[last changes] 2026-03-22
\item[year] 2026
\index{Year!2026}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package makes typesetting quantities found in thermodynamics texts relatively simple. The commands 
          are flexible and intended to be relatively intuitive. It handles several sets of notation for total, 
          specific, and molar quantities; allows changes between symbols (e.g., A vs. F for Helmholtz free energy); 
          and greatly simplifies the typesetting of symbols and partial derivatives commonly encountered in mixture 
          thermodynamics. Changes of one’s notes from one textbook to another can be achieved relatively easily 
          by changing package options.

          The package offers a collection of macros and environments which are intended to make typesetting thermodynamics 
          documents faster, more convenient, and more reliable. Macros include symbols for extensive, molar, specific, 
          and partial molar properties; excess and residual (departure) properties; partial derivatives; heat capacities, 
          compressibilities, and expansivities; saturation, mixture, and pure-component properties; Henry’s Law 
          parameters and activity coefficients; changes on mixing, fusion, reaction, sublimation, and vaporization; 
          and sets of all moles/mole fractions/masses/etc. being held constant in derivatives. Conversion of notes 
          between textbooks is trivial for textbooks supported by the package, and more general changes in notation 
          are also possible through package options.

\section[\texttt{thorshammer} -- Assessment based on AcroTeX quizzes]{\texttt{thorshammer} -- Assessment based on AcroTeX quizzes}\label{pkg:thorshammer}
\index{Package!thorshammer}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/thorshammer}
\item[name] \texttt{thorshammer}
\item[caption] Assessment based on AcroTeX quizzes
\item[author] Story, Donald P.
\index{Author!Story, Donald P.}
\item[copyright] D. P. Story (2020-2021)
\item[license] lppl1.2 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.2}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.2}
\item[version]  (2021-06-24)
\item[last changes] 2021-06-24
\item[year] 2021
\index{Year!2021}
\item[description] (no language specified) This package implements an idea by Thorsten G. for assessment using PDF quizzes produced by the  \href{https://ctan.org/pkg/exerquiz}{exerquiz} package. 
          Thorsten not only wanted to pose multiple choice, multiple selection, and fill-in type questions, but 
          also wanted to ask extended response questions that would be manually evaluated. Once the quiz is graded, 
          the instructor may optionally pass the quizzes through an Acrobat action sequence to extract the student’s 
          name and grade from the quizzes. The extracted information is saved to a tab-delimited TXT file. The 
          instructor can later merge this file into a larger spreadsheet.

\index{Package!threadcol}

\begin{labeling}{Web page on CTAN}
\item[Web page on CTAN] \url{https://ctan.org/pkg/threadcol}
\item[name] \texttt{threadcol}
\item[caption] Organize document columns into PDF “article thread”
\item[author] Pakin, Scott
\index{Author!Pakin, Scott}
\item[copyright] Scott Pakin (2013)
\item[license] lppl1.3 = The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3 (free)
\index{License!lppl1.3}
\index{License!The LaTeX Project Public License 1.3}
\item[version] 1.0
\item[description] (no language specified) The package combines a document’s columns into a PDF ''article thread''. PDF readers that support this 
          mechanism (probably Adobe Acrobat/Reader only) can be instructed to scroll automatically from column 
          to column, which facilitates on-screen reading of two-column documents.

          Even for single-column documents, threadcol supports the creation of multiple article threads, which 
          help organize discontiguous but logically related regions of text into a form that the user can scroll 
          through as if its contents were contiguous.
